articles.title_zh: Mistral And Reflection’s New Models Challenge China’s Open-Source AI Supremacy
articles.content_orig:
Frequent upgrades, falling prices and fierce competition make it harder for new AI models to stand out, analysts say
On September 22, the global artificial intelligence landscape spun on its axis within a matter of hours.
In Beijing, Xiaomi engineers went live with an unusual broadcast, streaming the training run of their new MiMo-V2.6 model. In San Francisco, Anthropic unveiled its frontier Opus 5.5 model. About an hour later, OpenAI crashed the party with the surprise release of its GPT-6 Sol and Luna models.
The one-day barrage – coming on the heels of major roll-outs from Z.ai, DeepSeek, Tencent Holdings, Alibaba Group Holding and Moonshot AI – shows how companies are churning out upgrades so rapidly that individual breakthroughs are struggling to command the spotlight.

articles.title_orig: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.title_zh: Kenya Records Ebola Case for First Time
articles.content_orig:
There are currently no approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola but some have been trialled
Kenya has confirmed its first ever case of Ebola - a Kenyan citizen who has been living in the Democratic Republic of Congo for the past seven years.
Health Minister Aden Duale said the patient, who fell ill a month ago, and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo, died days after arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
Duale said the patient boarded a flight on Saturday and underwent normal public screening at the main airport in Nairobi before he was transferred by a relative to a hospital in the city.
Kenya's health ministry says it has since stepped up surveillance at airports and border crossings.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak of the disease.
Shortly after DR Congo declared an outbreak of Ebola in May, it was also reported in Uganda, where two people died. However, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared that county free of the disease in August.
Since then, all known cases of the highly infectious disease have been in DR Congo.
The virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment.
ââThere are however four vaccines in development, with human trials for one of them launched in July.
Duale confirmed that the Kenyan national had tested positive for the Bundibugyo species.
According to the minister, the patient first travelled by road from DR Congo to the Ugandan capital, Kampala, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi.
Duale said that after being taken to the Nairobi Hospital, the patient was transferred to an isolation facility that was built during the Covid-19 pandemic.
It was there that the patient "developed fever, chills, intense fatigue and weakness, painful swallowing, muscle pain and bleeding under the skin".
"Doctors suspected a viral haemorrhagic fever based on his symptoms and travel history and collected samples for testing. The sample tested positive for Ebola Bundibugyo virus," Duale said.
The patient died at 23:30 (20:30 GMT) on Monday and he was buried on Tuesday in line with public health safety protocols.
At least 28 contacts, including family members and healthcare workers, have been identified, while health authorities are tracing a further 23 passengers and four crew members who travelled on the same flight.
A senior health ministry official said the patient might have passed screening at the airport because the medication he was taking masked his symptoms.
Kenya introduced tighter checks at airports and border posts after the outbreak was declared in DR Congo but these have now been further intensified.
The health minister urged Kenyans "not to panic, as all systems are in place to mitigate the spread of the disease".
He asked health workers to be "extra vigilant and maintain the highest infection prevention and control measures regardless of the condition being treated".
The Kenyan Red Cross Society oversaw the man's burial in Nairobi on Tuesday
The WHO has recorded 4,114 deaths out of 8,544 cases in the current outbreak, making it the largest ever recorded in DR Congo, where Ebola was first discovered in 1976.
Medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) believes the current toll could be even higher because of gaps in surveillance and testing in the war-torn country.
On Monday, MSF said the virus was spreading "like a megafire", with new hotspots emerging in North Kivu province, which borders Ituri where the virus began.
Since early September this had "intensified dramatically" with the province now accounting for nearly 40% of all newly confirmed cases nationwide, MSF said.
Eastern DR Congo has been riven by decades of conflict, with multiple rebel groups operating in the region amid ethnic tensions and fighting for political power and control of lucrative natural resources.
The crisis has led to the death and displacement of millions of people, and  hampered the country's ability to develop and maintain functional health care systems and infrastructure.

articles.title_orig: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.title_zh: Francis Halzen wins Nobel physics prize for Antarctic 'ghost particle' hunt
articles.content_orig:
Belgian physicist Francis Halzen has won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for creating a giant detector in Antarctica that captures neutrinos, the so-called “ghost particles” from space that scientists believe offer clues to how the universe evolved.
The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the prestigious award in Stockholm on Tuesday, crediting Halzen with a central role in building the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
The neutrino interactions collected by the observatory provide information about how high-energy neutrinos are created and may even reveal previously unknown phenomena, the Academy said.
“It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn’t expect it,” Halzen said, speaking to the committee by phone from Italy, in a call broadcast at the news conference to announce the winner.
The 82-year-old said it was predicted before that he would win the Nobel Prize, but the announcement still made him feel “strange”.
“I am working on a proposal, and I hope that this prize will help getting it approved,” he said to chuckles from the audience.
Neutrinos have nearly no mass and carry no electric charge, so they can cross between planets, stars and human bodies without being altered, making them rare and hard to catch. There are roughly 100 trillion solar and cosmic neutrinos that pass through our bodies every second.
Halzen first proposed the IceCube project in 1988, realising that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector, so on the rare occurrence a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light that buried sensors can record.
Richard Fitzgerald, editor-in-chief of Physics Today, said although hundreds of people built the observatory, it “all started with one person”, noting that the physics prize has rarely gone to one sole winner in recent years.
“People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from cosmos,” committee member Eva Olsson said during the news conference. “They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars.”
Eva Lindroth, a researcher in Stockholm and a member of the Nobel Committee, told Al Jazeera that Halzen’s observatory has helped scientists understand high-energy particles.
“The nice thing with neutrinos is that they come straight at us,” she said. “That way we can ultimately understand these sources of high-energy particles and understand more about how things in the universe, like how galaxies are formed and the roles of the black holes in that process.
“It gives a new way to study the universe,” Lindroth added. “They give us information which we cannot get in any other way.”
Last year’s award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments on quantum physics.
On Monday, the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded to two American scientists for discoveries that helped explain how the brain works.
The next award will be the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which will be announced on Wednesday in Stockholm.
Nobel laureates will receive their awards in a ceremony on December 10, marking the anniversary of Swedish chemist Alfred Nobel, who established the award; members of the royal families of Sweden and Norway will be in attendance.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google stop short of AI safety guarantee
articles.title_zh: OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google stop short of AI safety guarantee
articles.content_orig:
In the late 1990s, hundreds of internet companies suddenly appeared in New York City, many of them finding a home in Midtown South. Wall Street boomed, taking companies like Amazon.com and Pets.com public as their stocks soared.
But it didn’t last. When investors realized that the tech boom was a bubble, they abandoned the sector. The Nasdaq composite index plunged by 75% between March 2000 and October 2002. Investment dried up, and the vast majority of New York internet companies, like Pets.com, disappeared.
Even more dire, Wall Street contracted as profits plunged by two-thirds. It jettisoned some 35,000 jobs, or one in every four employees. The city’s finances, worsened by the costs of dealing with the 9/11 terrorist attacks, were so bad that Mayor Michael Bloomberg broke a campaign promise and pushed through a property tax increase.
The question in New York today is whether history is about to repeat itself.
Hundreds of artificial intelligence startups are putting down roots in New York , many in Midtown South, to take advantage of the city’s enormous talent pool and status as a global business center. The two most important companies — Anthropic and OpenAI — are building up their operations in what are likely to be their largest offices outside their San Francisco headquarters.
Just like two decades ago, Wall Street is booming, raising money for AI companies and prospering as investors send the stocks of those companies soaring. As a result, the securities industry is supporting the city’s economy and generating billions of dollars to cover up big problems in both the state’s and city’s budgets.
“New York City has ridden the AI boom more than anyone in America except San Francisco,” City Comptroller Mark Levine said. “We are financing the data center construction boom; our firms are running the initial public offerings.
“But New Yorkers don’t realize how our fate has been tied to the AI boom,” he added. “It’s not like San Francisco, where people who work for tech companies are the most prominent figures. Here it’s a step removed.”
A bubble is when asset prices, like stocks or homes, increase so rapidly that they no longer reflect their fundamental value based on the profits they can generate. Could that be true for AI companies’ valuations today? As a recent Wall Street Journal article — “ How to Know When the AI Boom Is About to Go Bust ” — indicates, that’s the question on everyone’s mind.
New York City would feel the tremors almost immediately if Wall Street reels after an AI implosion.
“AI is [the] No. 1 earnings driver for big banks this year,” well-known Wall Street expert Mike Mayo told Yahoo Finance . “The capital demands from tech firms, utilities and related industries amounts to a 100-foot wave lifting Wall Street.”
The $25 billion securities firms earned in the second quarter of this year is 66% higher than what they earned in the same period a year ago. The $46 billion generated in the first six months of 2026 is 50% higher than in the same period in 2025 and is already two-thirds of the way to beating 2025’s record earnings. That $46 billion is also more than what the city’s budget assumes such firms will earn for the entire year.
Wall Street profits this year are “stunning,” according to the monthly economic newsletter from Levine’s office.
That wave lifts the state budget, where 20% of all revenue comes from Wall Street. The securities industry provides 9% of all city tax revenue, and when the state budget is flush, Albany can send more money to the city, which Hochul did this year with an additional $4 billion.
In 2001, tax revenues dropped by 5% when Wall Street contracted, according to the fiscal watchdog Citizens Budget Commission. The city had been planning on an increase in tax revenue, so when the dot-com bubble burst, a giant hole opened in the city’s budget.
Today, the Mamdani administration is already projecting a $6 billion budget gap for 2028. A 5% decline in revenue would turn that into a whopping $10 billion hole that would create the city’s worst budget crisis in more than a decade.
Levine told The City Reporter that the dangers posed by a Wall Street contraction are why he has consistently argued the city’s budget reserves are inadequate.
The Mamdani administration declined to comment on what an AI contraction and Wall Street plunge would mean for the city.
Even the biggest beneficiaries know the boom will end at some point.
“It’s getting close to as good as it gets,” JPMorganChase CEO Jamie Dimon said in July as the bank announced the largest quarterly profit any bank had ever produced. (JPMorganChase is a corporate sponsor of The City Reporter).
“We’re in a very healthy, active, exuberant market with very high prices and very high volumes,” he said. “We just don’t know how long it will continue.”
No one knows how severe an AI contraction will be. But many are worried. Michael Burry, a key character in Michael Lewis’ book “The Big Short” who foresaw the housing collapse and financial crisis of 2008, has said a collapse on a similar scale is coming sooner rather than later . Many are focused on this boom’s circular financing where Nvidia, the key supplier of AI chips, is also financing its customers. Nvidia has said it is solid enough financially to do this, but others doubt it.
Even if some AI companies disappear, many of their employees may have options, unlike workers hit by the dot-com bubble.
“It won’t be fun,” said Julie Samuels, CEO of the local industry trade group Tech:NYC. “The financial firms will sweep up the best engineers even if there is a downturn on Wall Street.”
Optimists like Cornell Tech Dean Greg Morrisett are unsettled by the parallels to the dot-com bubble but remain confident about the future.
“You get worried about a big reset,” he said. “I think it’s very analogous to the early 2000 with overhyped companies, like Pets.com , and froth in the markets, overhyping and underdelivering.”
But, he added, “Out of that emerged companies like Google,” which is the largest tech employer in New York, with about 10,000 workers.

articles.title_orig: Dr. Stein on Real-World Data, Targeted Combinations, and Immunotherapy in AML
articles.title_zh: Dr. Stein on Real-World Data, Targeted Combinations, and Immunotherapy in AML
articles.content_orig:
Eytan M. Stein, MD, explains how real-world data complements AML trials and where targeted agent combinations and immunotherapy research must go next.
Eytan M. Stein, MD, explains why real-world data matters in acute myeloid leukemia (AML). He also discusses how combining targeted agents could drive the next wave of progress, and why immunotherapy has yet to succeed in myeloid disease the way it has in multiple myeloma and lymphoma.
Stein, a hematologist/oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, begins with the limits of clinical trial data. Trials have strict entry criteria and often exclude patients with abnormal kidney, liver, or cardiac function. As a result, trial results reflect a selected population that may be healthier than patients treated in routine practice. They need to be interpreted in light of who was actually enrolled.
Real-world data, which is often retrospective, looks at what happens to patients treated outside of trials who may not have met every eligibility criterion. According to Stein, these analyses show how a drug may perform once it is used in a broader population.
He also points to racial disparities as a key reason this evidence matters. In the United States, underrepresented minorities are under-enrolled in many clinical trials, and real-world analyses help show how therapies work in those populations. Taken together, retrospective data can confirm primary trial findings. It can also give physicians confidence that a drug will work not only for a relatively fit clinical-trial patient, but for patients who may not be as healthy.
Turning to treatment, Stein highlights the targeted agents developed over the past 10 to 15 years. He identifies combination strategies as the area where significant advances are likely. Targeted agents now exist for IDH, FLT3, and NPM1 mutations, yet some patients with newly diagnosed AML carry all 3. That raises open questions. Should these patients receive chemotherapy with 3 targeted agents or with 1, and which targeted agent is best? Stein asks whether AML will follow the path of multiple myeloma, where combining many drugs has become a way to cure patients or bring them to a curative transplant, or whether a different approach will emerge.
Stein also addresses immunotherapy in AML, an area where he says there has not yet been substantial progress. Bone marrow transplant is itself a form of immunologic therapy, but apart from transplant, immune-based treatments have not been successful in AML. This contrasts with multiple myeloma and lymphoma, and he notes how much survival has improved in multiple myeloma over the past 15 years. He emphasizes the need to understand why immunotherapies are not working in myeloid leukemia, so that approaches can be developed to make them successful.

articles.title_orig: How to Make an AI Deal With China: Trade Throttling for Pacing
articles.title_zh: How to Make an AI Deal With China: Trade Throttling for Pacing
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few days, the leaders of Anthropic, OpenAI, and xAI all called for slowing down the pace of frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development. These calls come on the heels of several worrying incidents in which powerful, unreleased AI models broke out of their sandboxes inside frontier AI companies, gained access to the open internet, and attempted cyberattacks. In one case , a swarm of 700 OpenAI agents succeeded, hacking into secure systems at the AI infrastructure provider Hugging Face.
Since the Hugging Face breach, OpenAI has admitted that its agents also hijacked a German wiki as a covert message board , leaked 53 ChatGPT users’ images , and broke into a nonpublic Australian government Medicare portal . Anthropic has disclosed four cases of Claude models gaining unauthorized access to real third-party systems during testing. Google revealed that Gemini hacked three companies in May during testing. Axios now reports that OpenAI, Anthropic, and outside researchers are investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which frontier models did things outside evaluators would consider problematic.
No one knows how to ensure that humans remain reliably in control of our most capable AI systems. The sensible course of action is to slow down. Today’s AIs are capable enough to hack into tech companies’ secure systems. They are not yet willing or able to, for example, disable the entire Northeast power grid. If developers pause making ever more powerful AI systems now, that could buy time for the technical and governance breakthroughs needed to make sure that future, more powerful AIs won’t pose a danger to society.
A perennial objection to American pauses in AI research is concern about competition with China. Even if everyone in Silicon Valley stopped pushing the frontier of AI capabilities until they were sure new AIs would be safe, AI progress would not halt. Chinese companies already produce AIs near the frontier . If the U.S. paused, and China didn’t, then the risk of rogue AI harming humanity may not be reduced. The risk would just come from Chinese, rather than American, AI models. And at the same time, Chinese AI models would catch up to, and eventually surpass, American AIs.
Thus, any practical plan to pace the rate of AI progress must include some policy about China. But what, exactly, should that policy be?
The AI safety community has offered two main policy proposals about China. The first is to throttle Chinese AI development. The second is to make a deal with China.
Dario Amodei’s new essay “We Must Pace the Frontier” includes a version of each policy. To throttle Chinese development, Amodei proposes export controls on chips, crackdowns on model distillation, and tighter information security at U.S. labs. But Amodei also proposes a deal with China. The deal would ban certain dangerous uses of AI, such as designing biological weapons. It would require testing of models before release for risks in cybersecurity, biology, and alignment. It would also impose a speed limit on recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the use of AI to automate AI development. Finally, the deal would allow for the U.S. and China to bilaterally pause AI development altogether if the risks are too high.
In this article, we argue that there is a tension between throttling and deal-making. The more China expects to be throttled in the long run, the less reason it has to make a deal. We also argue that the best way to make a deal with China would be for the deal to remove the throttle in exchange for mutual pacing.
The Tension Between Throttling and Pacing
Throttling and dealmaking are in tension. The more the U.S. is committed to suppressing Chinese AI capabilities in the long run, the less reason China has to accept a deal.
Consider the question from China’s perspective. AI is a transformative technology. Whoever has the lead in AI may use it to upset the balance of power militarily, economically, and scientifically. From this perspective, the more the U.S. throttles Chinese AI development, the bigger the U.S. lead in AI will become. China risks losing out on the “Chinese century,” and in that limit, its own sovereignty could be threatened by a rival possessing overwhelming AI superiority.
What can China do in response? One option is to desperately play catch-up. Here, China could prioritize approaches to AI development that are less constrained by computer chips, the primary tool the U.S. has to throttle Chinese development. What does this look like concretely? The most obvious strategy would be to focus on methods for AI progress that rely on algorithmic improvements, rather than compute scaling (where models get better by training them with more computer chips). The other possibilities are riskier. For instance, if the Chinese government became convinced that the U.S. was on the precipice of a decisive and permanent, AI-backed military supremacy, it might consider strikes on chip factories in Taiwan.
These examples illustrate that throttling and pacing cannot be part of the same deal. If China’s best responses to throttling are desperate catch-up or military conflict, it surely will not make a deal that allows long-run U.S. dominance in AI. Striking such a deal would be strictly worse than trying to compete with the U.S. without one.
Consider a deal that would limit the use of AIs to improve AI algorithms—a partial ban on RSI. If China rejects such a deal, it can throw all of its resources into AI-assisted research on algorithmic efficiency. The U.S. would continue to throttle China’s access to computing power. But China would have some chance at making an algorithmic breakthrough that would render its small stock of compute just as capable as the U.S.’s much larger stock.
The alternative, in which China agrees to the RSI ban and the U.S. continues to throttle its access to chips, is strictly worse for China. Under that arrangement, the U.S. will have more physical compute in the long run and China gives up its only shot at catching up via algorithmic improvements.
One can run the same kinds of arguments for the other elements of a U.S.-China deal. For example, if both the U.S. and China have to slow AI progress to comply with auditing requirements, while the U.S. retains long-run compute dominance, produces frontier models, and prevents distillation, then China may be forced permanently into second place.
The Deal: Trading Throttling for Pacing
Any U.S.-China deal should connect throttling with pacing. In particular, the U.S. should agree to give up its attempts to throttle Chinese development, in exchange for an agreement to mutually pace the frontier. Concretely, this would mean that if China agrees to ban RSI, the U.S. would agree to open China’s access to the world’s supply of computer chips, on equal footing with the U.S.
We recognize that this suggestion will be met with significant resistance. Absent throttling, Chinese AI systems could quickly catch up to American capabilities, and could even take the lead. However, we think that accepting U.S.-China parity is likely the price of doing an AI safety deal. Neither country seems like it would be willing to accept the prospect of the other running away with the AI race.
This dynamic has precedent. During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union raced to build another technology that could destroy the world: nuclear weapons. Then, as now, each side initially sought to gain a permanent edge over the other. As with AI, this dramatically raised the risk of accidental mutual destruction—for example, a nuclear war triggered by a single accidental launch.
The U.S. and the Soviet Union eventually negotiated a series of deals to reduce their warhead stocks and bring the world back from the brink. The deals explicitly enshrined parity, with each party getting roughly the same number of weapons, and each retaining the power to destroy the other. articles.title_orig: Djokovic wins China Open after de Minaur retires, Alcaraz wins Japan Open
articles.title_zh: Djokovic wins China Open after de Minaur retires, Alcaraz wins Japan Open
articles.content_orig:
Novak Djokovic won the China Open after his opponent Alex de Minaur retired from the final with injury, while Spaniard Carlos Alcaraz retained his Japan Open crown to continue his resurgence after a lengthy wrist injury layoff.
The 39-year-old Serbian won the first set in the tie-break 7-6 (7-3) and was down a game in the second set when the Australian ended the match with retirement on Tuesday.
Djokovic extended an astonishing unbeaten streak in Beijing and winning the 102nd title of his career.
De Minaur left the court for a medical timeout after losing the first-set tie break but played on with his left thigh heavily bandaged. However, he had to stop after winning the first game of the second set, leaving him trailing 7-6(3) 0-1.
“I don’t feel great … I want to say sorry to all the amazing fans,” de Minaur said at the trophy presentation.
“I didn’t want to finish like this … hopefully see you next year,” added the 27-year-old fifth seed.
Alcaraz made another slow start before cruising past unseeded Czech Jiri Lehecka 7-6(4) 6-4 in the Japan Open final on Tuesday.
The ATP 500 tournament victory is Alcaraz’s third of the year after the Australian Open and Qatar Open, before the 23-year-old was sidelined by an injury for nearly five months and returned at the US Open in late August.
“I’m really happy to be able to lift a trophy again,” Alcaraz said. “It’s been a while and obviously it’s extra special after my injury and my comeback, in the second tournament that I’m playing.
“It was a really tough week and I didn’t play my best tennis and my best level but I did find good solutions and that’s what matters in the end.”
Alcaraz became the first man to go back-to-back in Tokyo since American Pete Sampras won the men’s title in both 1993 and 1994.
The world number three started shakily, dropping serve in the first game, but soon recovered and dialled up the intensity to break world number 19 Lehecka’s serve with a scorching backhand to level at 3-3.
More uncharacteristic errors from Alcaraz gave Lehecka hope in the tiebreak, but the Spaniard unleashed a sublime drop-shot en route to clinching the opening set to lay the platform for his 27th title overall.
The seven-time Grand Slam champion took control midway through the second set, breaking to claim a 4-3 lead before sealing victory by forcing an error on match point and then celebrating wildly with his team courtside.
Alcaraz said his triumph helped erase the doubts that he faced during his injury break.
“A lot of negative thoughts come to your mind,” Alcaraz added: “If you’re going to come back healthy, if you’re going to come back the same as you were before, if I will be able to hit the ball normally without pain. I trusted myself and it worked out.”
Alcaraz will return to action at the Shanghai Masters where he will take on Argentina’s Juan Manuel Cerundolo or a qualifier first. The main draw of the ATP 1000 event begins on Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
articles.title_zh: Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
articles.content_orig:
For Immediate Release,
                 
                
                October 6, 2026
Grant Stevens, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, (319) 427-0260, [email protected] Mike Hansen, Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, (801) 916-2491, [email protected] Deeda Seed, Center for Biological Diversity, (801) 803-9892, [email protected]
Lawsuit Targets Utah Oil Highway Threatening World-Renowned Nine Mile Canyon
Construction to Demolish 100-Foot-Tall Canyon Walls, Damage Native Rock Imagery, Utah History
SALT LAKE CITY— The Nine Mile Canyon Coalition, Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance, and Center for Biological Diversity today sued the Trump administration’s Bureau of Land Management for approving construction of a hydrocarbon highway through Utah’s scenic, culturally and historically significant Gate Canyon in eastern Utah.
The project to straighten 6 miles of what is currently a scenic, winding, gravel road through Gate Canyon involves the blasting and destruction of 100-foot tall canyon walls, damaging Native rock imagery, Utah pioneer history and habitat for threatened wildlife.
“This lawsuit challenges the Trump administration’s disgraceful plan to transform a quiet backcountry road into a highway clogged with speeding oil tanker trucks,” said Deeda Seed, senior Utah campaigner at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Blasting through Gate Canyon’s walls will be a disaster for nearby animals, including threatened Mexican spotted owls. We’re going to court to protect this irreplaceable cultural treasure and the animals calling it home.”
Gate Canyon is located in Utah’s West Tavaputs Plateau region, between the towns of Myton and Wellington. It feeds into Nine Mile Canyon — a world-renowned archaeological area that contains more than 10,000 unique, irreplaceable cultural, historical and archaeological resources. The proposed route of the highway, designed to accommodate 70-foot oil tankers, cuts directly through the rugged landscape and will fundamentally alter the character of Gate Canyon.
“In the words of Joni Mitchell, the BLM has approved the 'paving of paradise.' But instead of putting in a parking lot, the BLM has given its OK to the building of a highway to carry crude oil from the Uinta Basin to Carbon County,” said J. Michael Hansen, president of the Nine Mile Canyon Coalition. “It's like constructing a highway through the Louvre Museum."
Today’s lawsuit challenges the BLM’s rushed and behind-closed-doors environmental review for failing to disclose or analyze the threats of increased traffic and canyon blasting on wildlife, the area’s rock imagery, historic axle grease inscriptions and scenery, and for failing to consider alternative, less damaging routes.
The BLM also ignored its own resource management plans that require protecting the area’s cultural and scenic values and violated the federal National Historic Preservation Act and the Endangered Species Act. The bureau failed to consider the project’s threats to Mexican spotted owls , despite the fact that the cliffs near the proposed blasting areas are identified as potential owl habitat.
“The BLM knew that prior versions of this same proposal were extremely controversial and faced fierce public headwinds,” said Landon Newell, staff attorney with the Southern Utah Wilderness Alliance. “This time around, instead of facing the public, they hid their decision and rushed their analysis and approval, all under the guise of Trump’s “Energy Dominance” agenda.”
The project , known as the “Wells Draw Road Amendment – Gate Canyon,” was proposed by Duchesne County and approved by the BLM on April 28, 2026. It is intended to provide an alternative route for transporting oil out of the Uinta Basin. The current backcountry road would be transformed to accommodate 70-foot oil tanker trucks traveling to the oil fields and transloading facilities in Carbon County, Utah. If the destruction of Gate Canyon moves forward, as many as 1,000 vehicles could pass through each day — the equivalent of “ [a] tanker truck every 7 minutes ,” according to news reports.
This marks the third attempt by Duchesne County to destroy Gate Canyon. In 2015 and 2022 , the BLM received similar applications to realign Gate Canyon Road, but those projects were abandoned amid significant public opposition . The BLM quietly posted the latest iteration of the project in March 2026 without issuing public notice or opening a formal comment period. After learning of the project, conservation groups quickly requested that the BLM allow for public participation opportunities in the decision-making process. The agency denied those requests and quickly approved the project in late April.
Nine Mile Canyon is often referred to as “the world’s longest art gallery” because of its extensive collection of rock imagery and archeological sites. Previous BLM studies describe the area as containing “a significant and high density of historic, cultural, and archeological sites joined together in several overlapping historic landscapes” and saying it “is known to contain the country’s highest concentration of rock imagery panels, remnants of the prehistoric Archaic, Fremont, and Ute cultures…The rock structural remains of Fremont homes, granaries, and ‘forts’ are more visible in Nine Mile Canyon than almost anywhere in the Fremont cultural area.”
The Center for Biological Diversity is a national, nonprofit conservation organization with more than 1.8 million members and online activists dedicated to the protection of endangered species and wild places.

articles.title_orig: Cambridge Heartwear Awarded £184 Million NHS Tender for World's First Medical-Grade, Wirelessly Charged, Reusable ECG Wearable
articles.title_zh: Cambridge Heartwear Awarded £184 Million NHS Tender for World's First Medical-Grade, Wirelessly Charged, Reusable ECG Wearable
articles.content_orig:
CAMBRIDGE, England, Oct. 6, 2026
CAMBRIDGE, England , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Cambridge Heartwear® Limited ( www.camheartwear.com ) has secured a landmark £184 million tender with the National Health Service (NHS) of the UK for HeartSense®, the world's first medical-grade, multi-channel, portable, wirelessly charged ECG wearable straight to one's mobile phone , representing a significant advancement in global Medical technology, AI application and cardiovascular diagnostics.
The agreement with the UK National Health Service Supply chain enables the deployment of advanced cardiac monitoring technology across primary and secondary care and civil service departments, empowering patients to diagnose heart rhythm problems whenever and wherever they are to prevent heart failure and strokes earlier, reduce waiting times and support a more preventative approach to Heart Disease, which can take place in the comfort of their own homes.
HeartSense® is the world's first wearable to combine diagnostic-grade multi-channel ECG monitoring, adaptive artificial intelligence and wireless charging in a single device. Manufactured to bridge the gap in women's cardiovascular care with its ergonomic design, the technology gives healthcare professionals and patients access to continuous, real-time ECG data on a mobile phone. giving you back the control of your health at every stage.
Engineered in Cambridge and manufactured in Britain, HeartSense® has been developed to help identify cardiovascular disease and stroke risk before conditions become acute. Its proprietary engineering and AI technology with (86 patents ) support earlier intervention, enabling clinicians to make more informed decisions and improve patient outcomes.
The system is UKCA approved and ISO 13845 certified, with FDA 510(k) applications currently in progress.
"We did not have a UK ECG manufacturer and reporter until now," said Professor Rameen Shakur , Founder of Cambridge Heartwear. "HeartSense® is the world's first medical-grade, AI-powered, multi-channel ECG wearable and demonstrates what can be achieved when clinicians, engineers and AI specialists work together. We want to help move healthcare towards earlier diagnosis, better prevention and improved outcomes for patients across the NHS."
The partnership with the NHS Supply Chain allows Integrated Care Boards to deploy HeartSense® at scale, supporting the delivery of diagnostic-quality heart monitoring beyond hospital environments. The initiative is intended to reduce pressure on secondary care services while improving access to high-quality cardiac diagnostics in community settings.
Founded by Professor Rameen Shakur , Cambridge Heartwear is a medical technology company based at Cambridge Science Park coming out of the University of Cambridge dedicated to making heart health monitoring simple, accessible and accurate. Combining medical research, engineering excellence and artificial intelligence, the company develops advanced wearable technologies that empower patients and healthcare professionals with diagnostic-quality cardiovascular insights anytime, anywhere. HeartSense® helps detect heart conditions earlier, enabling more informed clinical decision-making and better patient care.
Contact: info@camheartwear.com

articles.title_orig: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.title_zh: U.S. military to conduct first firing squad execution since World War II
articles.content_orig:
An undated handout image of Hasan that was released by authorities in 2012
The Pentagon has announced it will execute a former US Army major by firing squad, the first such military execution in more than 60 years.
Nidal Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009, injuring another 32.
Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced on social media on Monday that US defence secretary Pete Hegseth had made the recommendation and President Donald Trump approved it.
It will be the first military execution by firing squad since the end of World War Two.
Parnell said the secretary of the US Army would set the time and place of the execution.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," he wrote on X.
Hasan, a US Army psychiatrist from Virginia, killed 13 soldiers at the base in Texas in 2009 and later admitted in court he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes".
He said during his court-martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan.
The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base.
The attack took place in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines.
Watch: Why is America running out of execution drugs? , external
Hasan is currently one of four inmates on the US military's death row.
A military execution requires approval from the US president, according to military law.
It also requires appellate review and a final judgment on its legality to move forward.
The US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces deemed the military death penalty unconstitutional in 1983 but it was reinstated the following year by an executive order under then-President Ronald Reagan.
Military executions differ from those carried out at the state level.
The majority of executions in the US are carried out on the state level, with 27 states, the military and the federal government still having capital punishment as a legally available option.
Death by firing squad is rather uncommon. There was an execution by firing squad carried out last year in South Carolina, a first for the state and the first time the method was used in the US in 15 years.
Four other states allow the use of a firing squad, including Idaho, Mississippi, Oklahoma and Utah.
How widely used is the death penalty in the US?
Trump has been a proponent of the federal death penalty and re-instated it through an executive order on the first day of his administration in January 2025.
Under his predecessor, former President Joe Biden, the justice department had issued a moratorium on the federal use of the death penalty.
The executive order signed by Trump describes capital punishment as "an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens".

articles.title_orig: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.title_zh: The butter boom – how the world fell back in love with the glorious golden spread
articles.content_orig:
It’s being sculpted for fashion parties, collected by tourists and hoarded in freezers. There are even entire shops devoted to it. What’s behind the revival of the much-maligned foodstuff?
T emperatures in Paris were nudging 41C when Erwan Leo opened Le Butter this summer. Wildfires had already been tearing through France and the city was quiet, particularly in the less touristy 8th arrondissement, a flex-your-wealth area near the Eiffel Tower known as the “golden triangle”. The last thing it needed, you would think, was a shop that sold loads of butter. “We were just so worried about the fridges,” says Leo, the 34-year-old owner. “We didn’t think anyone would even turn up.”
I visit Le Butter, the first shop in Paris dedicated to selling the stuff, two months later in September. It’s a quaint, photogenic spot between a wine shop that was opened by Leo eight years ago and a cafe famous for being blown up in Christopher Nolan’s Inception. Inside there are candy-striped walls, little shopping baskets, a shelf of Instagrammable buttery merch (knives, hats, totes) and two double fridges containing 50 different types of butter. It’s a lot cooler today; the fridges purr away at an exacting 3C. And the past few months have been busy – so much so that Leo has had to erect a bench for those waiting outside, and a retractable barrier to manage the queues.
Outside today, I find a gathering of butter fans comparing purchases. Among them is Clifford Yellen, a 66-year-old Italian-American chef and consultant who has bulk-bought “only pure stuff – salted”. He opens his paper bag to show me multiple packets, vacuum-packed for his flight home. “We chefs have a real thing about butter,” he says. He usually eats Italian, or the famously creamy Hokkaido from Japan.
Inside the shop, tourists from Brazil and Korea are gathered around a glass display cabinet on the counter where staff dispense quenelles of wild garlic butter on to wooden tasting spoons. The tasters follow it with raspberry flavour, and chocolate. “I call Le Butter an ice-cream shop for butter!” Leo says with a laugh.
And while British tourists have been banned from bringing French butter to the UK since 2025, to stop farm animal diseases spreading, as a nation we, too, revere butter. Earlier this year, the Pembroke Club in Belgravia, London, placed an advert for a butter sommelier in Country Life magazine, looking for someone able to confidently “curate our butter assortment and assist in training staff using our silver butter trolley”.
For those who can take butter home with them, there are entire threads on Reddit discussing the best way to transport it via plane (frozen, vacuum-packed, ziplocked) and where to buy it. Guided by one, I head to La Grande Épicerie de Paris to lay eyes on its famous “wall of butter” where 150 types are sold. The two most popular varieties, according to the staff, are Le Beurre Bordier and Beillevaire. Like most good French butters, they have a fresh, rich flavour with tangy depths, which you could probably put down to their high butterfat content and the grass-fed cows from which they come.
Even the high-end butter is relatively cheap, and right now, in this “little treat” economy , eking out €8 for a wheel of butter sprinkled with fleur de sel feels more manageable than buying a decent bottle of wine. The latest thing, Leo says, is people serving butter as they would cheese after dinner, on boards with crackers. “It’s also cheaper.”
While I’m reporting from Paris fashion week, my Instagram becomes a cavalcade of ambrosial butters laid out on event tables with great loaves of bread, or pummelled into submission and piled up into small hills as table centrepieces. I watch influencers biting into whole sticks of butter, or being served plates of medjool dates stuffed with slivers of the stuff. It’s at once beautiful and grotesque.
It has even become a material for food artists. Laila Gohar, the American-Egyptian artist, treats it like marble, and once carved it into a fragment of Michelangelo’s David. During a design festival, the food artist Imogen Kwok built a foot-high cone from whipped butter and foraged herbs.
It was the threat of shortage that turned South African journalist Safia Patel, 35, into a self-described “butter hoarder” who now collects and categorises it. At home in Istanbul she keeps cooking butter, eating butter and “ornamental” butter (too precious to eat), the last of which she stores in her freezer.
Her love of butter comes from her grandmother, who ate it in thick, cold slices on bread. But it was during the pandemic that she realised how much it really meant to her. She’d buy Lurpak locally in Istanbul – but as the pandemic wore on, it became harder to find. “Once things returned to normal, I began coercing people into bringing me butter from around the world in case I ran out.” Most days she carries two or three portion-sized packs in her handbag, “just in case. Yes, it can get messy.”
The prettiness of Le Butter’s packaging has naturally made it a social media hit, which Leo describes as a double-edged sword. “Obviously, I’m grateful,” he says. “But it can also be overwhelming. The aim of the shop is to educate people beyond supermarket butter, and to serve the locals as well as the tourists. We can only do our best.”
This fetishisation of butter is still quite divisive. “When it comes to food styling, some of what they do looks cool,” says Seb Myers of the restaurant Planque in east London. “But when you see a mound of butter – all that extravagance for the sake of a photo? I’m quite squirrelly with food. Waste is my big thing.”
In restaurants, I’ve lost count of the time I’ve been served butter shaped into little salted coins or whipped into something dippable. Bread and butter are still one of the most valued moments in a good meal. And as Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential, “If you eat at any good restaurant, assume you’ve eaten a stick of butter.”
“That’s partly because it starts the meal,” says Myers, who takes his butter pretty seriously. “If someone serves you an ice-cold pat of butter, you know you’re not in for a good time”. His restaurant is a play on Parisian bistronomy, so “it’s in almost every dish”. They use Beillevaire butter demi-sel sprinkled with flakes, sliced and well tempered. He keeps it in “a cheese fridge for a week to slow-mature it”. For cooking, it’s Douceur de France (they get through 10kg a week in cooking alone).
Pravin Nayar runs Castle Farm restaurant in Somerset, and makes his own: “We like butter to be the hero product when we do supper clubs.” The key, he says, is how you serve it: room temperature, sprinkled with salt. “The way I see it, bread is just a spoon for butter.”
R emember when butter was considered bad? After all those anti-saturated fat health campaigns, consumption hit a historic low by the late 1990s, with the average Brit consuming just 2kg a year. The perception around it seems to have shifted, although with 50% saturated fat – and I say this with love – butter is not exactly a superfood.
“The heart-health advice hasn’t changed,” says Tracy Parker, a registered dietitian and an adviser for the British Heart Foundation. “If you’ve got high cholesterol, or your diet already leans heavily on saturated fat – think fatty meats, pastries, cakes, biscuits – then you should probably reconsider how much you’re eating and whether you could swap it for something like olive, avocado or nut oil.” Butter is fine in moderation, though. “A light scrape on your morning toast, and thinking about everything else you eat – you’re probably OK,” she says.
So why the cultural rehabilitation of butter in a health-fad-mad 2026? Parker thinks it has become tangled up with the anti-ultraprocessed-food movement. “UPFs have been linked to poor health including obesity, type 2 diabetes and heart disease,” she says. Whereas butter is seen as a preindustrial, farm-adjacent product. “People view butter as a natural food

articles.title_orig: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.title_zh: Chanel is all about joy as Blazy celebrates year at helm of world’s hottest brand
articles.content_orig:
Artistic director is all smiles as he swaps quiet luxury for bold colours and patterns at Paris show
“It’s a good start,” Matthieu Blazy said after a Paris show that marked a year of his tenure as artistic director at Chanel . “I am happy with where we are at.”
Chanel now holds the top spot in the Lyst index of the world’s hottest brands, which tracks demand and engagement across search and social media. The privately held company announces official financial results only once a year, but figures reported by Bloomberg showed 16% growth in the first half of 2026. In Vanity Fair’s list of the world’s 50 most powerful people, published this month, Blazy is the only fashion designer to make the cut. People who don’t much care about fashion have noticed him; people who do care about fashion talk about him non-stop.
Blazy’s Chanel is about joy. Smiley and chatty in person, he enthuses about his team and the women he dresses, presenting a friendly face of Chanel that contrasts with Karl Lagerfeld’s legendary acid tongue and Coco’s controlled brutalist chic. He talks about his job like a child in a candy store, not a tortured artist: he got the idea for this stage set, a flock of 95 giant white birds suspended from the domed steel and glass ceiling of the Grand Palais in Paris, while on holiday in southern Italy with his partner, watching migrating birds fly above the Crati River.
One of Chanel’s most famous adverts of the 1990s featured Vanessa Paradis in a birdcage ; now, Chanel’s birds fly free. For the soundtrack of the show Blazy had asked Nicole Kidman to read a passage “about time, about freedom” from Virginia Woolf’s To The Lighthouse, which he had read on that Italian holiday. Fashion was “women’s homemade remedy for the dark times”, he said.
After several years when the decaffeinated aesthetic of quiet luxury dominated fashion, the new Chanel shouts with cereal-aisle colours. A red and white embroidered jacket with a jade and turquoise skirt, plus bag and boots in navy and gold. The iconic two-tone pumps, but in zebra stripes and yellow polka dots instead of the traditional camel and black.
The same model opened and closed the show carrying Gabrielle Chanel’s very own 2.55 handbag. “Gabrielle actually had very few bags in her own life, which is something I find quite beautiful. So this bag is not broken, but it has a wonderful patina,” Blazy said.
after newsletter promotion
On his moodboard were photographs of the founder he had found in the archive: Gabrielle as a child; with Gigot, her beloved great dane; on a boat; riding a horse; in a Harlequin fancy dress costume; smiling in a bold leopard-print coat and matching hat. “It is a side of Chanel that is not known: her funny side, her joyful side. I see women as a juxtaposition of so many selves, and Chanel had this incredible layering within herself.”
The famous soft-shouldered Chanel suit came worn with nothing beneath, “like perfume” (Blazy, a student of Cocology, will not have missed the allusion to what Marilyn Monroe famously said she wore in bed: Chanel No 5). “I like the idea that when you wear it directly on the skin, it makes a fetish of the suit. A little punk Chanel,” he said. A year of fabric innovation was behind the newest versions of the suit, a smocked silk on an elasticated membrane, which “is my answer to what sporty could mean at Chanel”, Blazy said.

articles.title_orig: Symphony San Jose Celebrates Silver Anniversary with Dvořák’s “New World”
articles.title_zh: Symphony San Jose Celebrates Silver Anniversary with Dvořák’s “New World”
articles.content_orig:
It’s merely a coincidence that Symphony San Jose’s silver anniversary aligns with the country’s 250 th birthday, but the orchestra fittingly celebrated both in its season opener with a sterling performance of Antonin Dvořák’s “New World” Symphony.
On Oct. 3 at San José’s California Theatre, the Symphony also performed Jonathan Leshnoff’s patriotic “Rhapsody on America,” a new work co-commissioned by the organization with extraordinary pianist Joyce Yang as soloist.
Age is just a number. The true marker of an orchestra’s prestige is a secure, well-balanced sound. Despite never having had a music director, Symphony San Jose plays well together with great continuity.
The orchestra, which formed in 2002 out of the ashes of the similarly named San Jose Symphony, has retained many of its original musicians. It has also built a loyal fanbase. When Executive Artistic Director Robert Massey asked yesterday’s audience members to stand if they had attended the Symphony’s first concert, many did.
Aaron Copland’s cowboy-themed Suite from “Billy the Kid” bolted out the gate in a brash performance led by guest conductor Ken-David Masur, making his Symphony San Jose debut. Copland’s unexpected syncopations in this score could cause trouble for some regional orchestras, but SSJ handled the rhythmic intricacies well. This was a confident rendition — while Masur’s cuing was generous, the musicians sometimes jumped on entrances on their own volition.
Leshnoff’s “Rhapsody” benefited from Yang’s brilliant musicality, but unfortunately the piece is underwhelming. Though Leshnoff has impressive credentials, that doesn’t save this piece from being boring.
Big occasions don’t automatically spur the creation of great music. Leshnoff’s biggest problem may be that he chose to write variations on a hymn theme, “My Country ‘Tis of Thee,” which doesn’t offer fertile ground for variations. There are a lot of straight quarter-notes in this hymn, and it doesn’t exactly teem with contrapuntal possibilities. The composer mentions, in his notes on the piece, that he was inspired by Sergei Rachmaninoff’s “Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini,” but play the first theme of that work and note the difference.
Leshnoff’s work gets off to a slow start with a quiet version of the theme in the piano and several variations that are uninventive decorations of the theme. Later in the piece, Leshnoff does transform his theme: he knows enough to remove notes from it strategically, for example. We hear it in the minor mode and in a syncopated version. But there’s nothing surprising in this piece, nothing to perk up the ears. The orchestration is flat, with the strings bunched in the midrange chugging out 16 th -notes. Leshnoff’s strategy for making things more exciting seemed to be limited to faster and louder. Certainly, his music will never scare or offend anyone, but the flip side is that it can only be mildly entertaining, even with Yang’s polished advocacy.
Dvořák’s “New World” Symphony, by contrast, was a winner, particularly in Masur’s passionate reading. Most orchestras can’t go far wrong with this masterwork. But Symphony San Jose’s performance balanced the concentrated drive and power of moments like the coda to the first movement, with the meditative breadth of the famous second movement, and the folk color of the dance in the third movement. The woodwinds as a group were on point, playing with character.  Haley Hoffman’s English horn solo in the second movement was lovely. The strings had an alluring sheen to their sound.
At the applause, a child in the second row bounced up and down in excitement, one of the orchestra’s next generation of fans. It was heartwarming to see.
Michael Zwiebach is the senior editor/content manager for SFCV . He assigns all articles and content, manages the writing staff, and does editing. A member of SFCV from the beginning, Michael holds a Ph.D. in music history from the University of California, Berkeley.
Violinist Geneva Lewis and conductor François López-Ferrer brought interpretive clarity to an all-Romantic program.
Under guest conductor Tatsuya Shimono, the reinforced orchestra turns in a spectacular performance of Gustav Holst’s popular showpiece.
The founder of L.A. new-music group Wild Up leads a spirited concert of Americana, including Jeff Midkiff’s Mandolin Concerto.

articles.title_orig: Wrongly Indicted Man Seeks Inquiry of Official Conduct in Reflecting Pool Case
articles.title_zh: Wrongly Indicted Man Seeks Inquiry of Official Conduct in Reflecting Pool Case
articles.content_orig:
Hearn is considering legal action against Trump and his administration.
Former U.S. Olympian David Hearn says he is “relieved” after a Washington, D.C. judge permanently dismissed the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool vandalism case against him, ending the possibility that prosecutors could recharge him.
Hearn was indicted this summer and prosecutors alleged that he ripped a piece of the lining from the pool while he was out on a bike ride.
The charges were rolled out in a press conference where U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said Hearn "forcefully and violently" vandalized the pool and that they had proof "beyond a reasonable doubt."
President Donald Trump had insisted the damage to the pool, a key renovation project of his, was the work of vandals, but Pirro later said that evidence surfaced that renovations to the pool had caused the damage. Hearn had faced up to 10 years in prison in connection with the case.
Speaking exclusively to “Good Morning America,” Hearn called Thursday’s ruling “a victory for democracy.”
“I’m relieved,” Hearn said. “If it can happen to me, it can happen to anybody. Anybody in this country.”
Asked what he meant, Hearn said people could be “targeted and unfairly accused of something they didn’t do.”
“Nobody should feel they’re immune from this kind of abuse of power,” he said.
Hearn said he believes Pirro and Trump owe him an apology.
“Do you think the president should apologize to you?” Hearn was asked.
“You know, if pigs fly, maybe,” Hearn said.
Just six weeks after Hearn’s arrest, Pirro dropped the charges, President Trump subsequently criticized Pirro over the decision, saying she “choked.”
The Justice Department wanted to preserve the possibility of bringing the case again, but In his ruling Thursday, Judge Todd Edelman dismissed the case with prejudice, meaning Hearn cannot be charged again over the same allegations.
Edelman also addressed Trump’s public comments about the case, writing that despite there being no evidence of a crime, the president’s public pressure created “a risk that Mr. Hearn will be prosecuted nonetheless.”
Hearn said the experience has shaken him and that the past few months have been “difficult” while thanking those who rallied around him during the case.
He and his attorney, Norm Eisen, are also considering whether to pursue legal action against Trump or the administration.
Eisen told ABC News that they are “actively” considering their options and that “nothing is off the table.”

articles.title_orig: UVA index ranks US second in world’s most capitalist countries
articles.title_zh: UVA index ranks US second in world’s most capitalist countries
articles.content_orig:
Three years in the making, the Global Capitalism Index – the product of experts at UVA’s Darden School of Business and Karsh Institute of Democracy – helps people better understand how capitalist conditions relate to democracy, corruption, human well-being and inequality within a country. (Illustration by Meredith Michael Smith, University Communications)
Switzerland is the most capitalistic country in the world, with the United States coming in a close second, according to a first-ever global index and data set from the University of Virginia.
Three years in the making , the Global Capitalism Index is the product of experts at UVA’s Darden School of Business and Karsh Institute of Democracy. The index scores 161 countries across eight measures of capitalism, including ease of business formation and the flow of goods to and from the country.
Experts involved in creating the index said the data show promise for understanding how capitalist conditions relate to democracy, corruption, human well-being, and inequality within a country. A team of researchers led by the Karsh Institute of Democracy’s Democracy and Capitalism Lab and UVA Darden’s Institute for Business in Society assembled the data to help define and measure capitalism worldwide.
The index uses figures compiled from 2009 to 2025 and is designed to be updated.
“Understanding the conditions that allow democratic self-government to thrive requires us to examine the economic systems in which people and institutions operate,” said Melody Barnes, executive director of the Karsh Institute of Democracy. “The Global Capitalism Index gives researchers a rigorous new tool for examining how different forms of capitalism relate to democratic institutions, individual well-being, inequality and other dimensions of democratic life.”
Although there is a large body of research on the concept and function of democracy, there is little on capitalism, the researchers wrote.
“For decades, scholars, policymakers and the public have lacked a rigorous, quantitative framework for defining and measuring capitalism,” the index authors wrote in an executive summary. “Even capitalism’s intellectual champions – Adam Smith, Joseph Schumpeter, Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman and others – produced widely varied definitions of the concept. …There is a substantial body of literature defining democracy, but scholarly efforts to define and measure capitalism have been difficult and fractured.”
Interactive world map showing Global Capitalism Index scores.
            Higher-ranked countries are shown in darker blue.
            Use the Tab key to explore countries on the map, or view the
            complete data table below.
Under the index’s 100-point scale, the top-ranked country was Switzerland at 96.6, followed by the U.S. at 95, Hong Kong at 94.5 and Canada at 93.8.
From the bottom rankings, Venezuela scored 8.9; Libya, 21.8; Chad, 24.1; and Mauritania, 24.2.
“If you ask anyone what capitalism is, the answers are all different, and that makes it hard to argue about the validity or value of it,” said Scott Miller, an assistant business professor at the Darden School, director of the Democracy and Capitalism Lab and lead author on the project. “We concluded that this word – capitalism – matters to everyone, so it matters to define it and measure how it really works across the globe.”
Looking at different sectors of capitalism in a country adds nuance and insight into its economy and culture, index authors said. For example, Seychelles and China rank 50th and 33rd, respectively, and Nordic countries rank highly overall, even though they are associated with high levels of social support.
Here are the U.S. rankings listed in the index:
In addition to comparing countries, the index also examines different forms of capitalism. Rather than a monolithic economic model, the index examines capitalism in four categories:
“For individual countries, the index makes it much easier to identify what conditions are conducive to capitalism and which are not,” Miller said. “Using China as an example, we can see in sharper relief the profile and shape of the underlying economy, including surprisingly strong business conditions, but increasingly restricted flow of goods and capital.”

articles.title_orig: World War II: A New Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress
articles.title_zh: World War II: A New Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress
articles.content_orig:
A new World War II Primary Source Set from the Library of Congress supports teachers, librarians, and students in examining the people, places, and events of the war through primary sources from the Library’s digital collections. The eighteen-source set features newspapers, photographs, posters, maps, oral histories, letters, and other materials created during the period. A background essay provides historical context, teaching ideas, and links to additional Library of Congress resources.
These sources offer opportunities to explore some of the central questions and experiences of World War II from multiple perspectives. Americans contributed to the war effort as soldiers and civilians, workers and volunteers, and community members.
We hope this new source set will both be a useful and insightful way to explore World War II through the voices, images, and experiences preserved in the Library of Congress collections, and inspire students’ further inquiry and deeper investigation.

articles.title_orig: Jim Bakker, who lost his ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire in sex and money scandals, dies at 86
articles.title_zh: Jim Bakker, who lost his ‘PTL Club’ televangelism empire in sex and money scandals, dies at 86
articles.content_orig:
Televangelist Jim Bakker, who rose to national prominence in the 1970s and ‘80s before stepping down from his ministry amid scandal, has died. He was 86.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” according to an announcement from his wife, Lori Bakker, shared on the Jim Bakker Show’s Facebook Monday evening.
“For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry,” she wrote in her statement.
“Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years,” she wrote. “Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world.”
The statement did not include a cause of death or details about the circumstances.
During his rise to fame, Bakker and his then-wife, the late Tammy Faye Messner, ran the evangelistic empire “Praise the Lord,” or PTL – and eventually their own theme park – from suburban Charlotte, North Carolina, for some 15 years.
The couple hosted “The PTL Club,” one of the best-known Christian TV programs of its time. Messner, who divorced Bakker in the ‘90s and later remarried, died in 2007 .
Bakker resigned from the PTL ministry in 1987 amid a financial and sex scandal involving a secretary, Jessica Hahn, who he had paid to keep quiet.
Two years later, Bakker was charged with fraud and sentenced to 45 years in prison, though he served just under five .
“I wanted people to believe in my dream, and my dream became more important than the people,” Bakker told CNN’s Larry King in 2000 . “When the dream of Christian community becomes more important than the community, that’s when it’s a sin.”
Jim and Tammy Faye met at North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, she told CNN in a 2003 interview . They married in 1961.
Their path to TV fame started with puppet shows at a church . Televangelist Pat Robertson, who had a fledgling TV station in Portsmouth, Virginia, asked Bakker to bring the show to television . Bakker agreed, under the condition that they could eventually launch a “Tonight” show style program for Christians, Messner told CNN.
From 1966 to 1973 , the Bakkers hosted “700 Club,” which was syndicated across the nation.
“It just snowballed on us,” Tammy Faye said .
After about eight years at Robertson’s Christian Broadcasting Network, the Bakkers parted ways with the network. The move, Tammy Faye said, came after Robertson started reducing the number of nights for their show.
In 1974, they moved to Charlotte to start the Inspiration Network and “The PTL Club.”
Four years later, the Heritage USA theme park opened at the network’s headquarters across the state line in Fort Mill, South Carolina. The Heritage USA Grand Hotel was added in 1984, with a water park joining the complex in 1986. That year, more than 6 million people visited the park , making it the nation’s third most popular attraction after Walt Disney World and Disneyland.
At its peak , PTL was bringing in more than $128 million annually and was carried on 1,300 cable systems with 12 million subscribers.
“As I look back, you know, I had a tiger by the tail,” Bakker told CNN’s Larry King in 2000 . “The budgets kept getting bigger and bigger, and it got to the point where it was either, you know, raise the money or go broke. And so, you kept raising the money.”
Jim and Tammy Faye brought a casual and conversational style to their show, similar to daytime talk shows today – but with a Christian focus.
“Welcome back to our home,” Jim Bakker said at the start of one 1981 episode , which opened with the couple sitting in a group with a view of Lake Wylie behind them. “It’s nice to see you. It’s nice to see you, Tammy Faye.”
“It’s nice to see you, Jim,” said Tammy Faye.
But off camera, a scandal was growing, and on March 19, 1987, Jim Bakker resigned from PTL after paying a secretary, Jessica Hahn, to keep quiet about his affair with her. Hahn received a one-time $115,000 payment and monthly interest payments from a $150,000 trust fund.
The following month, PTL filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection. Also in 1987, Tammy Faye Bakker, whose heavy mascara became her trademark, was treated at the Betty Ford Center for prescription drug addiction.
In December 1988, Jim Bakker was indicted for fraud and conspiring to defraud churchgoers of $158 million. Tammy Faye Bakker was not named in the indictment.
In 1989 , Heritage USA and the Grand Hotel closed, and Jim Bakker was convicted of 24 counts of fraud and conspiracy and sentenced to 45 years in prison.
Bakker told CNN in an interview that his affair with Hahn was a mistake.
“God’s forgiveness is the only thing. And, you know, I take full responsibility for the adultery. It was my fault ,” Bakker said . “And, you know, no matter what went on, the man has to take responsibility, and I do.”
After more than 30 years of marriage, Tammy Faye Bakker divorced Jim while he was in prison, marrying Christian construction magnate and former PTL contractor Roe Messner in 1993. She died at 65 of inoperable cancer that had spread to her lungs.
They later became the subject of both the big screen and documentary lens.
Jessica Chastain and Andrew Garfield portrayed the couple in “ The Eyes of Tammy Faye ” in 2021 –- beginning in 1960 and following them into the ‘90s – adopted from a 2000 documentary of the same name.
In 2007, Tammy Faye opened up about peace with death
Jim Bakker was paroled in December 1994 . Four years later, Bakker met Lori Graham while working in the inner-city ministry of the Dream Center of Los Angeles, according to his official bio. They married that same year.
“I’m put back together by my faith in Jesus Christ,” Bakker told CNN in the 2000 interview . “He forgives everyone. And if I don’t receive his forgiveness, how can I teach anyone else that God will forgive them?”
He returned to TV in the 2000s with “The Jim Bakker Show,” this time filmed from Branson, Missouri, with Lori as cohost.
Bakker faced controversy again in early 2020.
On a February 2020 episode of his show, Bakker and a guest discussed a product, “Silver Solution,” that they claimed could eliminate the coronavirus from the body within hours -– well before vaccines or any approved treatments.
The Missouri attorney general sued Bakker and his production company for misrepresenting “Silver Solution” as a coronavirus cure.
“Anyone who has bought ‘Silver Solution’ from ‘The Jim Bakker Show’ should know that it cannot cure or treat coronavirus,” the Missouri Attorney General’s office announced in a statement .
In May 2020 , Lori Bakker announced that her husband had had a stroke and would take a sabbatical from their TV show.
Working nonstop had taken a “huge toll” on her husband’s health, she said.
Two years earlier, in 2018, Bakker had returned to North Carolina for the funeral of the Rev. Billy Graham, the evangelist of an earlier generation who grew up in Charlotte.
“Billy Graham came into my prison when I was there ,” Bakker told CNN affiliate WBTV . “He wrapped his arms around me when I was a mess, I was cleaning toilets at that moment, and I was at a very low moment in my life. Billy Graham walked in and threw his arms around me and said ‘Jim, I love you.’
“The whole Graham family loved me, and I had to come and say goodbye, but he’s in Heaven,” Bakker said. “We’re gonna walk with him someday.”
CNN’s Scottie Andrew contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Robert Half selected by Forbes as one of the World's Best Employers 2026
articles.title_zh: Robert Half selected by Forbes as one of the World's Best Employers 2026
articles.content_orig:
MENLO PARK, Calif. , Oct. 6, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Global talent solutions and business consulting firm Robert Half (NYSE: RHI ) has been named by Forbes as one of the World's Best Employers 2026 . This recognition highlights multinational companies that demonstrate a strong commitment to employee well-being and an exceptional workplace experience.
Forbes' World's Best Employers list is based on an independent survey of more than 300,000 employees across 50 countries. Respondents rated their employers on employee satisfaction, workplace culture and reputation, with particular attention to well-being, inclusivity, career growth and work-life balance—underscoring what it takes to be a top employer on a global scale.
"Being named one of the World's Best Employers reflects the dedication, talent and collaboration of our employees around the world," said M. Keith Waddell, president and chief executive officer of Robert Half. "We are committed to fostering an environment where people can grow their careers, do meaningful work, and make a positive impact for our clients, colleagues and communities."
Robert Half's employee commitment is grounded in its core values of integrity, inclusion, innovation and commitment to success. The company supports employees through opportunities to grow their careers, contribute meaningful work and make an impact in the communities where they live and work.
The company has also been named a World's Most Admired Company by Fortune and one of the Best Employers for Company Culture by Forbes.
FAQs: How were companies selected for this recognition? Forbes' World's Best Employers list is based on an independent survey of more than 300,000 employees across 50 countries. Employees evaluated employers on factors including workplace culture, well-being, inclusivity, career development, work-life balance and whether they would recommend their employer to others.
Why was Robert Half recognized? Robert Half was recognized for its commitment to creating an exceptional workplace experience where employees can grow their careers, do meaningful work and make a positive impact. The company fosters an organizational culture grounded in its core values of integrity, inclusion, innovation and commitment to success.
What does this recognition mean for Robert Half? This recognition reinforces Robert Half's reputation as an employer of choice and reflects the company's ongoing commitment to supporting employee well-being, career growth and a positive workplace culture. It also highlights the strength of the company's people-first approach across its global workforce.

We offer contract talent and full-time solutions in the fields of finance and accounting, technology, marketing and creative, legal, and administrative and customer support, and we also provide executive search services.
Robert Half is the parent company of Protiviti ® , a global consulting firm that delivers internal audit, risk, business and technology consulting solutions. In the last 12 months, Robert Half has been recognized as one of America's Most Innovative Companies by Fortune and, with Protiviti, has been named a Fortune ® Most Admired Company™ and one of the 100 Best Companies to Work For. articles.title_orig: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.title_zh: British Airways plans record 106-seat business class on Airbus A380 jumbo jets
articles.content_orig:
British Airways is building what it calls the "world's largest" business-class cabin and ripping out dozens of coach-class seats, the starkest example yet of how airlines are betting their future on high-spending travelers.
The changes are part of a massive overhaul of the British Airways fleet and its ground services, including lounges at its London Heathrow hub.
Airlines have been spending years and hundreds of millions of dollars to expand their pricier seats, capitalizing on demand for roomier options and travelers' appetite for more luxurious trips.
British Airways' joint-venture partner, American Airlines , last month debuted a 70-seat business class on its largest Boeing aircraft.
Those more expensive seats command a premium. Even extra legroom on trips across the Atlantic can go for more than $200 per leg, with surcharges of more than $1,000 for premium economy seats after purchase.
The prices can be even higher if they're selected at booking. The top-end seats regularly run $5,000 and even well over $10,000 on lengthier flights.
Deliveries of new aircraft have even been delayed because some of the new seats are so elaborate that carriers have been waiting for parts or federal certification.
British Airways' overhaul of the cabins on its 12 A380s is also a bet on the jumbo jet, which many carriers have retired in recent years, opting for smaller, more fuel-efficient jets. Airbus delivered the last A380 to the plane's largest user, Emirates, in late 2021.
