articles.title_orig: Economic Freedom of the World: 2026
articles.title_zh: Economic Freedom of the World: 2026
articles.content_orig:
The foundations of economic freedom are personal choice, voluntary exchange, and open markets. As Adam Smith, Milton Friedman, and Friedrich Hayek have stressed, freedom of exchange and market coordination provide the fuel for economic progress. Without exchange and entrepreneurial activity coordinated through markets, modern living standards would be impossible.
Potentially advantageous exchanges do not always occur. Their realization is dependent on the presence of sound money, rule of law, and security of property rights, among other factors. Economic Freedom of the World seeks to measure the consistency of the institutions and policies of various countries with voluntary exchange and the other dimensions of economic freedom.
The report is co‐​published by the Cato Institute, the Fraser Institute in Canada and more than 70 think tanks around the world.
This is the 31st edition of Economic Freedom of the World and this year’s publication ranks 165 countries and territories for 2024, the most recent year for which data are available.
Despite a precipitous decline in economic freedom since 2018, Hong Kong remained the world’s most economically free jurisdiction in 2024. It was followed by Switzerland (2nd), Singapore (3rd), New Zealand (4th), and the United States (5th).
Canada has now slipped from 9th to 18th, just ahead of Germany at 19th. The United Kingdom is 10th, Japan is 13th, France is 39th, Italy is 47th, South Korea is 53rd, Indonesia is 72nd, Mexico is 77th, Brazil is 85th, India is 88th, China is 110th, and Russia is 143rd. The 10 lowest-rated countries are: the Democratic Republic of Congo, Egypt, Malawi, Algeria, Iran, Myanmar, Libya, Sudan, Zimbabwe, and Venezuela in last place.
Overall, the index shows that global economic freedom fell following the pandemic as policymakers imposed new regulations, raised barriers to trade, expanded the size of government, and then printed money to pay for spending. While governments have begun to reverse these policies, economic freedom in the average country has not yet returned to pre-pandemic levels.
A preliminary estimate of US economic freedom in the first year of the Trump Administration finds increases in the size of government, weaker protection of property rights and the rule of law, and significant restrictions on trade freedom caused a 0.12-point decline in US economic freedom in 2025.
Nations in the top quartile of economic freedom had an average per capita GDP of $65,596 in 2024, compared to $9,552 for bottom quartile nations. Life expectancy is 80.7 years in the top quartile compared to 67.1 years in the bottom quartile.
The first Economic Freedom of the World Report , published in 1996, was the result of a decade of research by a team which included several Nobel Laureates and over 60 other leading scholars in a broad range of fields, from economics to political science, and from law to philosophy.

Asian countries have responded more aggressively than others to the energy supply crunch caused by the U.S. and Israeli war on Iran and now they are running out of resources to continue their response, the World Bank warned in a new report.
The report actually focuses on the potential of artificial intelligence to help Asian economies grow but names energy import vulnerability as one major headwind to that growth.
“Subsidies have been by far the most common policy response [to the crisis] among emerging and developing economies,” the World Bank said, adding that “Countries with substantial subsidies in place generally have had smaller increases in retail gasoline prices than non-subsidizers, but this relationship weakened considerably for headline inflation.”
Energy remains a spot of weakness for Asian countries due to their overwhelming dependence on imports but, according to the World Bank, AI can change that by motivating a shift towards greater domestic electricity generation, which would in turn lead to lower demand for imported energy commodities.
Meanwhile, Asian countries’ response to the energy crunch has led to lower prices at the cost of lower foreign exchange reserves, the lender also said. The longer the crisis continues, the greater the effect on their fiscal health would be, the World Bank warned, noting as examples Indonesia, Thailand, and Vietnam, which saw their dollar reserves decline by between 15% and 40% since the start of the war because of their crisis response actions.
These response actions, however, have had no effect on inflation anywhere in the world, and “headline inflation has sharply increased in many countries, even as core inflation has remained more subdued.” For Asia, however, there is hope for a reversal, driven by information technology generally and AI specifically, according to the World Bank.
“The region’s dependence on AI-related industrial activity has been a source of strength, but it could become a weakness if global AI activity slows or reverses,” the institution said in its report.
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV, ahead of World Youth Day in 2027, praises Korean courage
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV, ahead of World Youth Day in 2027, praises Korean courage
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff met with Korean clergy on Monday, marking the 25th anniversary of the Korean Pontifical College in Rome.
At a Monday audience celebrating the 25th anniversary of the Korean Pontifical College’s inauguration in Rome, Pope Leo XIV met with Korean clergy and reflected on their remarkable journey of faith.
As preparations gather momentum for World Youth Day in Seoul in 2027, the meeting provided an occasion to celebrate how the Church in Korea has grown into a dynamic land of missionaries.
The pope emphasized that the Korean Church’s vibrant growth rests firmly on the testimony of its martyrs. Through relentless persecution, devastating wars, crippling poverty, and national partition, Korean Catholics have continuously overcome incredible hardship.
“The Korean people have demonstrated throughout history an extraordinary strength of character,” Leo remarked.
The pope said it was a powerful testament to God’s grace that the faithful kept “the ability to go through the ordeal without losing hope and without letting suffering harden the heart.”
Drawing pastoral inspiration from history, Leo highlighted the tireless witness of Venerable Thomas Choe Yang-Eop. Known for walking endless miles across Korea to connect remote, hidden villages and bring them the light of the Gospel, Father Choe serves as an enduring model for modern ministry, the pope said.
The pope urged the assembled clergy to imitate Choe’s zeal: “In our time we have much need for men and women who have the courage to do good even when it costs them.”
Recognizing the diverse dioceses and backgrounds represented among the clergy, the pope called for a renewed commitment to synodality. By listening to one another and moving past regional differences, priests embody a unified Church walking together on the same path through Christ, he said.
Finally, looking ahead to hosting the world’s Catholic youth in 2027, the pope reminded the clergy to ground all their preparations in constant prayer, seeking the intercession of St. Andrew Kim Taegon, patron of Korean clergy.
“Young people from all over the world will arrive in a land where the Gospel has grown through the testimony of the martyrs,” Leo said.

articles.title_orig: The Kehlani World Tour: a dynamic but disjointed homecoming
articles.title_zh: The Kehlani World Tour: a dynamic but disjointed homecoming
articles.content_orig:
Editor’s Note: This article is a review and includes subjective thoughts, opinions and critiques.
On Saturday, Kehlani came home.
In front of a 20,000-person crowd, the Oakland native and R&B artist returned to the Bay Area to close out the North American leg of “The Kehlani World Tour.” Held at the Shoreline Amphitheatre in Mountain View, it was the tour’s biggest stop yet.
The concert itself was narrative as much as music. It followed Kehlani and her “crew” through a night of clubbing set in a futuristic world. As the “night” ticked on, Kehlani, who uses “she / they” pronouns interchangeably, took the audience along with her — in a “Zuber” (a futuristic Uber), on the dance floor and back to home again.
But if “The Kehlani World Tour” was a glimpse into the future, it was also a call into the past. Kehlani described the concert as a “family reunion,” and shouted out various members of her extended family in the audience throughout the night — from her team, composed of Kehlani’s friends from middle school, to her daughter, who they brought on stage to sing “Folded.”
“If there’s a lot of laughter, silliness and a lot of emotions tonight, bear with me because I’m just really happy to be home,” Kehlani said to the crowd.
The singer, who repeatedly called back to her past concerts, albums and iconic moments, also framed the concert as an homage to longtime fans, especially her “day ones.”
“I will just never ever forget my very first headline show at The New Parish in Downtown Oakland. I think the New Parish might fit like 200 people,” Kehlani said.
“I was there!” one fan yelled in response.
“So, to be here tonight, in what I think might be the biggest venue in the Bay Area besides a stadium, [it’s a] big deal,” Kehlani continued.
Perhaps because of her unique connection to the audience, Kehlani was unabashedly herself throughout the night. In exchange for that authenticity, however, the show felt choppy at times, failing to capitalize on  the momentum that openers Dixson, TheARTI$T, DJ Waseel and  Durand Bernarr built up. That choppiness was largely due to Kehlani’s frequent trips backstage for costume changes and interludes: Each interruption slightly dimmed the energy of the crowd.
The choppiness felt especially evident when Kehlani paused the show to introduce Ezra, a 19-year-old singer and the first artist signed to Kehlani’s new music label, Tsunami Mob. Despite it only being Ezra’s third time on stage, he was met with rambunctious applause and an army of flashlights — in large part thanks to Kehlani’s request that the crowd do so. More than anything, the moment felt like an ad. The audience, however, didn’t seem to mind — perhaps due to their fervent loyalty to the artist.
After Ezra’s appearance, Kehlani performed  “Toxic” and “Can I,” two fan favorites that captured her consistently melodic voice with a series of distinct riffs and “ooos” that only she could execute. Choreography also played a key role in energizing the night. Kehlani and her crew made full use of the double-decker stage — twisting a rhythmic jenga line up the stairs, twirling and spinning in pairs, sprawling themselves across railings. These moments came off more spontaneous than choppy, accentuating the club-themed, free-flowing framing of Kehlani’s show.
But while every moment might have seemed magical to longtime fans, Kehlani’s performance wasn’t for everyone. Despite the high-energy dancing, Kehlani left it to the crowd to belt out their favorite songs as she ad-libbed over a prerecorded track. This left more casual fans out of the loop. Coupled with the frequent interruptions and constant callbacks to her past, the performance lacked the consistency and broad appeal of a typical concert.
One of the more unexpected moments of the night came when Kehlani shared an intimate moment with a backup dancer, who she made out with and repeatedly pinned against the wall. (This scene lasted several minutes.)
Kehlani also paid tribute to R&B icons. She mixed “Distraction” with Janet Jackson’s “I Get Lonely,” playing Jackson’s music video in the background as her dancers replicated the choreography. It was a tasteful nod to one of her idols, and very much in theme with the concert’s broader journey down memory lane.
In a series of starts and stops, Kehlani offered a uniquely energetic and authentic performance — possibly puzzling some newcomers, but captivating an audience of loyal fans.
Hayden Thompson ’27 is an Executive Editor (Vol. 270). She was previously the Sports Managing Editor. Daniel Xu ’29 is the Vol. 270 Campus Life Editor for News. He was previously Vol. 269 Local Editor. Contact him at danxu ‘at’ stanford.edu.

articles.title_orig: Trump reverses course, says he won’t use taxpayer money for campaign-style ads
articles.title_zh: Trump reverses course, says he won’t use taxpayer money for campaign-style ads
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump has said he will stop using US taxpayer funds to pay for television ads he has fronted, following bipartisan pushback.
"The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," he said Monday on social media.
Trump said it is "a rather standard thing to do" but that he has decided to pay for the "Patriotic Ads" himself and with money he raised through his MAGA Inc super political action committee.
The ads, which praise the president and his policies, drew criticism and questions over their legality due to laws against using government money for political ads.
There have been more than a dozen ads over recent weeks, with some mentioning  Trump's tax cuts, US manufacturing and law and order. In them, Trump also vows to take action against the "deep state" and others he perceives as enemies.
In one ad, Trump says, "We will cast out the communists, Marxists, and fascists. We will throw off the sick political class that hates our country. We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all".
The ads come just ahead of the pivotal November midterm elections , when Democrats hope to take control of one or both chambers of the US Congress as polls continue to show Trump's approval rating falling. Midterm elections often serve as a verdict on how a president is doing - and typically the party of a sitting president tends to lose seats in Congress.
The White House has pushed back against criticism, calling the ads "educational" and saying they are not propaganda, but rather public service announcements.
They've pointed to previous administrations ads, like those under former Presidents Barack Obama on his healthcare plan and one under former President Joe Biden urging people to get Covid-19 vaccines.
But legal experts say past US government adverts have typically been about public health or national emergencies.
"It's difficult to see what legitimate government purpose is served by spending taxpayer dollars on ads whose only apparent purpose is to promote the president," legal ethics expert Margaret Dylus-Yukins has told the BBC.
Democratic Senator Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire introduced a measure, which was blocked by a Republican, denouncing the administration for using government funds for for the ads.
"It is the sense of the Senate that the advertisements promoting President Donald Trump that aired in September 2026, which included the direct language 'paid for by the U.S. Government,' should not be paid for by the United States government," the measure reads.
The ads have received criticism on both sides of the aisle.
Republican Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that while "I like the message ... it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars".
Senator John Kennedy, a Republican, said on CBS News on Sunday that politicians should not spend taxpayer funds on promotional ads.
"I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," the Louisiana lawmaker said.

articles.title_orig: World Teachers' Day
articles.title_zh: World Teachers' Day
articles.content_orig:
World Teachers’ Day is held annually on 5 October to celebrate all teachers around the globe. It commemorates the anniversary of the adoption of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers , which sets benchmarks regarding the rights and responsibilities of teachers, and standards for their initial preparation and further education, recruitment, employment, and teaching and learning conditions. The Recommendation concerning the Status of Higher-Education Teaching Personnel was adopted in 1997 to complement the 1966 Recommendation by covering teaching personnel in higher education. World Teachers’ Day has been celebrated since 1994.
It is a day to celebrate how teachers are transforming education but also to reflect on the support they need to fully deploy their talent and vocation, and to rethink the way ahead for the profession globally.
World Teachers’ Day is co-convened in partnership with the International Labour Organization, UNICEF and Education International.
In 2026, the Day marks the 60th anniversary of the 1966 ILO/UNESCO Recommendation concerning the Status of Teachers. Six decades on, as the Recommendation is being revised, new challenges have emerged for the profession, from digital technologies and climate change to inclusion, migration and displacement. These pressures affect several dimensions of the status of teachers: their symbolic status, when teaching is not sufficiently recognized or valued; their professional status, shaped by limited autonomy, support or voice in policy-making; and their material status, compromised by salaries, workloads and working environments that do not allow teachers to fully exercise their role.
Under the theme " Standing with teachers: 60 years of protecting the profession, advancing its status and shaping our futures ," the 2026 edition will centre on reviewing the current challenges related to teacher status and the strategies to address them, calling on society and policy-makers to protect, promote and elevate that status.
The global celebration organized at UNESCO Headquarters will feature high-level discussions on protecting and advancing the status of the teaching profession, as well as the award ceremony for the ninth edition of the UNESCO-Hamdan Prize for Teacher Development.
Other celebrations will take place around the world.
Joint Message from Mr Khaled El-Enany, Director-General of UNESCO, Mr Gilbert F. Houngbo, Director-General of the International Labour Organization, Ms Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, Mr David Edwards, General Secretary of Education International, on the occasion of World Teachers’ Day 5 October 2026.
"On this World Teachers’ Day, UNESCO, the ILO, UNICEF and Education International call on governments and partners to stand with teachers by advancing the status of the profession  and  ensuring  that  every  teacher,  everywhere,  is  empowered  to  help  build more inclusive, peaceful and sustainable societies."
5 October at UNESCO Headquarters, Paris, France

articles.title_orig: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.title_zh: SpaceX just locked up a NASA record no other U.S. spacecraft can touch
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX now owns every spot on the list of the five fastest trips a U.S. spacecraft has ever made to the International Space Station, and its newest entry beat the old mark by more than four hours.
Crew Dragon Grace docked to the forward port of the station’s Harmony module at 7:05 p.m. ET on October 1, just 7 hours and 55 minutes after lifting off from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral. NASA confirmed the milestone in a space station blog update , writing that the flight “marked the fastest launch‑to‑docking of a U.S. spacecraft in the history of the International Space Station.”
The previous U.S. record also belonged to Dragon. SpaceX’s uncrewed CRS-31 cargo mission reached the station in a little over 12 hours in November 2024. The fastest crewed trip before last week was Crew-11, which took 14 hours and 43 minutes in August 2025, according to Space.com .
A post that Elon Musk reposted on Monday filled out the rest of the ranking. Behind Crew-13, CRS-31 and Crew-11 sit Axiom’s Ax-2 mission at 15 hours and 35 minutes and NASA’s Crew-4 at 15 hours and 44 minutes. All five flew on Dragon.
SpaceX turned a heralding moment for Starship into its greatest
Crew-13 carried NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. NASA had projected a docking around 8 p.m. ET, as Teslarati reported the day before launch , and Dragon arrived nearly an hour early. Our launch day coverage noted that the flight was lined up to be the quickest Crew Dragon transit yet.
The speed came from timing more than hardware. SpaceX’s Julianna Scheiman said the station “was in an opportune spot in space,” which let Dragon start closing the gap almost immediately after reaching orbit. “This is close to the fastest it could be,” she added. Most Crew Dragon flights still take close to a day, using a series of Draco thruster burns to raise and phase their orbit before arrival.
Dragon’s next job at the station is a departure. NASA said Monday it is targeting 8:05 a.m. ET on Wednesday, October 7, for Crew-12 to undock, setting up a splashdown off the coast of California around 11:34 a.m. on Thursday. Clearing that port makes room for CRS-35, a cargo Dragon carrying the final set of iROSA solar arrays.
Dragon remains NASA’s only operational ride to the station while Boeing’s Starliner stays grounded, and the agency recently added Crew-15, Crew-16 and Crew-17 to SpaceX’s contract in a $946 million modification.
Gene has been obsessed with cars since before he could legally sit in the front seat. Writer, researcher, unofficial CS support, accountant, native suit guy when needed, and overall stick poker. He approaches every story the way he approaches a road trip: with too much enthusiasm, not enough planning, and a surprisingly good outcome. gene@teslarati.com
Tesla Full Self-Driving is really good. I have used it for over 76 percent of my driving since FSD v14 launched around this time last year, equating to about 76 percent of my miles using the suite. It’s truly the only way I prefer to travel, but admittedly I save some of the more fun drives for myself.
Even with all of the great things it has done for me, including saving me from being involved in an accident , there are still a handful of things that it needs to improve on. These issues recur from update to update, and while there have been some improvements, they still give me reasons to either soft or hard intervene.
A soft intervention means an adjustment that is needed without disengaging the suite, like manually using a turn signal to change lanes while the car still operates on FSD. What I’d consider to be a “hard intervention” is anything that requires me to disengage the suite altogether, like missing a turn or performing a maneuver I’m uncomfortable with. Of course, some hard interventions will be subjective.
Here are the five things I’d like to see Tesla really focus on through the final versions of v14 and hope to see completely improved with v15.
There are entirely too many instances of FSD traveling at a speed that is just totally outrageous. While some of these events can occur on Hurry Mode, I’ve even had issues with it on Standard from time to time, and despite wanting more aggressive maneuvers or a slight bit of urgency, I don’t want to worry about getting a ticket while doing it.
The two areas I notice it the most are in school zones and on local roads . When a Speed Limit changes from 45 to 35, FSD does not always slow down in a way that would appease local law enforcement. On Hurry, 52-55 is pretty standard for a rate of travel in a 45 MPH zone. When it changes to 35, FSD shows zero urgency to slow down to an appropriate speed.
School Zones have been a true pain point, and as recently as last week, I had an issue with it:
Threw FSD into Sloth to see how it handled this school zone. You can see well before I enter it, the car is traveling 34 MPH, one MPH under the limit.
Still not slowing down nearly enough.
@Tesla_AI, not 25, not 30…15 MPH in School Zones https://t.co/YQuQ8ydhKh
— TESLARATI (@Teslarati) September 29, 2026
Realistically, most Speed Limit issues are a soft intervention, as I simply scroll into a slower Speed Profile to get the car to slow down. School Zones are a hard intervention, as they require me to completely take over and travel at the posted 15 MPH limit. Even on Sloth, it simply does not get down to a low enough speed.
Parking is one thing that has really improved over time, but there are still some pretty considerable hoops Tesla needs to jump through to get it to a point where it can be unsupervised.
Parking preferences seem to be where a lot of these issues will be resolved, as most of my complaints come from the fact that the place FSD chooses to park are usually not where I would personally choose to park. This morning, for example, when I arrived at the gym, FSD chose to park next to a vehicle that was parked with its two tires in the spot that FSD picked.
This is a big reason Parking Preferences with Supervised FSD will be so valuable.
If possible, parking a little further away and being distant from people like this is worth it. https://t.co/3Ac71KQiQ3
— TESLARATI (@Teslarati) June 7, 2026
There were three spots in between that car and the nearest car, so FSD could have chosen the spot that would have given a one-spot buffer between the two vehicles. In a parking lot full of empty spots, don’t be that guy who parks next to a car.
Generally, parking performance is vastly improved from where it was a year ago; I rarely am adjusting how it pulls or backs into a spot on v14.3.10, but in earlier versions, I definitely had my problems. It’s gotten really good since, and this version has been the best in terms of parking performance. It’s more about the places FSD choose to park, and not necessarily the parking itself.
There are also no options or map data to allow you to choose a charger at a place like a grocery store if it offers charging. These are things that are a bit more complex, but they will be needed for unsupervised FSD operation.
Navigation was always going to be on this list, simply because it is one of the most inconsistent and mind-boggling things about FSD . Even after a year of intervening, sending voice notes, and overriding decisions, FSD still tries to take me out of my neighborhood the wrong way. You cannot turn left out of my neighborhood’s main entrance and exit, only right. Navigation still prompts a left turn out of my neighborhood’s main entrance and exit, instead of going around the neighborhood and exiting where a left turn is legal.
Tesla rolled out Preferred Routes with the Summer Update, and this has resolved some of the issues. I also found my own personal workaround:
🚨See if this cool Tesla Navigation Hack works for you!
I have used it to get out of my neighborhood legally with FSD, thus enabling completely hands-free drives! https://t.co/DlDsCQjxRI
— TESLA

Spanish PM Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election days after Congress voted against measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis
SÃ¡nchez's government had presented the measures in response to nationwide protests, triggered by the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home for failing to pay a sharp rent increase
The woman's rent was raised from â¬500 (Â£428; $572) to â¬2,650. It was later lowered to â¬1,650 - still â¬300 more than her monthly pension
SÃ¡nchez has been prime minister since 2018. Spain was not due to hold a general election until summer 2027 - here's what happened last time
Most polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election, which will take place on 29 November
SÃ¡nchez clearly wants to take the initiative - but it's going to be very tough for him to remain in power, writes Guy Hedgecoe in Madrid
Edited by Rorey Bosotti and Imogen James
Dan Woodland Live reporter
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has called a snap election on 29 November, bringing forward the vote which was originally scheduled for the summer of 2027.
The move follows weeks of protests across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants, sparked last month after an 87-year-old woman was evicted from her home in Madrid following a sharp rent increase.
SÃ¡nchezâs leftist coalition government failed to pass emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis on Friday - but is now expected to approve measures on Tuesday.
The premier's position has also been marred by multiple corruption investigations in recent months involving former members of government and even his wife and brother.
Opposition parties welcomed the snap election, with the leader of the conservative People's Party Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o declaring Spain will "at last" say "what it thinks", and leader of the far-right Spanish party Vox Santiago Abascal saying he was "glad" about the announcement.
Meanwhile, members of SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians expressed confidence that they would be re-elected and the prime minister would "pull off a comeback".
Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next vote, however they would be expected to need Vox's support to form a government.
This will be SÃ¡nchez's sixth election in 11 years, and if he is to remain in power, he needs to upset some tough odds, writes our reporter in Madrid .
We're ending our live coverage here, but you can read more in our news story .
With eight years in power, Pedro SÃ¡nchez is now Spain's second longest-serving prime minister in recent history.
His political career has been marked by dramatic twists and turns, including his resignation as Socialist Party leader in 2016 after losing the support of senior party figures. Just seven months later, he staged a remarkable comeback, returning to the leadership with the backing of grassroots members.
SÃ¡nchez has called an early election despite opinion polls suggesting he may struggle to secure enough support to remain in power.
Some analysts believe that focusing the campaign on Spain's housing crisis could help mobilise left-wing voters and steer the debate away from other challenges facing the government, including the situation in Ceuta and corruption allegations involving figures close to SÃ¡nchez.
It is not the first time SÃ¡nchez has taken a major political gamble. In 2023, he called a snap election after his party suffered heavy losses in regional and local elections.
Polls at the time also suggested he was heading for defeat.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, SÃ¡nchez ultimately secured enough parliamentary support to stay in office, thanks to agreements with left-wing parties and the backing of Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.
Opposition parties accused him of "selling out Spain" in order to remain in power.
The High Court of Justice of Madrid has rejected a request to disperse an encampment in Puerto Del Sol in the Spanish capital.
Protesters have set up tents in the famous square since 27 September, court documents show.
The court rejected the Community of Madrid's request for police to clear the square on Monday. A new hearing is expected to take place on Wednesday.
A trade union has also called on people to continue protesting in the street against issues with wages and housing ahead of the snap election.
The general secretary of the Workers' Commissions (CCOO) trade union confederation, Unai Sordo, says: "We must continue with a path of mobilisation, of street protests as we had announced, regarding wages and housing measures, and that will be our course in the coming months."
People in the streets of Madrid say they welcome news of the snap election called by Prime Minister SÃ¡nchez this morning.
âI think itâs good given the situation thatâs arisen", Raomon Diaz tells Reuters.
"Young people have been given little prospect for the future. And Iâd like to see a truly left-wing government finally come to power.â
Protester Florencio Diaz described the election announcement as a "great victory for the protests in the streets".
Florencio Diaz says Spanish people are struggling with the cost of living
"Weâre in a very difficult situation, with the cost of living rising and, above all, the abuse taking place in the housing market", he says.
However, Sandra - who is also protesting against Spain's housing crisis - expressed reservations about what the future holds.
âTo be honest, Iâm a bit worried about what might happen. But itâs certainly true that with the government we have, things arenât moving forward.â
Sandra says she's worried about Spain's future
The Spanish government is expected to approve measures on Tuesday aimed at tackling the housing crisis that parliament rejected last week .
The measures include a suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030 and an automatic renewal of rental contracts.
The government failed to pass them last week, after they were opposed by the People's Party (PP), Vox, and Junts.
Once the government approves the measures, SÃ¡nchez has 30 days to get them ratified. But the Madrid-based political newspaper Moncloa suggests that the prime minister's calling of a snap election could help him do this without congress, as parliament will be dissolved before those 30 days are up.
When congress isn't sitting, ratifying the measures falls to a committee which has a more favourable political make-up for SÃ¡nchez and doesn't require support from the Junts party, the newspaper says.
The deputy prime minister of Spain Yolanda DÃ­az has called for rent caps and a shortened workday
Members of Pedro SÃ¡nchez's cabinet and regional politicians have continued to react to the Spanish snap election.
The deputy prime minister of Spain, Yolanda DÃ­az - who is part of the Sumar movement - says in a post on Bluesky: "We are going to win again."
DÃ­az says the group will cap rents, shorten the workday and raise the minimum wage.
Health minister MÃ³nica GarcÃ­a says in a post on X that the "Spanish people will rise to the occasion and prevail over the resentment of international hate".
Meanwhile Justice minister FÃ©lix BolaÃ±os says on X that the prime minister "will pull off a comeback" and leave the People's Party and Vox "without a government".
Catalan President Salvador Illa Roca says elections will be a "moment to decide between continuing to advance or going backwards". "Catalonia will stand with Pedro SÃ¡nchez," he adds.
SÃ¡nchez celebrates beside his wife Begona Gomez, after winning the general elections in 2019
These will be the sixth elections that Pedro SÃ¡nchez has contested as Socialist leader since 2015.
He has only won two of those - the 2019 ballot which was repeated after being inconclusive - and yet he has been in power since winning a no-confidence motion against his conservative predecessor, Mariano Rajoy, in 2018.

articles.title_orig: Pixel 11 users might have Gemini call friends and family members
articles.title_zh: Pixel 11 users might have Gemini call friends and family members
articles.content_orig:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
How many phone calls have you put off just because dealing with another person can feel so tedious? AI has already promised to automate plenty of thankless tasks in our lives, and for a certain kind of person, maybe one of the most appealing possibilities there is making phone calls on our behalf. We just saw Google introduce Call for Me on the Pixel 11 series, and now we’re already getting an early look at what could be a big new expansion for what it’s capable of doing.
You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.
While Gemini is capable of dialing calls to connect you to pretty much anyone, if you want Gemini to actually do the talking on your behalf, Call for Me is built to handle calls to businesses in specific. It will patiently sit through hold music, and offer help with tasks like making reservations.
That sounds great, but it’s also fairly limited in its scope. If Gemini is a general-purpose language model, why not let it spread its wings a little bit and expand Call for Me to also support personal calls to our friends and family? Poking around some new updates, we’re finding early evidence for what looks like just that:
As you can see from those “Mom” and “John” examples on the introductory screen, this version of Call for Me would clearly be equipped to handle interactions beyond those with businesses. It does sound like Gemini may be a bit limited in what it’s able to do during these calls, largely just delivering messages or making basic inquiries, but we see how this could be really handy for things like dealing with people who are bad at responding to text messages.
Not everyone wants to talk to a computer, though. Thankfully, it looks like Gemini will also be giving people the ability to opt out of receiving these calls.
Alongside this expanded Call for Me functionality, we’re also able to pull up some granular permissions for app actions in that new write/delete section you see in the third screen above.
We’re able to surface similar menus for other apps, but so far this component still feels very much like a work in progress, with the options not properly functioning in our testing.
As for the expanded Call for Me functionality, we can’t say when Google might actually make this available — assuming it even does — but we’re already putting together some lists of contacts we’d love to try it with.

articles.title_orig: Digital Silk Road: China's Gulf Bet Meets US AI Chip Terms
articles.title_zh: Digital Silk Road: China's Gulf Bet Meets US AI Chip Terms
articles.content_orig:
Choose your language to begin.
Chinese direct investment in the United Arab Emirates exceeded $12 billion in 2025, according to the “2025 Statistical Bulletin of China’s Outward Foreign Direct Investment” released last month. Capital flows into Saudi Arabia expanded as well, cementing the kingdom as the second-largest destination for Chinese capital in the Middle East and North Africa.
This surge comes as Riyadh and Abu Dhabi execute a delicate geopolitical balancing act. The MBN Great Powers Index places both Gulf states solidly in the pro-U.S. camp, anchored by decades of military ties with Washington. Yet both nations also rank at the top of the Index for engaging with both, a strategic hedge as their commercial and diplomatic ties with Beijing expand.
Technology is where that balancing act is hardest to sustain, because it runs straight into U.S. policy. Washington will give Gulf countries access to its most advanced AI chips only if they remove Chinese technology from their core networks. That leaves Riyadh and Abu Dhabi weighing Chinese investment against the American chips they need to build their digital economies.
This past September alone, Chinese tech giant Alibaba Cloud pledged to scale up its data center capacity and expand localized AI services across the UAE. Meanwhile, Tencent and Alibaba’s Ant International announced new cross-border digital payment solutions in Saudi Arabia. In Riyadh, hardware giant Lenovo unveiled its first Saudi-manufactured laptop produced at its massive 49-acre (200,000-square-meter) facility, part of a $2 billion deal with Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund.
For Beijing, this digital-economy push aligns directly with its Digital Silk Road, the technology-focused extension of the Belt and Road Initiative designed to export Chinese telecommunications, cloud architecture, AI models and surveillance systems to a global market.
“This initiative is vital as it helps China expand and promote its goods and services globally through direct investments,” says Dr. Jamal Zarrouk, Managing Director of Boulder Economics Consultancy in Dubai.
“China possesses the capital, technical expertise, and industrial capacity required for large-scale infrastructure rebuilds, making it a primary long-term partner across the Middle East,” he adds, regarding long-term regional development,
In the Gulf, this strategy has found fertile ground. Both Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 and the UAE’s Centennial 2071 require massive investments in digital infrastructure, advanced computing, and deep capital investment.
MBN has tracked Chinese technology firms’ presence in the Gulf since 2010.
Before 2015, China’s technology footprint in the Gulf was limited almost entirely to basic telecommunications hardware sales from firms like Huawei and ZTE.
Following the 2015 launch of the Digital Silk Road, Chinese tech projects in the UAE jumped sixteen-fold to 81 active initiatives. The footprint expanded far beyond telecom into surveillance networks, AI applications, e-payments, and robotics, bringing in major players like Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, DJI, Yitu and Ant International Group.
Saudi Arabia recorded a similar sevenfold expansion to 56 projects, where artificial intelligence and telecom now stand on equal footing, and renewable energy is being boosted. Chinese solar manufacturers LONGi Green Energy and JinkoSolar took equity positions in Saudi solar parks, while SenseTime entered into a $206.5 million joint AI venture with the Saudi Company for Artificial Intelligence.
Yet this deepening digital relationship lands directly in the crosshairs of great-power competition. Affordable Chinese 5G networks and cloud centers powered the Gulf’s early digital push, but the shift toward gigawatt-scale AI compute has reshaped the geopolitical rules.
Washington views Chinese hardware in critical infrastructure as a major security threat and has laid down a strict condition on access to its most advanced chips: Gulf nations must first eliminate Chinese technology from their core networks.
That condition reveals the limits of the two countries’ strategic hedging. Washington approved Microsoft’s landmark $1.5 billion investment in Abu Dhabi AI firm G42 in 2024 only after G42 agreed to strip out its Huawei hardware and adopt U.S. technology standards.
Replacing Chinese infrastructure with Western chips and cloud systems carries high financial and operational costs. For example, G42 tore out $150 million worth of Huawei equipment and hired an outside auditor to confirm the cleanup. But both Gulf states appear willing to pay the price to guarantee access to cutting-edge AI processing power. Saudi Arabia raised its pledged U.S. investment from $600 million to $1 trillion in 2025.
In July, the UAE secured Country Group A:5 status from the U.S. Commerce Department for high-tech imports. The tier is generally reserved for close U.S. allies and lets approved Emirati government agencies and companies receive controlled American technologies without a license. In Saudi Arabia, state-backed AI firm HUMAIN is constructing high-performance data centers alongside American partners like Nvidia, AMD, and Cisco under strict U.S. export guidelines.
The result is a complex geopolitical triangle. Washington remains the indispensable security guarantor and undisputed leader in advanced AI silicon and defense technology. Beijing, meanwhile, offers cost-effective infrastructure, green technology, and massive commercial scale without political strings attached.
Riyadh and Abu Dhabi demonstrate that while frontier AI hardware demands strict supply-chain loyalty, they can still leverage their vast wealth and energy resources to remain central power brokers in a multipolar world.
How far that balance can stretch is the open question. Chinese capital is still flowing into the Gulf’s digital economy, while the region’s AI ambitions rest on American chips and the conditions Washington attaches to them.

articles.title_orig: Scandal-scarred televangelist Jim Bakker dead at 86: ‘Finished his race with faith’
articles.title_zh: Scandal-scarred televangelist Jim Bakker dead at 86: ‘Finished his race with faith’
articles.content_orig:
Disgraced televangelist Jim Bakker, who was as known for his scandals — including a $279,000 hush-money settlement to his church secretary — as he was his preachings, has died, his widow announced Monday. He was 86.
“It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening,” Lori Bakker wrote on “The Jim Bakker Show” Facebook page .
“For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry.”
Bakker rose to prominence after founding “The PTL Club,” a Christian television show he co-hosted with his first wife, Tammy Faye Bakker, from 1974 to 1989.
The couple’s multimillion-dollar South Carolina empire included the PTL Satellite Network, a Christian cable platform, and the Heritage USA theme park, which drew millions of visitors before shuttering in 1989.
But the kingdom crumbled in 1987, after a $279,000 hush-money payment Jim Bakker made to church secretary Jessica Hahn came to light. She accused the popular preacher of raping her in 1980.
Bakker denied the rape allegations — though he admitted to having sex with Hahn, insisting it had been consensual.
“Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world,” Lori Bakker’s statement added.
“Our family is grieving and we ask for your prayers and privacy during this time. Jim finished his race with faith. His voice, his vision, and his legacy will never be forgotten.”
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.title_zh: World Bank warns of AI concentration risks as it lifts East Asia and Pacific growth outlook to 4.5%
articles.content_orig:
The World Bank has raised its growth forecast for the East Asia and Pacific region on the back of artificial intelligence-related exports, while warning that its reliance on the AI boom leaves it vulnerable to a potential global tech spending reversal.
The region includes 23 economies, including China, Vietnam, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand.
The EAP economy is expected to expand 4.5% this year, 0.3 percentage point more than the bank projected in April, according to its latest report released Tuesday. Growth is forecast to ease to 4.4% in 2027 and 4.3% in 2028. Vietnam received the biggest forecast upgrade among major economies of the region, up 1.1 percentage point to 7.4%.
The region's strength, however, is highly dependent on AI-related manufacturing and exports. Trade growth, excluding AI-related goods, has been "weak or negative," the bank said. Those products accounted for more than half of the export growth in most of the region's economies and more than 70% in Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam.
China, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam shipped $1.4 trillion of AI-related goods in the 12 months through April, according to the report.
Official data showed that South Korea's exports grew 83.5% in September to a record $120.9 billion , with chips making up half of those shipments. Reflecting the dominance of semiconductors in the country's market, the World Bank highlighted that just two chipmakers — Samsung and SK Hynix — accounted for 43% of the benchmark Kospi index's value as of end-April.
The AI risk is on the spending side. AI-related capital expenditure has reached about 6% of U.S. GDP, similar to the 2000 peak in information-technology investment, and the current cycle "has risen faster than either previous cycle and is still gaining speed," the bank said.
The Bank for International Settlements in its annual economic report in June had warned that the boom's scale and pace bears resemblance to the dot-com frenzy of the 1990s and other "manias."
The financing driving the boom is also less transparent. Of the $2.9 trillion in AI capex planned for 2025-2028, $800 billion is expected to come from private credit, the bank said, where AI-related lending rose to 34% of activity in 2025 from an 18% average over the prior five years. Private credit portfolios have experienced markdowns, outflows and defaults this year.
Private credit markets are "less visible, and have not been tested by a severe downturn," the bank said.
That said, the AI boom supported by abundant liquidity could slow due to the latest tightening of financial conditions as major central banks raise rates for the first time since 2023, according to the report. The U.S. Federal Reserve raised rates last month , its first increase in more than three years, and signaled one more to hike this year.
A correction may not necessarily mean a bust for the AI supercycle, but that investment "had run ahead of realized demand," the organization said.
A slowdown by 1 percentage point in U.S. growth cuts other emerging-market growth by an estimated 0.6 percentage point, with the hit to investment about twice as large, the bank said. "A slowdown concentrated in AI would be material for East Asia because of the region's prominence in the AI supply chain."
Bank funding is the broadest exposure. Foreign-currency-denominated liabilities of banks appeared significant in some countries — 29.2% of GDP in Malaysia, 20.7% in the Philippines.
Taiwan's statistics bureau recently raised its 2026 growth forecast to 11% from 9.6% on AI demand, while warning in June that "if the high-tech sector faces headwinds, the negative impact on the local economy could be bigger than expected."

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | KKR Strikes Deal to Buy Private-Capital Fund Administrator Gen II
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | KKR Strikes Deal to Buy Private-Capital Fund Administrator Gen II
articles.content_orig:
Hg, the Manager of HgCapital Trust plc ("HgT"), today announces a full exit of Gen II Fund Services, LLC ("Gen II"), a global leader in private capital fund administration, to KKR.
The terms of the transaction have not been disclosed.
HgT, whose shares are listed on the London Stock Exchange, gives private and institutional investors the opportunity to participate in all Hg's investments.
This transaction values HgT's investment in Gen II at approximately £71 million. This would represent an uplift of £18 million (34% or 4.0 pence per share) over the carrying value of £53 million in the pro-forma Net Asset Value ("NAV") of HgT at 31 August 2026.

KKR to Acquire Gen II Fund Services for More Than $5 Billion from Hg and General Atlantic
NEW YORK, October 6 - KKR, a leading global investment firm, today announced the agreement to acquire Gen II Fund Services, LLC ("Gen II"), a global leader in private capital fund administration, for a total enterprise value of $5.1 billion. KKR is acquiring Gen II from Hg, General Atlantic and other minority investors through its Core Private Equity strategy. Led by CEO Steven Millner, Gen II has built an experienced leadership team that will continue to lead the company.
The strategic partnership with KKR is intended to support Gen II's next phase of growth as private market managers increasingly seek scaled, technology-enabled solutions to navigate more complex fund structures, investor needs and regulatory requirements. KKR plans to work alongside Gen II's management team to support the company's continued expansion in the U.S. and internationally, broaden its capabilities across asset classes and services and invest further in proprietary technology and AI-enabled solutions. KKR also plans to help implement a broad-based employee ownership program, giving all Gen II employees the opportunity to participate in the company's future growth.
Gen II is a leading fund administrator serving the private markets industry, providing fund administration services to more than 275 investment managers representing over $2 trillion in assets, alongside a growing suite of tax, compliance, treasury and technology-enabled solutions. Gen II was founded in 2009 by Steven Millner, Steven Alecia and Norman Leben, and has built a 17-year track record of service excellence and strong client retention.
General Atlantic and Hg co-led an investment in Gen II in 2020. Since then, the company has expanded its U.S. and European footprint, broadened its offerings and quadrupled revenue and EBITDA through strong organic growth and four strategic acquisitions.
"Gen II is exactly the type of financial services business we look for - a sophisticated sector leader with exceptional client relationships and a differentiated service model," said Chris Harrington, Partner at KKR. "The company has become the gold standard in fund administration through its white-glove service model and founder-led culture and is well positioned to benefit from the structural growth of private markets. We see significant opportunity to support the team as they expand globally and deepen their capabilities."
"At Gen II, our mission is to provide private markets managers with industry-leading fund administration delivered with unmatched client service and responsiveness," said Steven Millner, Co-Founder and CEO of Gen II. "KKR's ownership culture and long-term approach align perfectly with our vision for the future. Their resources and expertise will help our exceptional team capture the significant opportunities ahead to accelerate growth and continue to be at the forefront of our industry to serve our clients."
Justin von Simson, Partner and Stefanie Raiola, Director at Hg, said: "Gen II has become one of the most respected platforms in private capital administration, and we're proud of the role we've played alongside management and General Atlantic. Together we built a leadership team equipped to run a much larger, global business, and partnered on four acquisitions that took Gen II into new sectors, asset classes and services. Our value creation team worked closely with the business on its commercial strategy and the build-out of its Digital Solutions suite, including the launch of its GenVū client portal. We also drove AI and automation across client onboarding and bank reconciliations, capabilities now led by Gen II's own team. KKR is a natural home for Gen II's next chapter, and we wish the team every success."
Aaron Goldman, Managing Director, Global Head of Enterprise Technology and Caroline Woodworth, Managing Director, Head of Financial Services for EMEA at General Atlantic, said: "In Gen II, we saw a business with deep client relationships, an ambitious team and a culture of innovation and growth. Over the past six years, together with Hg, we have partnered closely with Steve and the management team to develop Gen II from a founder-led partnership into a true global platform. We have worked alongside the team on transformative strategic acquisitions that expanded Gen II's international footprint and broadened its service offering, invested in product and technology advancements and opened our network to introduce new managers to the business. Today, Gen II is a trusted partner to many of the world's largest GPs, and we look forward to seeing the team build on this progress as the company enters its next phase of growth with KKR."
KKR has extensive experience investing in and growing leading financial services businesses, reflected most recently with USI Insurance Services, which KKR announced an agreement to sell subject to closing conditions, and Integrated Specialty Coverages (ISC), which KKR exited in 2025. The firm has followed the fund administration sector for years and sees strong cultural alignment with Gen II's entrepreneurial, growth-oriented approach.
The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals and is expected to close in 2027.
Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP served as legal advisor to KKR. Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Robert W. Baird and UBS Investment Bank acted as financial advisors to the sellers, and Kirkland & Ellis LLP acted as legal advisor to the sellers.

The Supreme Court on Monday opened its new term by hearing arguments in a lawsuit filed in state court by the city and county of Boulder, Colorado, seeking to hold two major energy companies responsible for their alleged role in climate change and its impact. After nearly two hours of debate in Suncor Energy Inc. v. County Commissioners of Boulder County , it wasn’t clear whether a majority of the justices agreed with the energy companies that federal law prohibits Boulder’s claims. With Justice Samuel Alito recused from the dispute, a 4-4 tie would leave the ruling by the Colorado Supreme Court, allowing Boulder’s case to move forward, in place.
Monday’s argument was the latest chapter in an eight-year-old battle that began when Boulder filed a lawsuit in a state court in Colorado against two energy companies: Suncor, a subsidiary of one of Canada’s largest energy companies, which operates the only two oil refineries in Colorado; and ExxonMobil, the largest energy company in the United States. It is seeking compensation for some of the costs that it has incurred as a result of the alleged effects of climate change – for example, protecting its own property as well as that of its residents. Boulder contends that both energy companies have long deceived the public about the effects of climate change and the role of fossil-fuel products in creating those effects; it also contended that the companies played a role in climate change by producing, refining, and marketing fossil fuels.
After their efforts to move the case to federal court failed, the energy companies asked the state trial court to dismiss the case, but it turned down that request. The Colorado Supreme Court then agreed to decide whether Boulder’s state-law claims were trumped by federal law. It concluded that they were not, and its claims could go forward. The companies came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to weigh in, which they agreed in February to do.
Representing the energy companies, lawyer Kannon Shanmugam described Boulder’s claims as an “unprecedented effort to use state law to regulate global conduct.” The Constitution, he said, bars the application of state law to “certain inherently federal areas,” and the Supreme Court has long held that federal law governs interstate-pollution claims. Moreover, he added, a state cannot regulate out-of-state conduct “based solely on attenuated effects” that it might have within the state.
Chief Justice John Roberts appeared skeptical, however. He suggested to both Shanmugam and Sarah Harris, the principal deputy U.S. solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the energy companies, that it was not uncommon for lawsuits to be based on conduct that occurs outside a state but has broad “effects,” including within the state. He asked Harris “what makes this situation different from those” other cases in which the court allowed lawsuits to proceed in state court.
Harris answered that, unlike those lawsuits, Colorado would ban the production of fossil fuels anywhere in the country.
Roberts did not appear persuaded. “That’s a question of relief” for Colorado, “and what might be available,” he said. It did not, in his view, necessarily seem to go to the question of whether Colorado could bring the lawsuit at all.
Justice Elena Kagan also seemed dubious of the energy companies’ arguments. She told Shanmugam that Boulder’s “suit appears to be based on the old 1990s tobacco suits,” as well as more recent lawsuits against opioid manufacturers. Were those lawsuits also trumped by federal law, she asked?
Shanmugam pushed back, describing the tobacco and opioid lawsuits as different. He stressed that the injury at the center of Boulder’s case “is not suffered by the Colorado consumer in the traditional sense.” He then pointed back to the principle that federal law has traditionally applied to claims involving interstate air and water pollution.
Kagan remained doubtful, asking Shanmugam to point to the support for that argument in the text of the Constitution or federal law or in the Supreme Court’s cases. “Where,” she finally asked, “is the[re] anything for that?”
Representing Boulder, lawyer Kevin Russell echoed Roberts’ point, telling the justices that states have long had the power to provide court remedies for injuries that occur within their borders even when the conduct that caused those injuries occurred elsewhere. Applying state law, he said, has never been interpreted as projecting that law nationwide. And he emphasized that Congress has the authority to pass laws that preempt state laws if and when it wants to.
Russell faced tough questioning, however, from Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was the member of the court most supportive of the energy companies’ position. He pointed to a series of Supreme Court cases that, in his words, “make crystal-clear that interstate air and water pollution are matters for federal law” unless Congress specifies otherwise. In Kavanaugh’s view, those cases mean that state law generally does not apply to claims like Boulder’s, and Congress could believe that interstate-pollution issues are federal issues – and that it therefore does not need to pass new legislation to say so explicitly.
Several justices expressed concern about the possibility that allowing Boulder’s lawsuit to go forward would open the floodgates to even more cases in other states around the country. Justice Clarence Thomas asked Russell to describe any principles that might restrict whom state and local governments could sue.
Russell cited constraints on a state’s jurisdiction over particular defendants and a constitutional doctrine (known as the dormant commerce clause) that bars states from discriminating against out-of-state defendants, among other things, as possible limiting principles.
That prompted Thomas to ask whether, under Boulder’s theory, state and local governments could also sue “large retailers” of fossil fuels.
Russell acknowledged that “[n]othing in our theory prevents that,” but he added that “when lots of people act together to cause widespread harm, it is not uncommon for multiple different defendants to be potentially liable.”
Justice Amy Coney Barrett also sought to test the limits of Boulder’s theory, asking Russell whether Colorado could pass a law that sought to cap greenhouse-gas emissions in the other 49 states as well.
Russell agreed that such a law would be prohibited and sought to distinguish that scenario from Boulder’s lawsuit. He emphasized that, with the lawsuit, Boulder wasn’t trying to directly regulate the energy companies’ actions. The lawsuit, he argued, “doesn’t prohibit them from engaging in the conduct.” Instead, he said, “[i]t requires them to internalize a portion of the cost of their activities by paying for some of the damage that those activities inflict.”
Shanmugam picked up on these concerns in his rebuttal, telling the court that the “breadth of Boulder’s theory here is astonishing.” Indeed, he suggested, it would mean that on an upcoming visit to Colorado, Boulder could sue him “for refilling my car and thereby contributing to global climate change.” Moreover, he suggested, it would not be only state and local governments who could sue under Boulder’s theory, but “[a]ny individual who has suffered the effects of climate change.” “Climate change,” he concluded, “is certainly one of the most pressing issues of the day, but we would submit that this is exactly the wrong way to go about resolving it.”
However the court opts to resolve the case, the justices devoted relatively little time to whether the Supreme Court has the power to consider the energy companies’ appeal at all – a question that the justices had asked the litigants to address when they agreed to take up the case earlier this year. This means we can start getting more spaghetti computer models about this disturbance.
WESH 2 First Warning Weather Meteorologist Cam Tran said the area of interest could become a tropical depression by the end of the week.

Wind shear is forecast to increase across the northern Gulf later in the week. This could prevent anything stronger from developing, keeping the season hurricane-free.

articles.title_orig: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.title_zh: U.S. officials seeking details of reported Russian plague death, quarantines
articles.content_orig:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.title_zh: Teenager loses hand in blast amid French school protest clashes
articles.content_orig:
A teenager has lost a hand in a grenade explosion as the return of school protests in France sparked clashes with police.
The 15-year-old was seriously injured in the northern city of Lens on Monday. Unverified police reports said that he had picked up a stun grenade.
France had said it would close up to 500 schools as demonstrations over understaffed and rundown schools entered a third week. Critics have called for the authorities to temper their response to the protests amid claims of disproportionate police force being used against minors.
The youth, injured near the Auguste-Behal vocational high school, was taken to hospital in Lille. His life is not in danger, according to Pas-de-Calais prefect Francois-Xavier Lauch.
A police union source reported that the student appeared to have picked up a rubber sting-ball or ”de-encirclement” grenade, fired by riot police, in an attempt to throw it back before it exploded in his hand, the AFP news agency reported.
Public prosecutors said investigators have yet to establish whether the teenager picked up the device or whether it landed on him.
They have referred the case to police internal affairs, which is now engaged in six investigations into serious injuries that have occurred during the student protests.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray described the teenager’s injury as “humanly dramatic” but said he would not comment further until the circumstances were established. He said 190 students had been injured since the protests began.
The Lens incident has added to scrutiny of police tactics during the demonstrations. Amnesty International France has criticised what it described as disproportionate police force against minors, saying it was alarmed by reports of students being hit with batons and subjected to tear gas and rubber-bullet fire known as LBDs.
The rights group said many of those taking part were minors under 18 and called on authorities to ensure policing methods were proportionate and compatible with France’s human rights obligations.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told CNews television on Monday that the priority was to “restore order”.
The Education Ministry said 589 schools had been disrupted on Monday, down from 735 on Friday, according to figures reported by Le Monde. Earlier estimates had suggested between 400 and 500 of France’s 3,700 high schools could be fully or partially closed.
Nationwide demonstrations erupted at the end of last month at a high school in a Parisian suburb over teacher shortages, before spreading nationwide.
Geffray said on Sunday that 24 schools had been burned or ransacked during the protests, with 78 teaching staff injured.
Reporting from a high school in Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said students had set up a barricade in front of the building’s entrance using dustbins and fences.
“We’ve been talking to many of the students who have come out here, and what they say is that they are here to have their demands heard by the government. They say they are fed up with teacher shortages and often don’t have teachers for subjects like maths and English,” she said.
“They also tell us that they’re here to demonstrate to show solidarity with other high school students who are in perhaps poorer areas in France with less adequate facilities or in France’s overseas territories. They say all young people should have an equal right to education,” Butler added.
Unrest and confrontations were reported in several cities on Monday. News channel BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille, tear gas being used in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being set alight as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalised Lycee Vauquelin in Paris’s 13th district, said a “very determined” group wearing hoods and masks attacked her school.
While police and firefighters quickly put out the fire and the school was evacuated, suspending classes, Zerbib said it was “very violent and happened very quickly”, adding that the attack lasted 15-20 minutes.
Since September 28, about 5,000 people, mostly teenagers, have been arrested across the country and dozens have been injured.
Teachers and members of the public have also been attacked, while property damage costs are estimated in the tens of millions of euros.
Student unions have called for national demonstrations on Tuesday.

articles.title_orig: Aiming at fuel costs, Trump opens tax-exempt ‘red dye’ diesel to all drivers
articles.title_zh: Aiming at fuel costs, Trump opens tax-exempt ‘red dye’ diesel to all drivers
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order Monday that is intended to help bring down sky-high diesel prices by allowing anyone to purchase tax-exempt “red dye” diesel.
“Tonight I’m going to sign a historic executive order to officially waive the off-road requirement and allow anyone to purchase tax-free red dye diesel for any reason,” Trump said at a rally in Nebraska after he told the audience he didn’t “know what the hell” red dye diesel is.
Taxes on diesel are based on how it is used. Road diesel meant for long-distance transport is subject to federal and state taxes. But diesel intended for farm vehicles and machinery is typically tax-free and dyed red, so regulators and inspectors can tell it apart from road diesel.
A White House fact sheet about the order said Trump has directed the secretaries of transportation, agriculture, defense and the Treasury to work on expanding access to tax-exempt diesel and encouraging states to suspend their diesel taxes.
Diesel fuel prices have spiked because of the war in Iran, but dyed diesel fuel is cheaper because it’s exempt from federal and state excise taxes.
Trump said the order will save typical truckers more than $100 every time they fill their tanks and drive down the costs of other goods, including groceries.
Trump made the announcement at a rally in reliably Republican Nebraska, where GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts faces an unexpectedly strong challenge from independent Dan Osborn.
Osborn is one of several Senate candidates who could flip seats long held by Republicans. Voters in both parties this year cite high gas prices and the rising cost of living as their top issues.
In that frustrated, anti-incumbent environment, the Trump administration has been under intense pressure from Republican candidates to do something, anything, in response to diesel prices that have risen by more than 30% in recent months.
Diesel hit all-time high price Sept. 22 of $6.52 per gallon, according to AAA data. Since then, average prices have declined slightly.
But all told, since the Iran war began Feb. 28, the price of a gallon of diesel in the U.S. has risen by more than 70%.
The surge in prices is far more than the almost 45% spike in Brent crude oil and the 50% spike in unleaded gas prices over the same period.
While the war in Iran has disrupted oil shipments across the Middle East, it is the recent escalation of the Ukraine war that set U.S. diesel prices on a separate path from other energy commodities.
Ukraine’s successful targeting of Russian oil refineries with drones forced the Kremlin to ban exports of diesel at least through the end of this month.
In a bid to slow rising prices, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced last month that the Transportation Department would ease rules governing how many consecutive hours fuel truck drivers can work. The temporary adjustment is set to last 90 days.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.
Christina Wilkie is the senior editor of the NBC News Business and Economy Unit.
