articles.title_orig: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces expel Houthi rebels from several areas around key strait, officials say
articles.title_zh: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces expel Houthi rebels from several areas around key strait, officials say
articles.content_orig:
Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have "secured" the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the southern end of the Red Sea, at the start of a major offensive against the Iran-backed Houthi movement.
The Yemeni military also said in a statement that National Shield, Giants Brigades and Tihama Resistance forces had captured the Red Sea city of Mokha on Monday afternoon with the help of Saudi air strikes.
But in conflicting reports, unnamed Yemeni government and military sources told news agencies Reuters and AFP that the forces have only reached the city's outskirts.
The Houthis said they had struck Riyadh's international airport and other sites, but did not comment regarding Mokha.
Saudi Arabia condemned the attacks and reiterated calls for the UN Security Council's permanent members to support Yemen's government.
Four government sources told Reuters that Yemeni forces had reached the outskirts of Mokha late on Monday, and that Houthi fighters were now retreating.
Government military sources who spoke to AFP would not confirm the capture of the city, but said "our forces took control of the Dhubab military airfield and cut the road linking the Dhubab district to the Bab al-Mandab area".
Earlier, the Yemeni military also said its forces had seized Dhubab airport, 45km (27 miles) to the south, and were besieging Houthi fighters inside the nearby town.
Houthi-run media denied reports that government forces had also made advances in Dhubab.
The government said operations had also begun on other fronts on Monday, including the capital Sanaa, which fell to the Houthis at the start of the civil war 12 years ago.
Meanwhile, a Saudi-led military coalition said its fighter jets were providing "round-the-clock" air support to the pro-government forces and had destroyed 324 "high-value" targets since the start of the offensive.
Turkey and Pakistan, allies of Saudi Arabia, held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday and agreed to rapidly deploy military forces in Saudi Arabia in an invocation of their Mecca defence pact, according to a joint statement shared by Pakistan's foreign ministry.
Saudi air strikes killed a schoolgirl and a woman in the Sanhan and Saawan districts of Sanaa on Monday, according to Houthi-run Al Masirah TV.
Houthi spokesman Mohammed Abdul Salam said Saudi Arabia was committing "dozens of massacres" and that it must "bear all the consequences".
The Houthi-run Humanitarian Operations Co-ordination Centre warned civilian airlines that Saudi airspace, except for the skies above the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, was no longer safe because it had become "a theatre of operations".
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia and said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", in a statement to AFP.
On Sunday, the head of Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council announced the beginning of an offensive, dubbed Operation Yemen Dawn, aimed at retaking all territory held by the Houthis.
Rashad al-Alimi insisted that all opportunities for de-escalation had been exhausted and called on all forces to carry out their assigned missions "until the country is liberated from the grip of the Houthi terrorist militia".
It came after the Houthis reportedly cut a mountain road near the south-western city of Taiz, effectively leaving government forces and residents there surrounded.
The Houthis also said they had launched ballistic missiles and drones at oil facilities belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh and the Khurais area of Saudi Arabia in retaliation for dozens of Saudi strikes on their territory.
In addition to the strikes on Riyadh's international airport, the Houthis attacked an Aramco oil refinery, and Abha airport, as well as other sites, according to Yemen's Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree in a statement on Telegram.
According to BBC Verify, satellite imagery from Saturday shows thick, dark smoke coming from the site of a strike at the Aramco Riyadh Refinery, in the city's south-east.
A similar plume of smoke can be seen rising from the Khurais Central Processing Facility as well as from a potential strike point in satellite imagery from Sunday.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.
A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
Last month, the Houthis launched a surprise offensive along Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and quickly ousted pro-government forces from areas overlooking the Bab al-Mandab Strait, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim (Mayyun) Island.
They said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.
However, the seizure of the strait contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
At least 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry.
The UN says another 197,000 people have been displaced.

articles.title_orig: Students vandalize Cornell building over handling of gang-rape allegations
articles.title_zh: Students vandalize Cornell building over handling of gang-rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
Hall housing Michael Kotlikoff’s office spray painted as demonstrators demand resignation of college president
Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
Mass protests erupted at Cornell University on Monday, with students criticizing officials’ handling of gang-rape allegations , demanding the president’s resignation and painting “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” on an administration building.
Thousands of students and faculty gathered for a demonstration, sparked by the high-profile case of a former student known as Jane Doe, who said in a recent lawsuit that she was plied with drugs and raped at a fraternity house in 2024. The case has prompted international outrage and intense scrutiny of college fraternities and sexual violence on US campuses.
Protesters shouted , “Ban the frats” and held signs saying, “At Cornell, rapists are safer than women” and “Stop rape culture.” Some demonstrators directed their anger at Michael Kotlikoff, Cornell’s president, arguing he had failed to keep students safe and chanting , “Kotlikoff, resign!”
The demonstration took place after some students had smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall, a building that houses the president’s office, and painted messages on the facade at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported .
The messages in red paint read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED”. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The students who graffitied the building said in a statement to the student newspaper that they were protesting “the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”.
“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added. The students’ painted message was a reference to arguments that campus officials had treated pro-Palestine protesters more harshly than students accused of sexual misconduct, with four student demonstrators suspended in 2024, according to the Cornell Daily Sun.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, condemned vandalism in a statement on Monday.
“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
The student activists defended their actions in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”
The demonstrations escalated as Cornell faces widespread backlash for its handling of Jane Doe’s case, with critics saying the university had been too lenient with the accused men and had failed the victim.
According to lawyers for Jane Doe, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. Jane Doe dropped out of Cornell after the incident.
A third fraternity member, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reported on Saturday. Two more were reportedly given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university has said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.
One student protester who addressed the crowd on Monday said : “Too often, we are met with silence, we are met with statements, we are met with procedures, but not enough support. How much does it take for our university to stand with survivors?”
And a professor, according to the AP, said to applause: “Rape should not be inevitable.”
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, who is also under fire for his office’s handling of the original allegations, announced last week he was reopening the case. Van Houten said Jane Doe, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago. Jane Doe’s attorney has pushed back on those claims and accused the DA of failing to do a thorough investigation after the incident.
Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
Kotlikoff, the university president under fire, addressed the case in a video message on Saturday, saying the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Lewis County: All 11 measles cases are in one town
articles.title_zh: Lewis County: All 11 measles cases are in one town
articles.content_orig:
LOWVILLE, New York (WWNY) - All 11 confirmed measles cases in Lewis County are in one town, according to the county’s public health department.
“All of the cases that we know about are in the town of Lowville right now,” said Ashley Waite, Lewis County public health director.
Waite said there are both children and adults affected, some of whom are related to each other. All are unvaccinated, and none of the children attend public schools.
On Monday, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency over the growing number of measles cases across rural areas of New York.
Waite said the declaration will help slow the spread, as it will help health officials identify cases faster and provide more vaccines.
“When the governor declares a state of emergency, it’s opening up more resources for both the state health departments and the local health departments,” Waite said.
According to state data, there are no confirmed cases in Jefferson or St. Lawrence counties.
Health officials say the best way to prevent getting measles is to be vaccinated, which is 97% effective.
The CDC recommends everyone get two doses of the measles vaccine, first as a baby, and a second dose around the age of 4. Waite said if a child or adult is older than 4 and still needs the vaccine, it will still be effective to get it now.
“If somebody knows they’re not vaccinated, or wondering if they’re not vaccinated, they can reach out to their primary care provider. They can also reach out to us here at Lewis County Public Health and we can try to track down their immunization records, or we can offer the vaccine for them,” Waite said.
She said as long as someone is vaccinated, they should not worry.
“There’s little risk to the general public. The majority of our population is vaccinated,” Waite said.

articles.title_orig: Cornell University protests escalate with spray paint and broken glass
articles.title_zh: Cornell University protests escalate with spray paint and broken glass
articles.content_orig:
Student activists defend their actions as nonviolent, saying ‘property damage is not violent, condoning rape is’
Cornell University to take ‘serious look’ at fraternities after rape allegations
Student activists vandalized a Cornell University administration building overnight in response to the university’s handling of gang-rape allegations in a high-profile case that has dominated national news.
Students smashed a glass door at the entrance of Day Hall and painted messages on the walls at approximately 3am on Monday, the Cornell Daily Sun reported .
The messages, which read “SMASH THE PATRIARCHY” and “AT CORNELL RAPISTS ARE PROTECTED PROTESTORS ARE EXPELLED,” were written in red paint on the two walls surrounding the doors. The security camera above one of the messages was also painted over.
The actions were driven by a recent lawsuit alleging a 2024 fraternity-house gang rape and “in protest of the global systems of power that allowed this to happen in the first place”, according to a statement obtained by the student publication.
“We wanted to ensure that Day Hall, the center of Cornell’s administrative function, was not able to continue business as usual,” the statement added.
Kyle Kimball, a Cornell spokesperson, said in a statement that the concerns of the community were being heard, but condemned damaging school property.
“We understand the frustration and strong emotions being expressed across our community. Those concerns deserve to be heard, but damaging property is not the answer,” Kimball said. “We are investigating the vandalism at Day Hall and will address it in accordance with University policy and applicable law.”
The student activists defended their actions as nonviolent, in a manifesto obtained by the student publication. “We reject the dogma that would condemn our actions this morning as violent while excusing rape,” they wrote. “Property damage is not violent; condoning rape is.”
Protests led by student activist groups are expected to take place on campus today.
Meanwhile, Cornell is under immense scrutiny after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.
According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.
Two of the Chi Phi fraternity members were expelled and a third, who had already graduated, was barred from the Cornell campus, the New York Times reports . Two more were given suspensions and disciplinary probation.
Two other men, the outlet said, were ordered not to contact the sophomore, known in court papers as Jane Doe , and required to study sexual harassment, social media use and bystander intervention, and to write “reflection papers”.
The lawsuit also claimed that the seven fraternity members allegedly involved in the incident were “afforded the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by submitting essays to Cornell”.
The university said that claim does not accurately reflect what occurred. The accused men have denied all wrongdoing.
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.
Kathy Hochul , the New York governor, said on Thursday she was appointing Letitia James , the state’s attorney general, as special prosecutor to investigate the alleged gang rape at Cornell University.
Additionally, in a video message on Saturday, the Cornell University president, Michael Kotlikoff, said the school would take steps to prevent a similar situation in the ⁠future. That included “a serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”, Kotlikoff said.

articles.title_orig: Philippines Accuses PLA of Unsafe Close Encounter Over South China Sea
articles.title_zh: Philippines Accuses PLA of Unsafe Close Encounter Over South China Sea
articles.content_orig:
Published
					Oct 5, 2026 5:47 PM        		by The Maritime Executive
The Philippine military says that a Chinese fighter made an unsafe close approach to a patrol aircraft near Scarborough Shoal, a contested reef west of Luzon in the South China Sea.
According to the AFP, a Philippine C-208 light patrol aircraft was conducting a flight near Scarborough on Saturday when it was approached by two Chinese military aircraft. One of the Chinese planes, a J-16 jet fighter, approached repeatedly and moved in too close for safe operation, the AFP claimed - including maneuvers in front and in back of the Philippine plane.
The C-208 is a small, unarmed prop plane used for maritime patrols in Philippine service. The Shenyang J-16 is a fourth-generation strike fighter derived from the design of the Soviet-era Su-27.
"This incident is part of a recurring pattern of unsafe and coercive behavior against Philippine government vessels and aircraft conducting lawful operations," the AFP said in a statement. "The AFP will continue to conduct routine maritime and air patrols in the [western Philippine EEZ]."
The C-208 aircrew completed the mission and returned to base without incident, according to the AFP.
China claims the vast majority of the South China Sea as its own - including a large swathe of the Philippine EEZ - under its historically-derived "Nine Dash Line" claim and its more recent, geographically-based "Four Sha" straight-baseline theory. It seized control of Scarborough Shoal from Philippine forces in 2012 and has held it ever since. The Permanent Court of Arbitration in the Hague ruled in 2016 that these claims in the Philippine EEZ have no basis in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea; China refused to recognize the ruling and has continued to expand its presence in the region.
In accordance with China's views on sovereignty in the South China Sea, China's military and state media have an alternative account of Saturday's aircraft encounter. In China's view, PLA aircraft took action to expel a Philippine aircraft that "illegally intruded into the territorial airspace over China's [Scarborough Shoal]," 600 miles southeast of the Chinese mainland.
"[Scarborough Shoal] is China's inherent territory. The acts by the Philippine side seriously violate China’s sovereignty and are highly likely to cause unintended maritime and air incidents. We sternly warn the Philippine side to stop rights-violation and provocative acts immediately," a spokesman for China's Southern Theater Command said in a strongly-worded statement on Monday.

Video clips released by Chinese state media depicted the Philippine plane, but not the close approaches claimed by the AFP.

The naval and air forces dispatched by the PLA Southern Theater Command tracked and monitored the Philippine aircraft, and issued warnings to expel it in accordance with laws and regulations, Senior Captain Zhai Shichen, spokesperson for the #PLA Southern Theater Command (STC), said Monday. https://t.co/H3y91ihkAh

articles.title_orig: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.title_zh: Texas House Agriculture Hearing Lauds New World Screwworm Response, Warns of Mexico Spread
articles.content_orig:
Photo by Judy Gallagher via Flickr, CC BY 2.0.
A Texas House Agriculture and Livestock Committee hearing on Friday, October 2 covered a range of topics affecting the state’s agricultural industry, including New World screwworm (NWS) — celebrating the state’s success in stifling its spread and warning about a surge in cases in Mexico.
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) lists 52 cases of this flesh-eating livestock pest in the country since the first confirmation in June, 51 of which were found in Texas. One case appeared on the border between Texas and New Mexico, while one is fully within the latter state.
Based on both the USDA’s interactive NWS case dashboard and the Texas Animal Health Commission’s (TAHC) map of NWS zones, the majority of cases are located in West Texas, in counties including Val Verde, Edwards, and Crockett, while a significantly smaller portion is clustered near Roma.
While over a dozen cases occurred in July, August and September saw only four and three cases, respectively. So far in October, only one case has been confirmed — in a dog within Brewster County.
During the hearing, the committee heard testimony from various leaders in the state’s agricultural sector, who discussed a few interim charges assigned by Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows (R-Lubbock) for lawmakers to study ahead of the 90th Legislative Session.
The “invasive species” charge, which encompasses the focus on NWS while also addressing feral hogs and other parasites, reads : “Study the detection and management of invasive species and insects impacting Texas agriculture, including New World screwworm … Examine current prevention, response, and eradication efforts.”
Witnesses generally lauded Texas’ efforts alongside federal partners in preparing for the onslaught of NWS and in its response, while warning that the state is not quite out of the woods, as its neighbor Mexico continues to battle the infestation.
“Tremendous job we did in Texas getting through the summer. No question about it. It surprised the hell out of everybody,” said Thomas Lansford, representing the TAHC.
“But obviously, all hell is breaking loose in Mexico,” Lansford said.
The USDA is currently reporting 45,216 animal NWS cases through September 30 in Mexico, with 2,032 considered active cases.
Another TAHC representative, Dr. Lewis R. “Bud” Dinges, who is the Texas state veterinarian and the executive director of TAHC, similarly lauded the NWS response in Texas, saying, “None of the progress … would have been possible without the vigilance and participation of livestock producers, veterinarians, landowners, and other members of the public.”
But he added, “Our work will continue until the New World Screwworm is pushed out of Texas and back into Mexico. Until the pest is eradicated from Mexico, it will remain a risk to Texas and the United States.”
Since the first case was found in Zavala County in June, the USDA has released over 1.4 billion sterile flies as of October 1 to breed with the pests and prevent reproduction, a method that helped eliminate the NWS from the U.S. in 1966.
This method took center stage during the NWS discussion, as witnesses noted that the continued uptick in the pest’s presence in Mexico meant Texas could not yet rest easy, and that the outbreak would reduce Texas’ protection from the current sterile fly population concentrated in the Lone Star State.
Lansford continued in response to questions from Chairman Ryan Guillen (R-Rio Grande City) about the need for sterile flies to deal with outbreaks in other states: “With flies moving to the north and to the west, and Mexico … New Mexico is already in play … and then that brings Arizona and California into play.”
“If those states have cases, they’re going to take away what sterile flies we continue to disperse over our infested areas, and it's going to diminish what we have at our disposal,” he added.
The hearing concluded with general agreement among witnesses and lawmakers on the panel that while federal and local collaboration on the issue has proved successful, responders must remain vigilant as NWS spreads north and west through Mexico.
Mary Elise O'Bar is a reporter for The Texan , based in Southeast Texas. Her work has
been cited by The Hill, Newsweek, and congressional reporting. She
writes with a particular focus on social issues impacting  Texans,
and has spoken on various radio programs. She previously worked in
Washington, D.C. covering federal politics, and then in Austin
tracking the Texas Legislature. When she isn't reporting at local
events in Houston, she enjoys spending time with her husband,
reading, or exploring the great outdoors of Texas.

articles.title_orig: In a Major Boost for the Right, Another Bolsonaro Nears Brazil’s Presidency
articles.title_zh: In a Major Boost for the Right, Another Bolsonaro Nears Brazil’s Presidency
articles.content_orig:
Brazilians will decide in just under three weeks whether to reelect incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva or oust him in favor of Flávio Bolsonaro — the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro — as both advanced to a runoff after receiving the most votes in the first-round vote on Sunday.
But the results of the first round are recalibrating how investors are pricing what the final decision will be.
Speculators on prediction market platform Kalshi now give Bolsonaro a more than 80% chance of winning the presidency. Before Sunday's first-round results came in, he had about a 60% chance to win. On Polymarket , Bolsonaro's odds are now 85%, jumping from 63% before the first-round count.
While Bolsonaro was seen as a narrow favorite to win the presidency before Sunday's first round, he was widely expected to trail the incumbent Lula in that initial tally, according to polls before the Sunday vote . This was the case even as Bolsonaro was favored to win a runoff. However, Bolsonaro secured more than 47% of the votes, beating Lula's first-round total by nearly 2 percentage points.
If no candidate receives a majority of the votes in the first round of a Brazilian presidential election, the two who get the most votes advance to a runoff.
Brazilian assets were on the rise following the result.
The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) was up more than 12% on Monday. U.S.-listed shares of Itau Unibanco gained 15%, and shares of Banco Bradesco surged 19%. Brazil's local Bovespa index was up 8%.
Investors broadly saw Bolsonaro as more favorable to markets , as the candidate is promising greater fiscal discipline. In June, Brazil's deficit-to-GDP ratio was almost 10%.
Lula is running for a fourth term as president. He won back the presidency in 2022 — after a 12-year stint out of the office — when he defeated then-incumbent Jair Bolsonaro. Lula's campaign has tried to tie Flávio Bolsonaro to his father's efforts to contest his 2022 loss and brand the son as corrupt .
The runoff in Brazil will take place on Oct. 25.

articles.title_orig: macOS 27.2 reveals new clues about Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.title_zh: macOS 27.2 reveals new clues about Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro
articles.content_orig:
Apple is widely expected to release a new touchscreen MacBook Pro as soon as this month. This will mark the first-ever touchscreen Mac, and Apple is laying the groundwork in macOS 27.2 to accommodate touch gestures.
Apple released macOS 27.2 beta 3 to developers today, and it includes new references to upcoming support for touchscreen interactivity. As discovered by Aaron Perris for MacRumors , there are “gesture recognition tools” for several stock Apple apps:
macOS 27.2 beta 3 also adds a new long-press animation for the Dock, which could also be a hint at the forthcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro:
macOS 27.2 beta 3 introduces a new long-press animation for Dock icons, hinting at the upcoming touchscreen MacBook Pro pic.twitter.com/4zfZOxy8MO
Apple has gradually made a number of changes to macOS 27 in preparation for touchscreen support, including pull-to-refresh support for the first time. macOS 27 also added touch input to Sidecar, a feature that lets you use your iPad as a secondary display for your Mac.
Bloomberg has also reported on Apple’s work to optimize macOS for the impending touchscreen MacBook Pro. For instance, tapping a button or control will prompt macOS to dynamically display relevant touch options. Similarly, tapping the menu bar will automatically enlarge controls for easier touch navigation.
In addition to a touchscreen, the new MacBook Pro will reportedly have an OLED display and be “significantly lighter” than the current models.
Apple is expected to introduce the new MacBook Pro (or MacBook Ultra?) as soon as this month, though Bloomberg has cautioned it could slip to November.

articles.title_orig: Kathryn Hastie is exploring a whole new world of viruses
articles.title_zh: Kathryn Hastie is exploring a whole new world of viruses
articles.content_orig:
The new Hastie Lab is hunting for the antibodies we need in the fight against growing viral threats.
As a structural virologist at La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI), Kathryn Hastie, Ph.D. , has been one of the first to see some of the world’s tiniest proteins. Today, her office is teeming with them. She has 3D-printed models and colorful posters of the viral proteins that have defined her career so far.
“I love being able to see, basically at an atomic level, exactly what’s going on and how these proteins work,” says Hastie.
Structural virology is like enemy reconnaissance. When scientists have a clear view of a viral protein, they can guide the development of antibody therapeutics and vaccines to target and neutralize that virus. Viral structures give us the templates we need to stop infectious disease.
Hastie was recently named an LJI Research Assistant Professor. Her new lab will focus on “New World” Arenaviruses, a family of viruses that has become a growing threat in the Americas. These viruses include Junín virus, which causes a disease called Argentine hemorrhagic fever, and Machupo virus, which causes Bolivian hemorrhagic fever.
Hastie is ready for the challenge. She has spent years pushing the boundaries of what’s possible in structural virology.
Hastie devoted her early career to figuring out the structure of the Lassa virus glycoprotein. Lassa virus is a major health threat in West Africa, where it is spread by rodents. Lassa virus is a kind of hemorrhagic fever virus, which means it can cause severe flu-like symptoms, internal bleeding, and death.
Lassa virus uses its glycoprotein like a lockpick to enter and infect human cells. When Hastie started her research, scientists knew what the glycoprotein did. What they didn’t know was what it looked like or where it might be vulnerable to antibody counterattacks.
The Lassa virus glycoprotein is just unfathomably small. One glycoprotein weighs just 305.48 kilodaltons. You’d need just over 7 trillion glycoproteins to equal the weight of a grain of salt.
Hastie was determined to solve this protein structure through an imaging technique called x-ray crystallography. As she worked, the glycoprotein proved to be incredibly fragile and hard to stabilize for imaging work. “I didn’t know what the timeline would be,” says Hastie. “I just wanted to complete what I set out to do.”
It took nearly ten years, but Hastie succeeded. In 2017, she and her mentor, LJI Professor, President & CEO Erica Ollmann Saphire, Ph.D., MBA, revealed the glycoprotein structure in a groundbreaking paper for the journal Science .
“That’s this little guy right here,” says Hastie, as she points to a framed illustration in her office. The illustration shows an outline of the Lassa virus glycoprotein structure. The protein has a central hub with three spokes sticking out of it like blades on a fan.
Hastie and Saphire went on to demonstrate how human antibodies could bind to specific parts of the glycoprotein and neutralize Lassa virus infection. Their work suggests these same kinds of antibodies may be effective in future Lassa fever treatments. [Read: New Lassa fever therapy may be on the horizon ]
As Hastie starts her new lab, she’s gearing up to investigate a whole new world of viruses.
Lassa virus is just one species from the Arenavirus family. Arenaviruses are split into “Old World” and “New World” species. The most devastating Old World Arenavirus species is Lassa virus. New World Arenavirus species include Junin virus, Machupo virus, Guanarito virus, Sabiá virus and Chapare virus.
All of these spell trouble. “There are five major pathogenic species, meaning they infect humans and they cause hemorrhagic fever,” says Hastie. “Fatality rates are pretty high, 20 to 50 percent, depending on the particular virus.”
Hastie doesn’t plan to fight one viral species at a time. Several New World Arenaviruses cause disease in overlapping regions of South America, so scientists need antibody-based therapies that can work against multiple viral species at once.
Adding to the challenge: These viruses have developed pretty significant genetic differences over time. Hastie is looking for antibodies that can see past these differences and find targets that are shared between the viral relatives.
“These Arenaviruses are all really genetically diverse,” says Hastie. “One of the major challenges is finding an antibody—or a couple of antibodies—that recognize all of these diverse viruses and can stop their infection.”
Hastie is just the right person to hunt for answers. She has served as Director of LJI’s Center for Antibody Discovery for several years, where she led the development of a research pipeline to help find elusive, virus-neutralizing antibodies. LJI scientists have already used this pipeline to discover human antibodies against Ebola virus , measles virus , SARS-CoV-2 , and other viral threats.
Now Hastie is in a position to lead more independent projects—and she’s passing along what she’s learned through her challenges and successes in structural biology.
“One of my major roles in the lab is to provide support and feedback to the graduate students and post-docs. I talk to them about their projects and what went wrong, and we strategize ways to fix any problems,” says Hastie. “There’s a lot of failure in science. So you have to really love what you’re doing.”
La Jolla Institute for Immunology (LJI) was founded in 1988 as an independent, nonprofit research organization. LJI is based in San Diego, CA, and is home to world-class scientists solely focused on immunology. LJI scientists are harnessing the power of the immune system to defeat cancer, autoimmune, infectious, and neurodegenerative diseases. Our breakthroughs in immunology make life without disease possible. Visit lji.org for more information.

articles.title_orig: A Gift for World Homeless Day: PeaceHealth Deepens Its Commitment to The Way Station
articles.title_zh: A Gift for World Homeless Day: PeaceHealth Deepens Its Commitment to The Way Station
articles.content_orig:
Submitted by Unity Care NW
Almost two years ago, The Way Station Health & Hygiene Center opened with the intention of closing that gap. Showers, laundry, walk-in medical and mental health care, and respite beds for people recovering from a medical event, all in one place, aimed at interrupting the cycles that shorten lives.
This World Homeless Day , October 10, PeaceHealth is kicking off a community-wide giving campaign with a $30,000 community benefit grant in support of The Way Station Health & Hygiene program.
Rachel Lucy, community health director at PeaceHealth said, “The Way Station Health & Hygiene Center has exceeded expectations, serving many more individuals than originally estimated. Services offered at The Way Station go a long way toward restoring dignity and filling a local gap in access. We’re a proud partner.”
PeaceHealth isn’t new to The Way Station. It’s one of the four founding collaborators, alongside Unity Care NW, Opportunity Council, and Whatcom County Health and Community Services, that spent seven years planning the center before it opened in late 2024.
Their partnership shows up most directly in funding of 16 medical respite beds on-site, available for anyone discharging from PeaceHealth St. Joseph Medical Center who needs a period of rest and recuperation after a hospitalization. For someone experiencing homelessness, “respite” usually isn’t an option. There’s nowhere to rest, keep a wound clean, or follow up with a provider. These beds exist to offer a real chance to heal.
The respite program, operated by Opportunity Council with funding support from PeaceHealth, is built for a different need than the hygiene center and walk-in clinic next door. Guests recovering from a medical event get three meals a day, medication reminders, a bed, and a quiet place to rest, along with their own separate showers and laundry.
Once a guest is back on their feet, The Way Station’s Health & Hygiene Center, run by Unity Care NW, is right there: walk-in medical and mental health care, substance use disorder counseling, hot showers, laundry, and restroom access, no appointment required. “There’s not a long wait to get in,” says Mikel, lead Intake Coordinator at The Way Station. “We can do anything a primary care visit would do.” That ongoing access is what keeps a preventable infection from becoming an emergency room visit, and what keeps someone connected to care instead of falling out of it the moment they leave a respite bed.
That kind of ongoing access adds up. Anne, an Intake Coordinator at The Way Station, recently ran into a former guest while on a coffee run. He’d been unhoused for twenty or thirty years and had just moved into his own apartment. “It is so nice just standing in my kitchen,” he told her. “It’s like, oh wow, I have a kitchen now.” Anne doesn’t credit any single visit or service for that outcome. “That was all of us,” she says, “over time.”
Since opening, The Way Station has provided over 60,000 showers and connected nearly 2,000 guests to care.
PeaceHealth is starting off this campaign, but increasing the healthy years of life for people who are unhoused takes a community of people who care. A monthly gift to The Way Station Health & Hygiene Center is one of the strongest ways to be part of it. Your donation funds hot showers, clean clothes, and walk-in care for our unhoused neighbors, all year long, not just on World Homeless Day. Why give monthly?
Every gift, big or small, helps fund the same life-changing services that PeaceHealth’s grant supports: showers, laundry, and walk-in medical appointments that give people experiencing homelessness a real chance to get healthy, get stable, and get years of their life back.
Learn more about The Way Station here .

articles.title_orig: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.title_zh: Japan's prime minister calls China ‘an important neighbor’ amid tensions over Taiwan
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday called China “an important neighbor” and pledged continued dialogue with Beijing amid strained ties over her previous comments on Taiwan.
“China is an important neighbor, and our relationship has been built over many years despite existing challenges,” Takaichi said in a policy speech to parliament, according to the Japanese Prime Minister’s Office.
“We will comprehensively advance a ‘mutually beneficial relationship based on common strategic interests,’” she added.
Diplomatic relations between Japan and China have deteriorated significantly since Takaichi said in November that Tokyo could intervene if Taiwan were attacked, despite Beijing saying that the island is part of its territory.
Takaichi said Japan would clearly state its positions on issues in the East and South China seas, Chinese military activity around Japan, “coercive measures,” the safety of Japanese nationals and human rights concerns.
“We will maintain dialogue on shared challenges, protect Japan’s national interests and work toward a constructive and stable relationship,” she added.
Takaichi’s statement came a week after former Japanese Foreign Minister Takeshi Iwaya visited Beijing and met with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Vice Premier He Lifeng.
Wang urged Takaichi to “correct” her remarks on Taiwan and said bilateral relations needed to be normalized.
Relations between Japan and China have deteriorated significantly since Takaichi said in November that a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise collective self-defense.

articles.title_orig: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
articles.title_zh: France braces for national day of school protests after injuries and mass arrests
articles.content_orig:
France is braced for major protests on Tuesday, after organisers called for a nationwide day of action in support of students demanding more investment in education.
It comes after a week of demonstrations, which saw students blockading hundreds of schools, at least 190 students injured, and more than 5,000 people arrested.
One student had his hand blown off during a confrontation on Monday, while another was reportedly struck in the head by a tear gas grenade last week.
France's prime minister said the government had announced measures to address their demands, but the Union Syndicale Lycéenne (USL), a major organiser of the protests, said the government had offered "nothing concrete".
The organisation called on people to join their mobilisation on Tuesday in the face of "this political deadlock and what we describe as unprecedented repression of the movement".
Some other organisations have also shown their support for the students, with the teachers' union SNES-FSU urging its members to join Tuesday's protest.
The radical-left La France Insoumise (LFI) party leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon described the protests as the "most powerful high school and university student youth movement" since 1968 - a year of major unrest, which saw millions of workers go on strike.
The wave of demonstrations began in September in Paris and has spread across the country, with students protesting over a range of issues, including overcrowded classrooms, run-down buildings, and a lack of teachers.
The protests were started by high school students, who were later joined by university students.
On Sunday, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced a series of measures to "address the difficulties faced by secondary school students and education staff", promising "visible changes" in schools.
However, he also said: "We will make no concessions to violence. We stand by students and staff who have been assaulted, as well as police officers and gendarmes who have been injured."
The unrest has not only seen schools blockaded, but also rubbish bins set on fire. Education Minister Édouard Geffray said 24 schools had been "burned and ransacked" since the start of the protests.
Violent clashes between students and the police have led to some serious injuries throughout the course of the protests so far.
On Monday, a 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation near a school in the northern city of Lens. The student was transferred to a nearby hospital and his injury is not life-threatening, according to officials.
Last week, Eden, 14, was badly hurt in Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône after reportedly being struck on the head by a tear gas grenade.
The student suffered "a double jaw fracture" and had to undergo "extremely major surgery", according to his lawyer.
Speaking at a news conference on Monday, Eden's mother said her heart was "shattered".
"It's shameful, it's appalling, it's violent, it's horrific," French media outlet BFMTV reported her as saying.
"This should not happen. They are dealing with children who are asking for better conditions in which to study."
Among the 5,060 people arrested since the start of the movement, 87% were minors and 13% were adults, according to France's justice ministry .
Fourteen people have reportedly been placed in pre-trial detention, while 1,802 people are facing prosecution, including 319 adults and 1,483 minors.
The USL has accused police of using excessive force against the protesters. Responding to this allegation last week, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said the demonstrations had been policed in "an extremely proportionate manner".
While France's next presidential election is still months away, the protests and the response by French authorities have been heavily politicised.
The government and hard-right politicians have blamed the hard left for fuelling the protests. Lecornu said LFI was being "irresponsible" in calling for the movement to expand.
The leader of the hard-right National Rally, Marine Le Pen, has also criticised the left for its response.
"This is no longer about high school student protests. It is about riots organised by professionals and overseen by deputies from La France Insoumise," she said, calling for a new anti-rioting law to be passed.
Meanwhile Mélenchon, the LFI's party's presidential candidate, has been blaming the police for "abuses of power", calling on people to take to the streets to "protect the youth demonstrations".
The left-wing mayor of Marseille, Benoît Payan, condemned the "unacceptable violence" in his city. While young people were "legitimately concerned" about their future and public services, they must express themselves calmly, he said.

articles.title_orig: SSPI Explores US-China Space Law, Export Controls, and Cross-Border Regulatory Frameworks
articles.title_zh: SSPI Explores US-China Space Law, Export Controls, and Cross-Border Regulatory Frameworks
articles.content_orig:
On October 5, 2026, Space & Satellite Professionals International (SSPI) released Episode 5 of its Collateral Risk podcast series, examining the legal, regulatory, and policy friction impacting cross-border commercial space ventures between the United States and China.
Hosted by SSPI Executive Director Tamara Bond-Williams, the episode features a discussion with Fuhua Ni, Founding and Managing Partner of Shanghai Zenith Law Firm, focusing on navigating export controls and establishing formal industry channels between regional space ecosystems.
China’s commercial space sector has expanded rapidly following initial market liberalization policy shifts in 2014, yet its domestic legal and regulatory infrastructure remains distributed across multiple government agencies and regional jurisdictions. During the discussion, Ni detailed how international commercial law practices interface with complex space law structures, highlighting the operational constraints imposed by trade compliance regimes including the International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), Export Administration Regulations (EAR), and the Congressional Wolf Amendment.
The episode also evaluates a proposed Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) report assessing potential avenues for bilateral US–China space cooperation, alongside the challenges of managing dual-use technologies where commercial systems support national security functions.
The broadcast forms part of SSPI’s broader The Defense of Space sector campaign, launched alongside the Collateral Risk podcast series to address the strategic exposure created as military operations integrate commercial low Earth orbit (LEO) constellations. The initiative investigates legal frameworks governing satellite targeting during conflict, the extent of US commitments to defend commercial space infrastructure, and operational implications surrounding NATO’s Article 5 space declarations.
To build durable cross-border industry relationships and facilitate regulatory dialogue, Ni is currently leading the preparatory group to establish an official SSPI China chapter. The professional network aims to provide commercial space operators, legal professionals, and policy analysts with a structured forum to address emerging space governance, mediation, and arbitration protocols as commercial space assets become increasingly central to global commerce and national security architectures.
Satnews is a leading provider of satellite news, events, publications, research and other satellite industry information in both commercial and military enterprises worldwide.

articles.title_orig: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.title_zh: What impact will climate change have on malaria?
articles.content_orig:
Climate change could make a number of infectious diseases worse. I expected malaria would be one of them.
That’s concerning, given the huge global burden that it already carries: it kills almost half a million children every year.
But a more complex story emerges from the scientific literature. One where rising temperatures could actually reduce the burden of malaria in some areas, while making it worse in others.
What impact has climate change already had on malaria? Will it make the global fight against it harder or easier in the future?
These are the questions that I want to answer here.
Before we look at how climate change could change the dynamics and distribution of malaria in the future, we need a quick primer on the global burden of the disease today.
This is important because climate change could cause a decline in malaria in some regions, while increasing the prevalence in others. The impact on the overall global burden of malaria will mostly depend on what happens in the worst-affected regions today.
Malaria is an infectious disease present across much of the tropics and subtropics. In the map below, you can see the band of new infections across South America, South and Southeast Asia, and Africa.
The difference between sub-Saharan Africa and other parts of the tropics, though, is huge. Infection rates in sub-Saharan Africa are around 100 times higher than in South America and 50 times higher than in South Asia.
The fact that severe malaria is mostly an African story today is even clearer when we look at where people die from it. More than 95% of the 600,000 people who die from malaria every year live in sub-Saharan Africa. You can see this regional breakdown below. 1
But this chart also makes clear that within sub-Saharan Africa, there are substantial differences in the burden.
Around half of global deaths occur in West Africa — countries like Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Liberia. The rest are split between the central and eastern parts of the continent. Southern Africa has extremely low rates of malaria.
This dominance in West Africa is not just about population (we might expect more deaths in denser areas). As you can see in this map of death rates , those living in West Africa are at a much higher risk of dying from malaria.
These are the important background facts to make sense of this article’s focus. Most deaths from malaria occur in sub-Saharan Africa. Within the continent, West Africa is hit the worst. And children are most at risk: tragically, around 70% of malaria deaths are among children. That’s almost half a million children dying of the disease every year.
To understand the link between malaria and climate change, we need to know the basics of the disease’s “perfect conditions”.
Several mosquito species in Africa carry and spread malaria. A dominant one is Anopheles gambiae . It carries and spreads the parasite Plasmodium falciparum , which is what infects humans.
Over many decades, scientists have studied the ideal conditions for these mosquitoes to thrive. The spread of malaria peaks in these species at around 25°C. 2 Transmission drops close to zero below 16°C and above 34°C.
That means the suitability of malaria forms a bell-shaped curve like the one below. It spreads best at 25°C; this suitability drops on either side of it, and eventually becomes negligible.
Temperature is not the only thing that matters. How established malaria already is in a given country or region does, too. As do rainfall patterns: female mosquitoes lay their eggs in standing water, and larvae need water to develop. So, rainfall creates favorable conditions for malaria to spread. There is a limit, though: heavy, persistent rain often washes larvae away, preventing them from developing. An area with moderate rainfall is therefore a good breeding ground for malaria to spread.
Humidity can also have an effect. Adult Anopheles dry out in low-humidity air, so they often live longer in wetter, more humid seasons (and when they live longer, they do a better job of spreading the parasite).
The world has already warmed by around 1.4°C since pre-industrial times. 3
What impact has this already had on the prevalence of malaria?
A recent paper by Colin Carlson and colleagues, published in Nature , estimated the impact of historical climate change on the burden of malaria so far, and projected how this might affect it in the future under different warming scenarios. 4 The paper focused on the burden on children in Africa — as we established earlier, this is the most affected demographic, both in terms of cases and deaths.
They estimate that over the last century — from 1901 to 2014 — climate change has led to a small increase in the prevalence of childhood malaria across sub-Saharan Africa. By “increase”, they mean that rates were slightly higher than they would have been compared to a hypothetical scenario without climate change . The prevalence of malaria has actually declined in recent decades, but for reasons unrelated to climate.
Across the region, this increase was estimated at roughly 1 case per 1,000 children aged 2 to 10. To put this into context, around 24% of children (or 240 in every 1,000) in this region were estimated to carry the malaria parasite at the end of the study period. So, the overall impact has been relatively small and is quite uncertain. 59% of the study’s simulations showed an increase in malaria prevalence, with uncertainty ranging from a reduction of 4 cases per 1,000 to an increase of 6 cases per 1,000.
The bigger impact has been in changing the prevalence of malaria across different parts of the continent. Hotter temperatures might not have led to a large increase, on average, but they have affected its distribution.
Climate change has probably led to a decline in malaria in West Africa, but an increase in the southern and eastern parts of the continent. The following map summarizes this change: you see blue in the West but red, marking an increase, in the East and South.
Remember that West Africa is where the burden of malaria has been, and still is, the highest. A decline there due to climate change has been almost entirely offset by an increase elsewhere on the continent, which is why the effect, on aggregate, is very small.
The chart below shows malaria prevalence in two scenarios: the realistic one the world has lived through, and an alternate reality without human-driven climate change. Malaria has declined in West Africa due to climate change, but has increased in the other three subregions.
To understand why climate change has made things better in West Africa, but worse elsewhere, let’s return to our bell-shaped curve of where malaria thrives.
The study by Carlson and colleagues found results very similar to previous studies on the optimal conditions for malaria-carrying mosquitoes: transmission peaks at around 25°C.
In 1901, the average temperature in West Africa was around 26°C — very close to, but just past, the ideal temperature. 5 Climate change has increased temperatures, pushing them away from the optimum and down the slope.
What has happened elsewhere? East and Central Africa started below the optimum, at around 22°C, and Southern Africa far below, at around 17°C. Higher temperatures in all of these regions have pushed them closer to the optimum. East and Central Africa now sit at around 24°C, and Southern Africa at around 18°C.
It’s this temperature effect that has driven these diverging patterns across sub-Saharan Africa. The authors of the study did not find a discernible signal of climate change in historical drought and flood trends.
What’s crucial is that, while climate change has, on net, probably increased the burden of malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, its impact has been small compared with the many interventions and investments made to control and alleviate malaria. Malaria cases and deaths have not increased, but fallen substantially over the longer term.

articles.title_orig: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Is Awarded for Discoveries in Neuroscience
articles.title_zh: Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine Is Awarded for Discoveries in Neuroscience
articles.content_orig:
The Nobel Prize medal in Literature that was awarded in 1996 to Polish poet Wisawa Szymborska, photographed in Krakow, Poland, on January 15th, 2025.
The unveiling of the 2026 Nobel Prizes is now underway.
The Nobel committees announced the year’s first winners on Monday, awarding the prize for physiology or medicine to a trio of scientists who the committees said have “laid the foundation of a new era in neuroscience.”
The news kicks off a week of announcements for the prestigious prizes, which are awarded each October to individuals or groups for outstanding contributions across six fields: physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace, and economic sciences.
The committee will continue revealing the winner or winners of one category every weekday until the final laureate is announced. The physics award will be given on Tuesday; chemistry on Wednesday; literature on Thursday; peace on Friday; and economic sciences next Monday, Oct. 12.
Winners will receive a diploma, a medal, and 12 million Swedish kroner—the equivalent of roughly $1.2 million—during the award ceremonies in Stockholm and Oslo in December.
The peace prize, often the most closely watched of the awards, will be given to one of 287 candidates who were nominated this year, the Nobel committee said .
Last year, the honor was awarded to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado to honor her work fighting against dictatorship and promoting democracy in her country for nearly 25 years. Machado later gave her medal to President Donald Trump , who has long coveted and publicly campaigned for the prize, after the U.S. ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in a military raid in January.
Read More: Meet the 2025 Nobel Prize Winners
The committee, however, issued a statement in the wake of the gesture declaring that laureates cannot share or transfer prizes .
“The decision is final and applies for all time,” the committee wrote .
Trump has again been nominated for the peace prize this year, but is not expected to win the award amid the U.S.’s ongoing war with Iran .
Here’s what to know about the 2026 winners who have been announced.
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were awarded the Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine for their pioneering discoveries in optogenetics, a method that uses light to determine how cells operate in the brain or even to exert control over those processes.
“Optogenetics provides opportunities for mapping the brain in a way that we could once only dream of,” said Per Svenningsson, chair of the Nobel Committee for physiology or medicine.
Hegemann is a professor of biophysics at Humboldt University in Berlin. Nagel teaches plant physiology at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. And Deisseroth is a professor of behavioral sciences at Stanford University.
The laureates' use of optogenetics will allow researchers to “discover exactly which of the nerve cells in a complicated bundle control different brain functions,” such as those related to pain, social behavior, thirst and hunger, and reward and attention, the committee wrote .
Nagel said in an interview with the Nobel Institute that he was “very surprised” upon receiving the news and that he thought it was “too early to get this prize in medicine optogenetics,” given his belief that other medical discoveries have benefited a greater number of people. Hegemann said to the institute that he was “overwhelmed” upon receiving the news.
Deisseroth, who has similarly said he was “quite surprised” to receive the honor, told Stanford Medicine that he “couldn’t be happier,” noting that “the trio that the committee picked spans the progression from the early algal explorations all the way to advanced neuroscience experiments.”
“So this prize really captures the full journey of discovery,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Modern World Baltimore moving to former Wishbone Reserve
articles.title_zh: Modern World Baltimore moving to former Wishbone Reserve
articles.content_orig:
The former Wishbone Reserve/Get Shredded space in Hampden isn’t staying vacant long after the tenants moved out in September .
The operators of Modern World Baltimore, a bottle shop at 1006 W. 36 th Street that features non-alcoholic and specialty goods, snacks and gifts, announced on Instagram that their business will be moving to the former Wishbone Reserve/Get Shredded building at 3811 Falls Road in late November or early December – and it will have company.
“We will not be alone in this huge new space!” they said. “This will also house our new project, Heads Up Gallery, a home for Outsider and Weirdo art.”
Wishbone Reserve, a vintage and antiques store, opened in Mount Washington in 2015 and moved to Hampden in 2018. The operators of Modern World Baltimore said they will remain open in their current space – the former Hampden Junque emporium operated by Michal Makarovich — until the end of November.
“We are so excited for this new venture and the ability to stretch our legs a bit,” they said. “Thank you Baltimore for continuing to support us. You will not want to miss what’s coming!”

articles.title_orig: Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf
articles.title_zh: Discovery of a second-generation planet candidate accreting onto a white dwarf
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
Many white dwarfs accrete the debris of disrupted planetary bodies, detected in the form of metal enrichment in their atmospheres, dusty or gaseous circumstellar discs, and photometric transits from debris. The composition of accreted debris has been shown to be diverse yet overall closely resembles Solar System bodies. Here we report the discovery of a white dwarf accreting material that is unlike any Solar System object. The atmosphere of HS 0209+0832 is strongly enriched in trans-iron elements including zinc, copper and niobium but depleted in the canonical rock-forming elements silicon and iron. The composition of the accreted object is consistent with a candidate second-generation planet, formed from the stellar material ejected during the giant phase. The key abundance signature that differentiates it from a first-generation planet is the high enrichment of s-process elements. Photospheric helium and the absence of terrestrial rock-forming elements implies that the white dwarf is accreting from the escaped atmosphere of a photo-evaporating giant planet candidate. This is further supported by the detection of a sinusoidal photometric period of 4.399 ± 0.026 days at an amplitude of 0.120% ± 0.018%, which we attribute to thermal emission phase variability from a planetary day–night cycle or a transiting cometary tail of an evaporating gas giant. The discovery of this second-generation planet that is chemically distinct from first-generation material demonstrates that close-in planets around white dwarfs can form after the main sequence.
HS 0209+0832 is a hot, young white dwarf with an effective temperature of T eff ≈ 35,000 K, a cooling age of t cool ≈ 5 Myr and a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere with an ~1% trace of helium 1 . Such a mixed composition is unusual for a white dwarf of this temperature because helium should sink out of the atmosphere within months 2 , 3 . A far-ultraviolet (FUV) spectrum obtained in 1999 with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph (STIS) onboard the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) revealed the presence of carbon, aluminium, silicon, calcium, titanium, nickel and zinc in the atmosphere 4 , as well as ~100 lines that could not be identified. Whereas the presence of helium and metals indicates ongoing accretion, the nature of that external source remained unexplained 4 .
In the 25 years since that study was published, the origin of photospheric metals detected in many other white dwarfs has been unambiguously confirmed as planetary debris 5 , 6 . This motivated a reanalysis of the observations of HS 0209+0832 obtained with HST/STIS, the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) and the Ultraviolet and Visual Echelle Spectrograph (UVES) mounted on the Very Large Telescope (VLT), along with the broad-band photometry from Pan-STARRS and the Gaia parallax ( Methods ). In a first step, we determined T eff = 35,800 ± 500 K, a surface gravity of log g = 7.90 ± 0.02 and a helium abundance of log(He/H) = −1.90 ± 0.20 (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Extended Data Table 1 ). With these parameters fixed, we computed extensive grids of synthetic white dwarf spectra 7 using detailed lists of metal transitions in the ultraviolet (Extended Data Table 2 ). We matched most of the previously unidentified lines to transitions of copper and niobium, with the latter identified using five Nb III lines and 57 Nb IV lines (Fig. 1 ). We carefully examined archival FUSE 8 spectra of 33 known metal-enriched white dwarfs with temperatures 20,000 K < T eff < 77,000 K and confirm non-detections for niobium within that sample.
The FUSE and HST spectra (both black) of HS 0209+0832 contain many lines of C, Al, Si, Ca, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb as well as strong hydrogen and helium lines. The unusual structure of the He II line is not well reproduced by the model, which could be caused by additional absorption from circumstellar gas. We show the model fit used to obtain metal abundances in red.
We measured the photospheric abundances ( Methods ) for nine metals and calculated upper limits on 15 metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). We excluded any lines originating from the interstellar medium in our fit (Extended Data Table 4 ). At the temperature of HS 0209+0832, radiative levitation can support certain elements against gravitational diffusion. We investigated this effect for all detected elements, as well as for N, P and S for which we determined upper limits ( Methods ). We selected these volatiles because they are commonly detected in hot white dwarfs 8 , 9 ; thus, it is unusual they are not observed in HS 0209+0832. We find that, for the measured abundances, radiative levitation is negligible for Ca, S, Ti, Ni, Cu, Zn and Nb. Assuming a steady state between accretion into and diffusion out of the white dwarf atmosphere, we computed the diffusion fluxes for each element. We adopt these mass fluxes as being representative of the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832, as they correct the photospheric abundances for the differential sinking timescales of individual metals (Extended Data Table 3 ). By contrast, the abundances of C, N, Al, Si and P are subject to radiative support. These elements must still have an external origin 10 , 11 , but our analysis cannot determine their mass fractions within the accreting material.
We compare the abundances of the parent body accreting onto HS 0209+0832 to the entire sample of white dwarfs accreting rocky material 12 and to Solar System meteorites 13 , but find no compositional matches (Fig. 2 ). Whereas silicon and iron are two major components of planetary bodies in the inner Solar System, with a combined mass fraction of ~48% in the bulk Earth 14 , we detect only traces of silicon in the atmosphere of HS 0209+0832, compatible with the support provided by radiative levitation, and no iron. By contrast, the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 is rich in nickel, which shares many geochemical properties with iron, and we measure a nickel-to-iron ratio of Ni/Fe > 2.09, compared with ~0.05 within CI chondrites 15 and the bulk Earth 14 . We find that the trans-iron elements are strongly enhanced relative to calcium compared with solar abundances, particularly niobium, which is over three orders of magnitude more abundant than in the Sun.
We show the number abundances of the metals (Z) in the material accreting onto HS 0209+0832 (red stars) with respect to calcium, normalized to bulk Earth (BE) 74 (solid black line) for all detected metals and metals with strict upper limits. The error bars represent 1 σ uncertainties, and the arrows represent upper limits. The dashed red lines represent the predicted abundance from radiative levitation alone. For comparison, we include the solar abundance pattern 75 (dashed black line), comet Halley 76 (black points) and the abundances of several white dwarfs accreting bulk Earth-like 5 , core-rich 77 , mantle-rich 78 and icy 16 material (green, blue, brown and purple points, respectively).
Most enriched white dwarfs are depleted in volatile elements such as C, N and S, but a minority are volatile enriched, which can be due to accreting either icy bodies 16 or the atmosphere of a giant planet 17 . The only volatile detected in HS 0209+0832 is carbon (Extended Data Fig. 2 ), with a high photospheric abundance that is compatible with fiducial predictions from radiative levitation. However, there are both theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that our fiducial radiative levitation predictions overestimate the importance of this effect. articles.title_orig: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.title_zh: How to protect your attention in an always-on world
articles.content_orig:
Margaret Canter, Ph.D (left) and Maree Jones (right) There was a time when the internet was a briefly visited place. People logged on, did what they needed to do and logged off. That time is gone, and society’s attention now has completely shifted to the online world as digital technology has evolved.
As director of Social Media Strategy at the University of Alabama at Birmingham , Maree Jones has watched the shift happen in real time. Spending 16 years in a field that never stops, Jones has seen technology go from sitting on desks to riding in people’s pockets from the moment they wake up until they go to sleep. Drawing on her years of expertise in an always-online world, Jones provides insight on how to protect attention and focus in the workplace.
The challenge of protecting attention is a workplace concern, and it also is a critical component in mental health and emotional well-being.
Margaret Canter, Ph.D., clinical psychologist and professor of pediatrics in the UAB Marnix E. Heersink School of Medicine and Children’s of Alabama, speaks on the connection between attention and mental health, and shares her insight on attention protection and focus recovery. Canter’s work focuses on providing integrated behavioral healthcare to the pediatric clinic's patient population, which is children from birth through 18, and their families.
According to Canter, attention is a valuable resource because humans can give their attention to only one thing at a time, meaning what individuals choose to focus on and attend to must be worth it.
“When someone is able to focus and sustain their attention, they learn more and can be more efficient in completing their work or tasks,” Canter said. “If we are stressed or anxious about things getting accomplished, we may be preoccupied with those things’ getting done, which would negatively impact our attention.”
Difficulty paying attention and trouble focusing are symptoms of both anxiety and depression. If one already has difficulty paying attention, feelings of anxiety can become heightened, with mood and self-esteem being negatively impacted.
“In the age of social media, productivity isn’t just about how much work gets done. It’s also about how often we’re asked to stop what we’re doing and mentally shift to something else,” Jones said.
Likewise, if someone is already having feelings of anxiety and depression, individuals may not have the motivation to make the effort in their work, tasks and other responsibilities.
Jones says that part of what makes constant connectivity so draining is not the volume of work; it is the volume of decisions. With access to all kinds of information, the mind can be easily susceptible to burnout, and it can be hard to determine which information should be attended to. This persistent hum of pressure can be especially draining for people whose jobs depend on staying informed.
“Burnout has become an increasingly important conversation because we’re finally beginning to understand what long-term exposure to that pace feels like,” Jones said.
Smartphones allow access to all kinds of information at any time and place, including consuming the news via social media instead of traditionally. Because news segments are delivered in 30-second to three-minute intervals, sustaining attention for longer can be more difficult.
“When they’re wanting to read about a news topic or event, I encourage individuals to find one or two sources or individuals they trust and limit their exposure,” Canter said. “If we are intentional about our attention, we will not have the constant stream of information negatively affect our productivity and mood.”
In her role, Jones has the potential to be exposed to thousands of notifications a day. Each one, she says, carries a hidden cost of deciding on what and which information needs to be attended to.
For Jones, she has learned to recognize the warning signs that technology has taken the wheel. The antidote starts with treating attention as a resource worth guarding.
“By the end of the day, people who largely do digital work can feel exhausted because they’ve spent the day managing interruptions and making thousands of tiny decisions,” Jones said.
“Protecting my attention has become just as important to me as managing my calendar, because attention is what allows me to do meaningful work.”
For many people, including Jones, simply spending less time online is not an option. Being online is the job. So instead of avoidance, she recommends building boundaries around intention and learning to let technology work for her, instead of against her.
“I’ve adopted a mindset of being intentional with my time online rather than constantly immersed in it,” Jones said. “Sometimes that means giving yourself permission to mindlessly scroll but setting a timer. Sometimes it means unfollowing accounts that consistently leave you feeling anxious or discouraged.”
Some recommended ways to protect attention include the following:
When people are feeling stressed, they often seek distractions to take their minds off whatever is stressing them. While often associated with unproductivity, distractions can be a tool for attention protection and getting through a tough moment.
“Distraction is an excellent coping skill and one that I often use with children and teens in therapy,” Canter said. “Sometimes we need to get through a tough moment without doing something that would make the situation worse. However, it is important to remember that sometimes you need to come back to whatever is upsetting you and work through it, so it does not cause future problems.”
Having to respond to multiple people, whether digitally or in-person, can be taxing on the mind and attention. To balance responsiveness and attention, Canter encourages having windows of time when they are truly offline. This powerful strategy helps rebuild attention stamina and allows individuals to have higher-quality responses when coming back online.
“As a parent, I try to not have my phone with me during the time I’m helping my kids get ready for bed,” Canter said. “When I’m successful, I’m able to be more present for my kids, which feels good, and we are more efficient in completing the bedtime routine because I am not distracted by whatever it is I’m looking at or whoever I’m talking to on my phone.”
One of the biggest barriers to setting boundaries in terms of responsiveness, Jones says, is the fear of seeming unavailable.
“In workplace culture, we sometimes unintentionally equate responsiveness with value,” Jones said. “Responding quickly doesn’t always mean you’re doing your best work.”
According to Jones, the healthiest teams she has worked with communicate expectations and preferred boundaries clearly. Everyone understands what requires immediate attention and what can reasonably wait. That creates trust without requiring individuals to be constantly interrupted.
“For any communication methods, expectations should be discussed with your manager and your team,” Jones said. “Different jobs require different response times, and having those expectations clearly defined removes a lot of unnecessary stress.”
Digital fatigue is real, and much of it is fueled by the belief that instant communication should always be the norm.
“Just because technology makes instant communication possible doesn’t mean every conversation needs to happen instantly,” Jones said. “Digital work is cognitive work, and sometimes what feels like burnout may actually be decision fatigue.”
Away from work, Jones guards her attention just as carefully, keeping few apps on her phone and even fewer with permission to send notifications.
“Every notification is essentially asking, ‘Can I interrupt what you’re doing?’ Very few apps deserve that permission, especially in my free time,” Jones said. “Just because I work in social media doesn’t mean I have to live in social media.”
