articles.content_orig:
A Republican super PAC is shifting strategy.
Senate Republicansâ top super PAC is making a tactical change, pausing its ad campaign in North Carolinaâs Senate race and launching a new one in Kansas.
Senate Leadership Fund is plowing seven figures into Kansas to help incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall against Democrat Adam Hamilton. After spending more than $30 million in North Carolinaâs Senate race, the super PAC is putting further spending there on hold. A Trump-aligned group also has no further spending on the books past this week either, according to  Ad Impact.
âSLFâs job is to maintain the majority and this move reflects the most effective and efficient use of resources to do exactly that,â said a person familiar with the plans. The group also recently boosted its spending in Senate races in Ohio and Iowa.
The move to shore up Marshall and put North Carolina on the back burner reflects a shifting Senate battleground map â and Republican Michael Whatleyâs struggles in North Carolina against former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper. Another GOP group cut millions in North Carolina ad reservations last week and some Republicans have been urging their allies to concentrate on other Senate races.
In Kansas, Hamilton is running surprisingly close to Marshall, who is seeking a second term in a state where a Democrat hasnât won a Senate race in nearly a century.
The new SLF ad hits Hamilton as a âtwo-face extremistâ and is aimed at eroding his centrist credibility with voters, dinging him on his immigration record and linking him to Democrats like Kamala Harris and Hillary Clinton and calling him âtoo-extreme for Kansas.â
Senate Republicans currently hold 53 seats, including North Carolina and Kansas, and can afford to lose up to three seats to keep the majority.

articles.title_orig: AI industry insiders voice alarms to NYC council as local governments take up safety concerns
articles.title_zh: AI industry insiders voice alarms to NYC council as local governments take up safety concerns
articles.content_orig:
Former Google DeepMind researcher Alex Turner warned that "misaligned" artificial intelligence could prove more dangerous than China's aggressive development push during a New York City Council meeting on Monday.
"China is not our only potential adversary," he said. "With reasonably high chance, we are racing to build and grow our own adversary here at home, which is misaligned AI. Misaligned AI is everyone's adversary, including our own, and one day may be more powerful than China."
The comments followed a question from New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin on how to balance frontier model development in the context of the technology race with China.
Anthropic whistleblower Jacob Coxon, who raised early concerns about the dire risks of artificial intelligence , called out the industry's "extremely reckless" approach to development during the meeting.
"On the current path, I think it is more likely than not that humanity loses control to these AIs, and it could end in human extinction," he told a packed room.
Following a month of intense debate surrounding the risks posed by advanced AI models, senior leaders from Anthropic , OpenAI, Google and Meta testified under oath about the potential dangers of the technology and outlined current safety measures.
Anthropic sent Logan Graham, the head of its Frontier Red Team, to testify, while OpenAI was represented by Morgan Dwyer, the company's head of policy development and operations. Google's director of AI and emerging tech policy, Alice Friend, and Meta's AI policy director for legislation, Shane Cahill, also attended.
Menin appeared frustrated at times with the lack of direct responses to questions, including one on legal liability when AI models cause serious financial harm or even death.
"I'm going to take it then that neither of the four of you, no company here, can quantify the risk of something cataclysmic happening," she said, calling the answers "troubling at best."
Google's Friend spoke in support of a "comprehensive" federal framework to address mounting AI risks, citing national security concerns.
"As I said in my opening statement, we've long said if it's illegal without AI, it's still illegal with AI," she said.
Both Coxon and former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo warned of the dangers that the "move fast and break things" culture at the AI companies poses with such a transformative technology.
Coxon said that method works for a "photo-sharing app" but not "for building the most powerful technology ever built."
Kokotajlo called on the AI industry to increase transparency and slow the leading model development during his testimony, echoing the stark warnings raised by industry experts in recent weeks.
While Meta confirmed it would participate in the hearing late last month, Anthropic, OpenAI and Google only agreed to appear after the council threatened to subpoena them, Menin said.
Elon Musk's SpaceXAI was the only company called to testify not in attendance, even after the city issued a subpoena to SpaceX CEO Elon Musk last week, requiring that he or another representative of the company's AI unit, SpaceXAI, testify.
This is in "direct violation of the subpoena" issued by the council last week and the council plans to "pursue this matter in court," Menin said.
Top AI labs, most notably OpenAI and Anthropic, are facing heightened scrutiny over their safety and security practices after Coxon quit his job at Anthropic and set off a firestorm on social media by claiming that the company, and OpenAI , are " gambling with our lives ."
Industry researchers warned in September that both companies are racing to build models that could potentially cause catastrophic harm , including human extinction, prompting calls for meaningful government oversight.
Menin opened the meeting by singling out the federal government's light-touch approach to AI after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary accord with tech leaders in Washington last week.
"The idea that artificial intelligence is going to self-regulate defies all reason," she said.
Rogue AI fears began swirling over the summer after OpenAI disclosed that two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached the open-source developer platform Hugging Face . Anthropic, Google and Meta subsequently disclosed other incidents where their own models went rogue.
Last month, Menin called for the rare "Council Committee of the Whole" to ask companies to explain the threats posed by AI and weigh in on potential legislative solutions.
"Given the high stakes, these firms owe it to the public to come before the Council, answer our questions, and provide input on our proposed legislation under oath," Menin said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: US and German scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on light and brain
articles.title_zh: US and German scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on light and brain
articles.content_orig:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was jointly awarded on Monday to Karl Deisseroth , Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel for their work in optogenetics, a field of neuroscience that looks at the activity of individual neurons to link them to specific behaviors.
Here & Now host Robin Young spoke with Deisseroth, one of the three Nobel winners and professor of bioengineering and psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University, shortly after he learned he had won the prestigious prize.
“It was very disorienting, unexpected," Deisseroth, a Boston native, told Young. "I had I'm a bit of a night owl, but I was working late, and I had just gone to bed and was at the interface between sleep and wake. And then the call came, and so I was not sure if it was a dream or not. I'll tell you that.”
“What we figured out was how to use light to control cells in the brain.
"And so, this is different from how you normally think about light as an imaging tool to look at things. In this case, it's totally different. We're using light to make things happen, to turn cells on or off, but deep within a brain that's functioning in an animal or even a person that's moving and behaving and living.
"And this is so powerful because what we can do, the way this works is we make cells sensitive to light by introducing a gene from algae. From single-celled algae that gives rise to a light responsive ion current, a flow of charged particles, which is electricity. So basically, long story short, we can use light to create electricity in exactly the cells we give the gene to."
And maybe change the way the brain is reacting to something?
“Yes, for example. So normally, we take for granted the choices we make and the priorities we think. Of course, survival-drives like hunger and thirst will do what it takes to make them happen. If we need to nurture our young or if we need to be aggressive or defensive, we'll do the right thing.
"In reality, all these actions and priorities are set by cells, and the cells are competing with each other and deciding what to do based on the connectivity of the neural circuits. And what optogenetics has let us do is to tease that apart and say, ‘OK, here's why this action is taken, here's why this priority is rising to the top, and here's how to change it.’
"So, it's interesting to get to that level of understanding of why we do what we do."
You're also a psychiatrist, and we’re reading that your work made you very frustrated because you couldn't explain to patients why they were having their suffering. Is that part of this?
“Yes, it is very much so. So, psychiatry is probably the field of medicine that is most in need of explanatory power like that. Why is something happening? What is the biological basis for it? And this is in part not through any lack of effort or trying, but because the brain is very complicated. It's very hard to study, very fragile and intricate.
"And what optogenetics does is it gives us the tools to pierce through that intricacy. Optogenetics is fast. Optogenetics is precise, just like the brain. So, we can keep up with the brain and make things happen.
"As a psychiatrist, it's so exciting to look at this and think, ‘Oh, this is a way we can come to a deeper understanding of ourselves.”
How can the discovery be used to treat people?
“It's already been tested in human beings who are blind, and this is a disease called retinitis pigmentosa where there's loss of cells that's due to neurodegeneration.
"And optogenetics has been used to confer light sensitivity back on these people and let them see things that they couldn't see before. And that's just one of many examples.
"But once you understand the cells that matter, which is something we've lacked for so long in psychiatry. Once you understand the cells that matter, you can design any kind of treatment. You could design a medication that targets those cells grounded for the first time and knowing what matters. And that’s the real power of optogenetics as it tells you what matters."
This was edited for clarity.
Hafsa Quraishi produced and edited this interview for broadcast with Michael Scotto . Scotto adapted it for the web.
This segment aired on October 5, 2026.
Robin Young brings more than 25 years of broadcast experience to her role as host of Here & Now.

articles.title_orig: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
articles.title_zh: Trump: U.S. willing to help Russia with potential pneumonic plague outbreak
articles.content_orig:
A 28-year-old lab researcher at a Russian institute dedicated to studying plague and dangerous pathogens died of pneumonia of an “unknown” origin.
The Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute operates in Siberia, where several other people are quarantined. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that oversees infectious disease, has downplayed the link between the researcher’s death and her work, but the case has prompted questions about the type of plague that causes pneumonia.
The US State Department and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said they are monitoring the situation closely. The World Health Organization said Monday it’s in contact with Russian health authorities to verify what happened, what testing is underway and any potential international public health implications.
Dozens quarantined after researcher at Russian plague laboratory dies of ‘unknown’ infection
“Based on unofficial information available, the public health risk to the general population appears to be low,” a WHO spokesperson said, adding that its risk assessment would be updated once more information was available.
Pneumonic plague is a rare, deadly lung infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Scientists consider pneumonic plague the most dangerous form of the infection.
There are other forms of plague stemming from Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body.
The most common form, bubonic plague, often develops after a flea bite or when the bacterium enters through a cut or break in the skin. The infection triggers swollen, painful lymph nodes and can progress to septicemic plague.
Septicemic plague infects the bloodstream, potentially leading to organ failure, it can also come directly from a flea bite.
Pharyngeal plague attacks the throat after someone eats infected meat.
Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that passes directly from person to person. Respiratory particles carry it when a person coughs or sneezes. Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it.
The last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the United States dates back to 1924, during an outbreak in Los Angeles .
With pneumonic plague, particles lodge in the lungs and can trigger severe pneumonia, making breathing difficult. Symptoms can begin within 24 hours of infection.
Other symptoms include fever, chills, headache, body aches, dizziness, weakness, fatigue, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Without treatment, it is nearly always deadly.
Doctors can treat plague with at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Most commonly they use ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin, and streptomycin. Patients that get antibiotics within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving.
Doctors may also support someone with supportive care and provide supplemental oxygen, fluids and encouragement to rest.
Although plague vaccines have been in use since the 19th century, it wasn’t clear they offer protection from pneumonic plague.
The WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination , except for high-risk groups such as laboratory personnel who are constantly exposed to the risk of contamination.
Although people may be most familiar with plague from reading the Bible or historical literature — or as a metaphor to describe broader pestilence and poverty, according to infectious disease expert Dr. Tyler Evans — it persists today.
Known as the “Black Death” in the 14th century, the infection killed more than 50 million people in Europe. While antibiotics have made it more manageable, it remains present on every continent except Oceania.
Since the 1990s, most human cases have occurred in Africa, according to the WHO.
The last US death from pneumonic plague occurred in Arizona in July 2025, according to the CDC . The young man worked with sick cats and is believed to have contracted the infection from the animals. No one else exposed to the cats reported getting sick.
Evans, who wrote “ Pandemics, Poverty and Politics: Decoding the Social and Political Drivers of Pandemics from Plague to Covid-19 ,” says the risk for plague is “getting worse as the result of ecological changes and particularly with the US pulling back on our public health infrastructure and measures.”
Plague, at least, can be quick to diagnose, he said. And “the antibiotics, first and second line, are very effective for this.”
WHO has said the risk to the general population appears to be low.
People with pneumonic plague feel sick very quickly, which can slow potential spread, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center.
“It’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” Dalal said. People can develop symptoms as early as 24 hours after exposure.
There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, he said, so by the time an infected person would reach the US they would likely already be exhibiting symptoms.
“Of course, you have to be careful, and you should keep this at the back of your mind … The world is a little village now, as I say — connected to each other. But at this point in time, compared to what we have been seeing, like during the Covid pandemic, this is not of that magnitude as of now, and hopefully remains contained as it is.”
For people around patients with plague, WHO recommends avoiding direct contact with those who are sick and urges caution around infected body fluids.
Workers caring for patients with pneumonic plague must wear standard protective equipment and may also take preventive antibiotics.
In case of exposure, health officials will also monitor family members and other close contacts of an infected person and provide them with antibiotics before they become ill. They also recommend routine hand-washing with soap and water.

articles.title_orig: Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform-FL: 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards Finalist
articles.title_zh: Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform-FL: 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards Finalist
articles.content_orig:
Quebec City — Technimount EMS (Technimount), a leading provider of mounting solutions for medical devices, is proud to announce that its Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL has been selected as a finalist for the 2026 EMS World Innovation Awards.
Designed specifically for critical care air transport, the Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL transforms a LifePort AeroSled TS stretcher, typically used for adult and pediatric patients, into a neonatal transport system within seconds. The platform securely mounts the Dräger Isolette TI500 incubator while allowing care teams to quickly return the stretcher to standard patient care when neonatal transport is no longer required. By eliminating the need to dedicate a stretcher exclusively to neonatal care, this solution helps air medical teams to optimize equipment utilization while increasing operational flexibility.
At the heart of the system is Technimount’s proprietary XClamp Technology, which remains installed directly onto the stretcher without interfering with its regular use. When neonatal transport is required, the platform can be rapidly installed without tools. A dual quick-release latch system, one securing the platform to the stretcher and the other anchoring the incubator, allows for fast installation and removal. Engineered with the space constraints of aircraft environments in mind, the compact platform remains within the dimensions of the AeroSled TS while providing a secure solution for neonatal transport. The system has been rigorously tested to meet applicable sections of FAA regulations 14 CFR §§ 23 and 25.
The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL is also designed for seamless compatibility with Technimount’s Xtension Pro Assistant – LP, a previous EMS World Innovation Awards-winning solution. Together, the systems provide teams with the ability to securely manage the incubator and essential medical devices required for neonatal critical care throughout transport.
“Being selected as an EMS World Innovation Awards finalist for a tenth year is an important recognition of the work our team continues to put into solving real challenges faced by critical care transport professionals,” said Carl Bouchard, Founder and CEO of Technimount System. “The Neonatal Transport Incubator Platform – FL was developed to give air medical teams greater flexibility without compromising safety or efficiency, and we are proud to see this innovation recognized by the EMS industry.” Concluded Mr. Bouchard
Technimount EMS is a leading provider of mounting systems designed to safely secure medical devices during transport. Technimount EMS addresses the safety needs of patients and staff during ground or air emergencies and Critical Care Transport, establishing itself as a standard in the Emergency Medical Services industry.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Hits Record as Key Supplier’s Revenue Booms on AI Demand
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Hits Record as Key Supplier’s Revenue Booms on AI Demand
articles.content_orig:
There's a simple reason the Nasdaq-100 Index closed at new records Friday: The world's biggest company notched its first record since May.
Nvidia , which accounts for 13% of the Nasdaq and 8% of the S&P 500 Index ,  added 1.3% Friday, ending seven weeks of sideways trading surrounding a high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and corporate executives leading what Trump calls "super intelligence."
The rally puts the value of Jensen Huang's semiconductor business at just under $5.7 trillion, and based on the price of options trading at Nvidia, it will likely cross the $6 trillion threshold by the end of this month. It should be a comforting notion for equity bulls. Currently, there is about a 50% chance Nvidia will reach a $6 trillion valuation between now and the end of this month, and a 13% chance it happens this week, according to market-maker pricing of deltas on Nvidia options expiring this week and Oct. 30, which measure the sensitivity of options pricing relative to moves in the stock. The odds it happens between now and Dec. 18 is about 67%.
They're also implying about a 1-in-16 chance Nvidia could hit $7 trillion by Nov. 20. Based on the current share count, Nvidia would need to touch $248 to cross the milestone.
"Nvidia's buyback announcement was a bright spot," Ben Emons, managing director at Highline Asset Management, wrote in a note to clients last week. "The buyback is not just a payout but a capital-allocation event that asserts confidence in long-run AI demand."
It's important to note when using deltas to gauge a range of possibilities that the same size move in the opposite direction is also just as likely. While that's largely the case for Nvidia, some of the stock's call options are currently trading with a higher implied volatility than the equivalent puts, Barchart data shows. Such "call skew" is a sign that traders have a bias toward hedging for a rally.

You may have watched the moon block out the sun during a solar eclipse , but have you ever seen it do that to a planet? Early Tuesday (Oct. 6) morning, skywatchers across much of eastern North America will have an opportunity to watch a crescent moon pass directly in front of Jupiter. The rare alignment won't happen again for 11 years.
During the event, known as a lunar occultation, Jupiter will disappear behind the moon for up to about an hour before suddenly reappearing. The occultation will be visible before dawn from much of the eastern and central U.S., Canada and the Caribbean, while parts of Africa will experience the event during daylight, according to In-The-Sky.org .
The moon will be a beautiful waning crescent, just 20% illuminated, and Jupiter will shine brightly alongside it. The pair will rise together in the east early Tuesday morning and gradually appear to move closer as the moon travels eastward against the background stars.
When the occultation begins, Jupiter will remain hidden behind the moon for roughly an hour. No telescope will be needed to watch Jupiter disappear and reappear. However, a pair of binoculars or a small telescope will make the event much more dramatic.
Through a telescope, Jupiter will look like a tiny disc rather than a point of light and will take about a minute to disappear completely behind the moon. An easy way to photograph the event is to use a smart telescope to image the moon. (Here's everything you need to know about lunar photography ).
Below are the times when Jupiter will disappear and reappear in 10 major cities Tuesday morning, according to the International Occultation Timing Association .
Outside the occultation path, Jupiter won't disappear at all. Instead, it will appear to be skimmed by the crescent moon — still a potentially spectacular sight that could produce some amazing photos. From across much of the world, the crescent moon and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together.
Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.
The next lunar occultation of Jupiter visible from North America will occur on Nov. 27, 2037, according to When The Curves Line Up .

He is the author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners and co-author of The Eclipse Effect , and leads international stargazing and eclipse-chasing tours. His work appears regularly in Space.com, Forbes, New Scientist, BBC Sky at Night, Sky & Telescope, and other major science and astronomy publications. articles.title_orig: Trump approval at record low; Hispanic voters sour on Republicans, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
articles.title_zh: Trump approval at record low; Hispanic voters sour on Republicans, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
articles.content_orig:
A new poll from the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos has found that United States President Donald Trump’s approval rating remains at a record low as the midterm elections approach in November.
The six-day survey, completed on Monday, found that just 32 percent of US voters approve of the job Trump is doing as president.
While that low rate has held steady since September, the latest Reuters-Ipsos poll suggests his support among Latino voters is continuing to slide.
Trump’s approval rating shrunk this month to 24 percent among Hispanic voters , its lowest point in either of his two terms in office.
The Republican leader had previously made substantial inroads with that constituency.
The Pew Research Center estimated that Trump and his Democratic rival, Kamala Harris, were within three percentage points of each other in the 2024 presidential race, earning 48 percent and 51 percent of the Hispanic vote, respectively.
That rate marked a significant jump for Trump over the 2020 election, when he only earned 36 percent of the Hispanic vote.
Experts have credited the boost in Hispanic support with helping Trump win the 2024 race. His 2020 bid, by contrast, ended in defeat to Democrat Joe Biden.
The Monday poll found that Trump’s gains among Hispanics have largely evaporated.
About 52 percent plan to vote for the Democrats in the November midterms, compared to 26 percent for Republicans.
The upcoming midterm is largely viewed as a referendum on Trump’s second term and will decide whether the Republicans maintain their majorities in the US House of Representatives and the Senate.
Democrats have seized on Trump’s low approval ratings, hoping to translate frustration with the president into voter momentum for their party.
A Democratic majority in one or both houses of Congress would place substantial constraints on Trump’s agenda for the remainder of his time in office.
But Trump has also faced rumblings from within his Republican Party as the November 3 midterms approach.
One Republican incumbent, Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, released a campaign advertisement last month that addressed Trump directly, saying, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
She cited Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown as a source of tension. “Some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she said, pointing to the detention and deportation of immigrants with no criminal record.
Experts have also warned that the president’s shrinking popularity, driven in part by concerns about the cost of living and his decision to launch a war on Iran , could weigh down Republican candidates in key races across the country.
Still, Trump has continued to express confidence about the prospects of his Republican Party in the upcoming midterms.
He has also defended his decision to place himself at the centre of the Republican election campaign strategy. Trump recently launched a 32-day blitz of cross-country rallies ahead of the November 3 midterms.
“Just so you understand, they all want me to go,” Trump said, denying that some Republicans would prefer he keep his distance. “They all want me to go campaign.”

articles.title_orig: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.title_zh: Will Powerful Countries Back the UN Chief the World Needs?
articles.content_orig:
As the United Nations continues its search for a new leader , Binaifer Nowrojee, president of the nonprofit Open Society Foundations, described the kind of secretary-general that the world wants. But is it the same person that the five permanent members of the Security Council — Britain, China, France, Russia and the US — want, PassBlue asked her.
“We need a secretary-general that is bold, that is not scared to speak truth to power,” Nowrojee told PassBlue on Sept. 24, during an interview that touched on many global issues, including the race to choose the UN’s next top diplomat.
The 15-member Security Council ultimately recommends a candidate to the General Assembly for approval this year, as planned. But the process is currently going through an informal straw-poll phase to assess its candidate of choice.
The latest poll was held by the Council on Sept. 29, after three in July, August and early September, respectively, and like the others before it, the P5, as they are known, have yet to publicly show their hands on who they want to lead the 81-year-old UN. Each P5 has a veto, which can block a substantive Council decision despite majority support and thus end a candidate’s aspirations. A nominee needs to have at least nine votes from the Council and no veto to win the coveted recommendation to the Assembly.
Aglaia Balta, Greece’s permanent representative to the UN and the Council’s monthly rotating president, said on Oct. 1 that members would be consulted on using color-coded ballots in the next two straw polls, slated for midmonth and end of the month. The color ballots distinguish the P5’s votes from those of the 10 elected members, revealing whether a candidate faces opposition from a permanent member without identifying which country cast the no vote.
The candidates, now numbering seven, after Michelle Bachelet of Chile dropped out on Sept. 20, have been straddling a tightrope in their respective campaigns, avoiding statements that could put them at crossroads with the P5. Despite the balancing act, some P5 have publicly signaled reservations about candidates. Bachelet, Chile’s two-time president, announced her withdrawal after poor results in the first three informal ballots.
Opposition from Washington was a hurdle she could not surmount because of her perceived pro-abortion stance and other matters. (Relevant US officials, for starters, never met with her, according to a diplomat familiar with her campaign.) China has said it would prefer a woman secretary-general. That could complicate the bids of candidates like Rafael Grossi of Argentina, Macky Sall of Senegal and Olara Otunnu of Uganda. Grossi also faces a potential block from Russia, which has reportedly suggested it may oppose candidates with European Union or NATO citizenship.
Besides being Argentine, Grossi holds Italian citizenship. Maria Fernanda Espinosa, a candidate who is a former vice president of Ecuador and is backed by Antigua and Barbuda, has Spanish citizenship. So far, Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett have led the informal polls, but neither has emerged as an obvious consensus choice for the Council to recommend to the General Assembly. Color-coded ballots will better reveal their chances.
The interview has been edited for clarity and condensed for brevity. Some questions have been reordered for better flow.
PassBlue: Given the UN’s financial crisis, political tensions and struggles to resolve conflicts and fund development work, would a woman secretary-general step onto a glass cliff?
Binaifer: The United Nations has carried us well for the last 80-plus years, and there’s been great steps forward on a variety of issues through the UN and a rules-based world order, and people still want that. Governments still want that, but we are now at a point where the world is different. When the UN was set up, it was four or five empires that actually set it up and have presided over it. So there are inequalities and privileges that were built in that no longer fit today’s world.
Today, we don’t have a world of four or five empires. We have a world of 193 countries that sit and want a place at the table. Demographics are different. Eighty-five percent of the world’s population is now sitting in the global majority, only 15 percent in Europe and the United States. The UN has reached the end of how it can function in the way it’s functioned, and a reset is required, and that is the case for any organization.
The most important thing we need right now is a secretary-general who is visionary and bold and is ready to take this organization into the future. As the first woman to lead the Open Society Foundations, it is incredible to me that over 80 years, not a single woman has served as the UN secretary-general.
It is symbolic of the types of exclusions that have limited the abilities of the UN, even as it has espoused equality, even as it espoused human rights principles; it’s an important thing that it walks the talk internally of what it needs to do. We need a secretary-general who will lead us into the future that this next generation is going to live in.
PassBlue: What does the world need from the next secretary-general that might conflict with the P5’s priorities?
Binaifer: We need a secretary-general that is not scared to speak truth to power, that substantively can identify the key issues we need to focus on in this next century and is not scared to make some of the hard decisions that will require. We also need a secretary-general that is a bridge builder. They still have to work with member states. They still have to build coalitions around the agendas. But let’s not have a secretary- general that relinquishes the entire reform agenda and limits it only to budgets and headcounts. We have a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to press a reset button. Let’s do it properly.
PassBlue: How do you see African countries engaging in multilateral, bilateral and trilateral AI discussions and using the technology?
Binaifer: First of all, we know Africa is the youngest continent, and every one of those young people has a phone in their hand, so we know that there’s a lot of familiarity and that young Africans are leaning into technology. They’ll lean into artificial intelligence. They may not be the architects of the structure, but they will be the users, and they will innovate and find ways to have this integrated into their lives.
What we want to ensure is that the harms that we are seeing in places where children or hate speech, those kinds of things, that African governments take steps to put in a regulatory environment, because now we know those lessons. We see Australia stopping social media for children under 16. We know that women politicians, for example, get much more hate and abuse online compared to male politicians. So African governments can actually make policy decisions to limit the harms but also benefit, to have their young people benefit from the good possibilities that that technology and artificial intelligence will bring.
PassBlue: How can African countries move beyond consuming technology to creating economic benefits for young people and for their national economies?
Binaifer: There’s huge innovation in Africa on many levels. Take a place like Kenya, where technology for money transfers with M-Pesa happened long before other countries were doing it, and you find very savvy tech people in Gen Z organizing protests on social media to call on the government to do things about their issues. We also see innovation in organizations like Gearbox in Kenya or others, and the difference between the US and Africa in terms of why does innovation actually appear in the US in the tech space. Because the US government has invested in providing funds for innovation.
Innovation doesn’t just pop out of thin air, and if African governments want to engage their citizens more and engage their young people with talent, they also need to invest in them, an

articles.title_orig: Lucid's Q3 deliveries fall 6.7% as EV maker cuts production to align with demand
articles.title_zh: Lucid's Q3 deliveries fall 6.7% as EV maker cuts production to align with demand
articles.content_orig:
Lucid Group reported a 6.7% decrease in year-over-year vehicle deliveries during the third quarter, after the embattled all-electric vehicle maker cut production to better align with slower customer demand.
The U.S. automaker, which is heavily backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, on Monday said it delivered 3,806 EVs and produced 2,954 vehicles from July through September. Those results compare with deliveries of 4,078 EVs on production of 3,891 vehicles in the year-ago quarter.
Deliveries of Lucid vehicles are 3.4% higher through the third quarter than a year earlier. Production has climbed 33%, as Lucid ramped up vehicle production through early this year.
Lucid's highest quarterly production of nearly 7,900 units occurred during the fourth quarter of last year, followed by 5,500 during the first quarter of this year.
Shares of Lucid closed up less than 1% on Monday at $4.17 and were little changed in extended trading following the delivery data. The stock is off more than 60% this year.
The third quarter of this year was the first since Lucid cut production at its plant in Arizona from two shifts to one amid an "operational reset" under new CEO Silvio Napoli, who started leading the automaker in June.
The turnaround plan includes identifying $1.4 billion in cash flow improvement opportunities this year.
They include approximately $600 million to $800 million in vehicle inventory, $500 million in capital expenditures, and $200 million in operating expenses, the company said when reporting its second-quarter results in August.
Lucid said Monday it would report its third-quarter results on Nov. 9 after markets close.

articles.title_orig: Instagram Is Toying With A Read-Only Mode For Plus Subscribers
articles.title_zh: Instagram Is Toying With A Read-Only Mode For Plus Subscribers
articles.content_orig:
That’s a nicer name than ‘stalker mode.’
Instagram is internally developing a possible new feature that seems tailor-made to allow for nefarious behavior. Leaker and reverse engineer Alessando Paluzzi posted on X with the discovery of an Instagram feature billed as "read-only mode." According to the uncovered screenshots, this option allows for a session where "you can't like, comment, message, follow or view stories" on the social network, which would allow a user to browse the platform without leaving any type of paper trail about what they were viewing. It appears to be a concept for Instagram Plus accounts from the images shared.
#Instagram is working on a new perk for Instagram Plus: Read-Only Mode 👀
ℹ️ Browse a profile in read-only mode, preventing you from liking, commenting, messaging, following, or viewing stories. pic.twitter.com/eQIDjAnn1c
— Alessandro Paluzzi (@alex193a) October 3, 2026
A spokesperson from Instagram told Engadget that read-only mode "is an internal only exploration, not testing externally at all." So this feature is far from launching if it ever does, and tech platforms will regularly try out features that never see the light of day for users. But it also doesn't suggest whether there's any acknowledgement internally that this type of reduced visibility could be used for stalking or other criminal purposes. Hopefully the team can sufficiently address those safety concerns before any potential external tests or launch.

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says the world should accept some ‘bad things’ happening with AI as the industry signs on to Trump’s voluntary safety pact
articles.content_orig:
Following a controversy-filled summer in which OpenAI’s models executed more than one unauthorized hack, CEO Sam Altman said the world should accept some “bad things” happening with AI for the sake of all the good the technology will bring.
During Politico’s Decoded podcast , he was asked where his and OpenAI’s view of new AI rules differed from that of Anthropic and its CEO, Dario Amodei.
“We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency,” Altman replied.
The comments come as debate intensifies over how much regulation and what safeguards should be applied to AI while Congress has yet to pass a law dealing with the technology. Fears over the tech recently increased after an Anthropic researcher resigned last month and warned AI companies are “ gambling with our lives ” by rushing AI development toward potentially self-improving systems that could threaten humanity.
Anthropic has advocated for AI regulation, and Amodei last month called for a global slowdown in AI development to address the tech’s risks. Altman and other AI executives agreed with him on slowing down .
In August, OpenAI also backed a California law requiring AI companies to publish a public safety framework and a plan for mitigating catastrophic risks, as well as to report any loss of control of an AI model. It even asked for that law to go beyond reporting to include monitoring of AI models during their development.
OpenAI president Greg Brockman also joined other AI executives in signing an agreement at the White House last week to establish voluntary standards for the industry.
Still, that falls short of calls for tougher regulation coming from other AI leaders like Amodei, who has proposed an FAA-style regulator that could require testing and auditing of AI models or block or reverse their release if they don’t meet the bar for public safety.
In the interview with Politico, Altman said it would be impossible to avoid every bad thing that AI could be used for. The alternative would be to severely restrict access to the technology, which he said would be unacceptable.
“I wouldn’t take a trade of saying, like, we’ll make sure there’s no major hacks, there’s no kind of, like, misuse of this technology, there’s zero scams, there’s zero all the other bad things that will happen, because I think people will do tremendously, orders of magnitude, more good stuff than bad stuff,” he added.
Altman said AI companies should tread carefully, though, and draw a line when it comes to “catastrophic risks,” which have recently taken on renewed significance given recent hacks by AI models on third parties.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to Fortune ’s request for comment.
Concerns over the possibility of AI escaping human control have recently accelerated following hacks executed by OpenAI’s models on open-source AI platform Hugging Face and the Australian government . Anthropic last month also said it had discovered four incidents in which its AI models had gained unauthorized access to third-party systems during cybersecurity evaluations.
While much of the AI safety debate has centered on losing control of AI, Altman said restricting access to AI too severely in the name of safety could be harmful too.
“That also is a way that this can go horribly wrong because people are shut out of the kind of power and benefits and control and agency over the future they should have,” he added.
The CEO said AI developers should strike a middle ground instead.
“Accept bounded risks, accept risks that we understand in exchange for the benefits, and liberty, agency, all those things,” he said. “But don’t accept, like, the really catastrophic risk.”

articles.title_orig: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.title_zh: What to know about pneumonic plague after woman in Russia dies from mysterious illness
articles.content_orig:
The death of a 28-year-old woman who worked in an anti-plague laboratory in Russia is raising concerns about what caused her illness.
The woman died Friday, according to the World Health Organization, with no cause of death confirmed. A Russian official said the woman died of pneumonia of “undetermined” origin and did not link her death to her work at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East. The U.S. State Department said, however, that it’s monitoring reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague in the Irkutsk region, in southeastern Siberia, in coordination with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Key details remain unknown, including whether the woman was infected with plague at all and, if so, whether it was naturally occurring plague or bacteria studied in the lab. Scientists also don’t know how quickly her illness progressed and what treatment she received. Nearly 200 people that came into contact with the woman are under precautionary medical observation, according to Russian media.
“Maybe it’s going to come out that she died from something unrelated and it was just a coincidence” that she worked in an anti-plague lab, said Lisa Morici, a microbiologist and immunologist in the Tulane University School of Medicine.
Dr. Ashish Jha, the White House’s former Covid response coordinator, told NBC News in an interview, “If there were weapons programs, biological weapons programs in these labs, that would be much more concerning to me.”
“We need to understand that now,” he added.
The situation is still rapidly unfolding. But here’s what we know about the pneumonic plague, how it spreads and how dangerous it is.
Plague is an infection caused by Yersinia pestis bacteria. Known as the “Black Death” during the 14th century, the plague triggered several global pandemics over centuries before the discovery of antibiotics.
It presents in three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic and septicemic, according to the World Health Organization . All three are caused by Yersinia pestis, but they occur in different parts of the body.
Bubonic is the most common form, Morici said. It is primarily transmitted through bites of infected fleas or direct contact with infected rodents, which can cause painful, swollen lumps in the lymph nodes. It is usually not contagious.
Left untreated, however, it can spread to the lungs and become pneumonic plague, which can pass from person to person through respiratory droplets, Morici said.
Septicemic plague occurs when the bacteria grow and spread in the blood.
Pneumonic plague can spread through the air when an infected person or animal coughs or sneezes.
The respiratory droplets don’t travel very far, maybe three to six feet, said Dr. Dave Wagner, director of the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “They drop to the ground pretty quickly.”
It’s the rarest form of the disease, according to WHO.
Dr. William Schaffer, an infectious diseases expert at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, said close contacts are most at risk. Pneumonic plague isn’t something that spreads “distantly across a room, but to face-to-face contacts,” he said.
“It’s highly unlikely for most people to get the pneumonic form of the disease,” Morici said.
Covid, for example, spreads like wildfire through the air, traveling beyond six feet.
“It’s nothing like the Covid-19 pandemic,” she said.
While pneumonic plague is the rarest form of the disease, it’s also the deadliest.
“It’s the one that’s so frightening because it can kill so quickly,” Morici said.
It progresses remarkably fast, Wagner said. Symptoms typically appear within one to two days of exposure, and patients require treatment within 48 hours of showing symptoms to prevent fatal complications. Symptoms can include shortness of breath and coughing or blood in the phlegm.
Because of how rapidly it attacks the respiratory system, public health experts consider this strain the most likely candidate for a biological attack, according to Morici.
People with pneumonic plague are often quarantined, she said. Health care workers will often wear personal protective equipment, such as an N95 mask, or even a full body suit in case of accidental exposure.
“We’re using the strictest levels of biocontainment,” she said.
Antibiotics are highly effective against plague, including pneumonic plague.
“This is why we don’t have big plague outbreaks anymore,” Wagner said.
Schaffner said there’s no evidence to suggest that the plague bacteria are evolving in a way to become resistant to antibiotics. “We will not turn 2026 into the Middle Ages, where the Black Death caused vast amounts of death throughout Europe. That will not happen.”
Wagner said he has no reason to believe this suspected case of plague is “going to take off and spread.”
“The plague that we have today is the same plague that was the scourge of humanity for so long during great pandemics,” he said.
About seven cases of plague are reported in the U.S. each year, according to the CDC . Most occur in rural parts of the Southwest, including Arizona, California, Colorado and New Mexico. These are areas where Yersinia pestis bacteria naturally circulate among wild rodents like prairie dogs and their fleas.
Most people are treated quickly with antibiotics and recover. Deaths from the plague in the U.S. are rare but do happen.
Last July, a man in Arizona died of pneumonic plague after he was exposed to sick cats. Within a week, the man went to an emergency department with shallow breathing, a fast heart rate, chest pain and a dry cough. Despite getting antibiotics and oxygen, the man died within eight hours of his admission to the hospital. Testing later showed he had pneumonic plague .
Berkeley Lovelace Jr. is a health and medical reporter for NBC News. He covers the Food and Drug Administration, with a special focus on Covid vaccines, prescription drug pricing and health care. He previously covered the biotech and pharmaceutical industry with CNBC.
Erika Edwards is a health and medical news writer and reporter for NBC News and "TODAY."

articles.title_orig: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.title_zh: Chiang Mai conference opens to explore “Being Church in the World Today”
articles.content_orig:
A gathering of World Council of Churches (WCC) commissions and reference groups on Life, Justice and Peace opened in Chiang Mai, where ecumenical leaders will explore what “ Being Church in the World Today” means.
Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, general secretary of the World Council of Churches adressed the Joint Conference of WCC Commissions and Reference Groups on Life, Justice and Peace on the openning day of the conference in Chiang Mai, Thailand, 5 October 2026.
WCC general secretary Rev. Prof. Dr Jerry Pillay, in his opening address, offered a WCC perspective on ecclesiology, mission, witness, and hope.
“ Humanity faces wars and armed conflicts, growing inequalities, displacement and migration, ecological destruction, technological disruption, artificial intelligence, religious and political polarization, declining confidence in institutions, and profound questions concerning human dignity and the future of life itself,” he said. “ At the same time, Christianity itself is experiencing major transformations.”
The church is God's before it is ours, reflected Pillay. “ Here unity is not an ecclesial luxury,” he said. “ It is related directly to Christian witness.”
He further noted that a divided church struggles to proclaim a reconciled Christ. “ This is particularly important for the ecumenical movement,” he said. “ The WCC ’ s understanding of unity cannot be reduced to organizational uniformity.”
Dr Prawate Khid-arn, assistant general secretary for ecumenical relations of the Church of Christ in Thailand, prayed that the meeting will renew people ’ s hearts, deepen their commitment, and give them fresh energy and courage for the journey ahead.
“ May our discussions lead not only to words and recommendations, but also to meaningful actions that bring hope to those who suffer, restore human dignity, strengthen justice, care for God's creation, and contribute to genuine and lasting peace,” said Khid-arn. “ May the Holy Spirit guide your conversations, inspire your discernment, and strengthen our common witness.”
Rev. Grace Moon, general secretary of Christian Conference of Asia, noted the context of the meeting in Asia—a region full of spiritual richness, cultural diversity, and resilience, yet also a place where many still face challenges like inequality, displacement, violence, discrimination, and climate change.
“ Our Christian faith means we cannot ignore suffering or injustice—we are called to stand with those who are hurting, excluded, or silenced,” said Moon. “ We cannot solve these problems alone.”
Moon further noted that climate injustice, conflict, and discrimination are all connected. “ Our calling goes beyond charity—it is about working together for justice, healing, and the well-being of all people and creation,” said Moon.
The conference marks the second time that WCC commissions related to the Life, Justice, and Peace programme are meeting - the first such gathering was held in Geneva in 2024.
The first day of the conference currently underway began with pilgrimage encounters, giving participants an opportunity to meet local communities and organizations in and around Chiang Mai working on issues including clean air, migration, HIV and health justice, and interfaith dialogue.

articles.title_orig: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.title_zh: Middle East oil exports surpass pre-war levels despite tensions, data shows
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil exports from the Middle East have risen above pre-war levels on four of the seven days in the last week of September, provisional data from ship-tracking firm Kpler showed.
However, senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) commander Ali Fadavi said in a televised interview on Sunday night that only three to four million barrels of oil per day (bpd) are now moving through the route, dismissing the amount as “negligible” when compared with pre-war traffic.
Fadavi said, for the first time, no US vessels were present in the Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, the Sea of Oman or even the northern Indian Ocean and US warships are “100 percent vulnerable” to IRGC attacks.
Kpler data showed crude exports from the region exceeded pre-war levels on September 24 and between September 27 and 29, rising to 19.5-22.5 million bpd.
Around that time, Iran claimed success in attacking ships – including US Navy vessels – near the Strait of Hormuz, saying the strikes had forced Washington to move its warships further from the Iranian coast.
Before the US-Israel war on Iran began, exports averaged 18 million bpd between March 2025 and February 2026.
According to Kpler data, the overall tally for crude, oil products, chemicals and non-gas liquids averaged 22.4 million bpd in the seven days to September 30.
On October 1, the seven-day moving average for crude exports was at 18.5 million bpd. This includes transits via the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, exports from terminals and ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman.
The number of liquefied natural gas cargoes exiting the Strait of Hormuz also rose in September to its highest monthly level since February.
The figures exclude any vessels that might have crossed the strait with their automatic identification system transponders turned off to avoid detection.
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or in the Gulf of Aden since October 2.
On Sunday, Iran’s top negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States accepts Tehran’s seven-day plan to reopen the waterway.

articles.title_orig: Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27
articles.title_zh: Command-line tool quickly removes Apple Intelligence from macOS 27
articles.content_orig:
A new tool is allowing Mac users the ability again to easily turn off Apple Intelligence with one click and free up to 12GB of storage.
Unlike with previous versions of macOS, macOS 27 Golden Gate doesn’t have a toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. That makes disabling AI features that you may not want more difficult. It also means that the AI models necessary for running Apple Intelligence will take up space on your disk , even if you don’t use them or if you go through your settings to individually find and disable AI capabilities.
In response, a developer known as Om Lahore on GitHub last week created RemoveMacAI, a command-line tool that allows macOS 27 users to “turn off Apple Intelligence on macOS 27″ in a way that is “fully reversible,” per the GitHub page . They said that Apple’s Intelligence models take up “about 12GB,” but the models can actually take up over 30GB, The Verge noted.
RemoveMacAI “turns off Siri, Writing Tools, Genmoji, Image Playground, the ChatGPT extension, and all the summaries, then it deletes the models and stops macOS from downloading them again. Dictation still works because it’s a separate setting,” the developer said in a Reddit post first spotted by MacRumors .
On Reddit, RemoveMacAI’s developer said the tool is open source and further explained how it works:
It uses a configuration profile you approve in System Settings plus Apple’s own asset service, so [ System Integrity Protection ] stays on and nothing in /System gets touched directly. removemacai revert removes the profile, and macOS downloads the models again when you turn a feature back on.
The dev also said you can remove only the Apple Intelligence features you don’t want and keep the others.
Some users on Reddit have reported that the tool works, and it has 1,700 stars on GitHub as of this writing.
Interest in RemoveMacAI demonstrates the aversion that some users have to some or all of Apple Intelligence’s features, despite growing focus from Apple on AI-driven device and software upgrades in its computers and other devices .
“Reminds me of all the de-crufting you’ve always needed to do when you install Windows. Looks like we’ve gotten to the point on macOS too, where you need to run third-party scripts on a new OS installation to gain back control of your system resources and remove unwanted crapware,” a Hacker News user wrote in response to RemoveMacAI.
Although many users are happy to leverage Apple Intelligence in their gadgets, RemoveMacAI is a simple way for the rest to regain control over Apple Intelligence’s presence on their computers that Apple previously offered.

articles.title_orig: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.title_zh: World Mission Sunday 2026 | October 18
articles.content_orig:
About / Offices / Vocations
About / Offices / Vocations
Posted on October 5, 2026 in News
Dear Brothers and Sisters in Christ,
On October 18, we celebrate World Mission Sunday, a powerful reminder of our shared responsibility to proclaim the Gospel to all nations. It is a day when Catholics around the world unite in prayer and solidarity to support the missionary work of the Church.
We are all called to be a part of this mission work. In his last words before ascending to heaven, Jesus told us, “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (Mt 28:19), and for 2,000 years the Church has been at work in this task. And we are far from finished! Two-thirds of the people alive — 5.5 out of 8.1 billion — still have no relationship with Christ or his Church. Bringing people to Jesus is the work of the Church, and all of us together have a part to play. Today, we have a singular means to do so: World Mission Sunday.
The second collection we take up on World Mission Sunday helps extend the Church’s missionary work to places where the Church barely exists, where the Gospel has never been heard before, and where the Church is too young, too persecuted, or too poor to sustain herself.
On World Mission Sunday, we stand in solidarity with the missionaries, priests, religious sisters and brothers, and lay leaders serving in the 1,130 mission dioceses — spanning Asia, Africa, Latin America, Oceania, and the Middle East — that depend on our prayers and financial support to continue proclaiming Christ and building His Church.
The year’s World Mission Sunday celebration is unlike any other in our lifetime for two reasons.
First, this World Mission Sunday marks the 100th anniversary of its establishment by Pope Pius XI in 1926. This centenary is an opportunity to mark it with renewed missionary zeal. This year’s theme, “One in Christ, United in Mission,” chosen by Pope Leo XIV, invites us to rediscover the profound unity we share in Christ through baptism and how our baptismal identity overflows into the mission to bring others into communion with God and us.
Secondly, the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen on September 24 reminds us of the importance of the missions. While many know him best for his TV presence, books, and charismatic eloquence, he repeatedly said, “My greatest love has always been for the missions of the Church.” For 16 years, as National Director of The Pontifical Mission Societies in the United States, he poured his talents into World Mission Sunday and distributed the proceeds diligently to the missions. We can surely count on his intercession for World Mission Sunday 2026.
Pope Leo XIV recognizes how important World Mission Sunday is for the Church. He spent a large part of his priestly ministry as a missionary in Peru, serving communities in the Andean highlands and rural villages, and has noted how dependent he was on the support of the Church universal through World Mission Sunday.
Last year, he became the first pope in history to record a short video that could be played before Mass, in which he appealed, “Please help me help missionaries everywhere.” That’s what World Mission Sunday does: to help Pope Leo care for the 1,130 missionary dioceses and territories under his supervision through the Dicastery for Evangelization.
Please respond to his appeal as generously as you can. Visit pontificalmissions.org/wms-2026 for full details.
I am praying that World Mission Sunday will be a blessing for our diocese and help foster increased zeal for the missions within all of us. Let us pray together that the Holy Spirit will renew in us the fire of the early Church, that we might truly be One in Christ, United in Mission, and that we will grow in missionary awareness, solidarity, and responsibility.
In Hope, united in Christ’s mission,
Most Rev. James V. Johnston, Jr. Bishop of Kansas City-St. Joseph

articles.title_orig: Hofstadter’s butterfly turns 50: a fractal hiding in quantum matter
articles.title_zh: Hofstadter’s butterfly turns 50: a fractal hiding in quantum matter
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Indu Satija celebrates the 50th anniversary of the publication of Douglas Hofstadter’s eponymous, iconic butterfly and explains its enduring, magnetic appeal
In the mid-1970s a graduate student wrestling with a deceptively simple quantum problem uncovered one of the most haunting images in modern physics. The pattern seemed almost impossibly intricate: delicate wings assembled from infinitely nested bands and gaps, a self-similar pattern born from the motion of electrons in a crystal under a magnetic field. First published in 1976 ( Phys. Rev. B 14 2239 ), it came to be known as Hofstadter’s butterfly, after its discoverer Douglas Hofstadter .
Half a century later, the butterfly has not faded into scientific nostalgia. If anything, it has become even more important – reappearing in new materials, new experiments and in places no-one imagined when it was first plotted. Recent research by Kazuki Ikeda from the University of Massachusetts and Yaron Oz at Stony Brook University suggests that related patterns may even surface in the physics of black holes ( J. High Energy Phys. 2026 38 ).
Each new realization adds another chapter to a story that is not really about a single graph, or even a single discovery, but about the unity of patterns across the physical world. A structure first seen in a simple model has become a symbol of how richness can emerge from basic rules, how beauty can arise from constraint, and how the quantum world still harbours forms strange enough to surprise us.
What makes Hofstadter’s butterfly so compelling is the remarkable story of its birth and, more importantly, how far it has travelled from its original birthplace. Like many scientific breakthroughs, its discovery was fairly obscure initially and owed a great deal to luck. In 1974 Hofstadter – son of the 1961 Nobel-prize-winning nuclear physicist Robert Hofstadter – had just dropped out of graduate school at Stanford University in the US and was “in despair” according to friend and physicist Francisco Claro .
Having just completed a PhD with the renowned solid-state physicist Gregory Wannier at the University of Oregon, Claro suggested that Hofstadter should approach Wannier as well. As it happened, Wannier had been struggling with a problem that had puzzled him for years: he could not obtain an analytical solution to Harper’s equation , which describes the motion of electrons on a 2D crystal lattice subjected to a perpendicular magnetic field.
Named after P G Harper , who was a graduate student of Rudolf Peierls at the University of Birmingham, UK, this classic “magnetic problem” displayed a mysterious sensitivity to whether the magnetic flux was a rational or irrational number. It was a feature that immediately captured Hofstadter’s imagination and, with the rational–irrational dichotomy echoing in his mind, Hofstadter began his PhD studies at Oregon by immersing himself in solving the problem.
But he soon found himself equally stuck. Frustrated by the analytical approaches often discussed at the time, he pursued a different path: numerical computation. Using a programmable Hewlett Packard desktop calculator that by today’s standards looks laughably primitive, he displayed the numerical solutions graphically as the energy of electrons versus magnetic flux Φ per unit cell of the lattice. At that moment, he became convinced that he had uncovered the true structure of the problem. “All at once my eyes were opened,” Hofstadter recalls.
What he found was a complex recursive shape (or fractal in today’s terminology) hidden within the energy spectrum of electrons in a magnetic field. Resembling a butterfly, Hofstadter brought his hand-plotted diagram, which he codenamed “Gplot”, to Wannier, who was not impressed. According to Hofstadter, Wannier dismissed the result as “numerology” and even threatened to withdraw the PhD student’s funding.
But after nearly a year, Wannier came to recognize the validity and significance of Hofstadter’s work, ultimately awarding Hofstadter his PhD and accepting the butterfly as a legitimate description of the energy spectrum of electrons moving on a 2D lattice in a magnetic field. Wannier even added to the butterfly’s story with a paper titled “A result not dependent on rationality for Bloch electrons in a magnetic field ( Phys. Status Solidi b 88 757 ). This work, along with further studies with Claro, introduced a set of integers uniquely labelling every gap in the graph, providing a simplified description of the spectrum ( Phys. Rev. B 19 6068 ).
Ruby celebration Douglas Hofstadter (right) pictured in 2016 with colleagues Indu Satija (centre) and Francisco Claro (left) all wearing T-shirts emblazoned with Hofstadter’s butterfly to celebrate its 40th anniversary. (Courtesy: Indu Satija)
Born in 1945, Douglas Hofstadter discovered his eponymous butterfly while a PhD student at the University of Oregon in 1975, using computational modelling to make his breakthrough (see main text). Four years later Hofstadter published his Pulitzer-prize-winning popular-science book Gödel, Escher, Bach , which tackles cognition, mathematics and symmetry.
Currently a professor of cognitive science and comparative literature at Indiana University in Bloomington, US, Hofstadter is still active as a researcher and wrote a follow-up book I Am a Strange Loop in 2007. On the golden jubilee of the now-famous butterfly named after him, Hofstadter provided the following comment to Physics World .
“This graph was first computed using a programmable desktop calculator and was first plotted by hand using coloured felt-tip pens. I was just extremely relieved that by showing that my ‘Gplot’ graph was made of distorted copies of itself, I would at last be able to get a PhD thesis. I had no idea that Gplot would go on to become well known as the Hofstadter butterfly, and that variations on the theme would proliferate like wildfire over the coming decades.”
“As the years have gone by,” he continues, “articles about Hofstadter’s butterfly have grown more and more numerous and harder and harder for me to follow. For better or for worse, these theories are all way beyond me, but remembering the first wingbeats of the butterfly’s flight cheers me up.”
Hofstadter’s butterfly is more than a beautiful graph. It is a map of what happens when quantum particles are caught between two competing kinds of order: the regular periodicity of a crystal lattice and the circular orbits of a magnetic field. When these two scales contend with one another, the energy spectrum does something extraordinary. Instead of varying smoothly, it fragments into a hierarchy of allowed and forbidden energies, referred to as bands and gaps, respectively.
Zoom in on one region and new structures emerge. Zoom in again and the pattern repeats, endlessly varied yet ruled by strict mathematical order. It is one of the rare instances in which fractal geometry appears not only in abstract mathematics or artistic imagination, but in the measurable behaviour of matter itself.
The deep connection between this theoretical pattern and real-world matter became clear through an exotic quantum phenomenon known as the integer quantum Hall effect . It was discovered experimentally by Klaus von Klitzing at the Max Planck Institute for Solid-State Physics in 1980 – a breakthrough that earned him the Nobel Prize in Physics five years later.
The classical Hall effect is what happens when a voltage is produced in a bulk conductor at right angles to an applied magnetic field. Similarly, the quantum Hall effect is the appearance of a voltage across opposite faces of a thin 2D semiconductor when a current is passed along the plane of the material and a magnetic field applied perpendicularly it. But there is one big difference in the quantum version.

articles.title_orig: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
articles.title_zh: Flydubai co-pilot originally planned attack for July, investigators believe
articles.content_orig:
Police and security agencies in multiple countries scramble to piece together background and intentions of Hamam al-Hammami
Investigators believe the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.
The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe.
Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.
Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.
Israeli media have quoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near ⁠Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar , said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.
In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”
Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia , where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.
The investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are examining reports that the co-pilot studied in both nations about 10 years ago.
Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, but left the airline after being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.
Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.
A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.
Netanyahu has claimed Hammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.
Nine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.
An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.
“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.
“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, a co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.
Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.
Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.
The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.
Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.
“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”
